Name: compositional_subliminal_geometry
Title: Do Subliminal Traits Add Up? Compositional Geometry of Hidden Trait Transmission and a Steering-Vector Defense
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning is mediated by teacher-specific activation steering vectors; therefore multiple traits transmitted through the same number/code data should combine according to the vector-space geometry of their steering directions (superposing when parallel, transmitting independently when orthogonal, canceling when anti-parallel). This compositional structure predicts a cheap, model-agnostic defense: blending outputs from teachers whose steering vectors span a spread of directions collapses the net transmitted vector, suppressing all hidden traits while preserving overt task quality.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025/Nature 2026) introduced subliminal learning for single traits and showed it requires matched base models. Blank et al. (2026) showed single-trait transmission is well-approximated by a single steering vector (steering-vector distillation). The 'divergence tokens' paper (2025) found early layers are critical and empirically noted that mixing multiple same-bias teachers weakens transmission, but gave no geometric explanation and studied only same-direction mixing. LLS (2026) selects data subsets to elicit single hidden effects via log-linearity. Persona Vectors (2025) monitor/steer single traits at deployment. No prior work studies (a) whether multiple *distinct* traits transmit simultaneously through the same numeric data, (b) how transmitted traits compose as a function of the geometry (angle) between their steering vectors, or (c) whether this geometry yields a principled, deployable defense. We turn the steering-vector hypothesis into a quantitative compositional theory and an actionable orthogonal-blending defense, distinguishing our work from all single-trait, mechanism-only prior studies.
Abstract: Subliminal learning—the transmission of behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls, or misalignment) through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences—poses an unexpected safety risk for model distillation. Recent work suggests this transmission is mediated by a single teacher-specific steering vector added to the student's activations. We take this account seriously and ask a simple new question: if traits are vectors, do they compose like vectors? We test whether multiple distinct traits can be transmitted simultaneously through the same numeric data, and whether the transmitted behavior is predicted by the geometry (cosine similarity) of the underlying steering directions. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5, Llama-3.2) and LoRA fine-tuning affordable in an academic lab, we construct teachers carrying pairs and triples of traits (animal/tree/color preferences plus safety-relevant traits), generate filtered number and code datasets, and measure trait transmission to students. We predict and test three regimes: parallel steering vectors superpose (amplified transmission), orthogonal vectors transmit independently (both traits appear), and anti-parallel vectors cancel (neither transmits). We further validate that measured transmission strength scales with the dot product between each trait's steering vector and the fine-tuning activation-gradient direction. Building on the cancellation regime, we introduce Orthogonal Data Blending, a defense that mixes outputs from teachers whose steering vectors span diverse directions, collapsing the net transmitted vector. We evaluate transmission rates, overt task quality (MMLU, code pass@1), and defense robustness, offering both a predictive geometric theory and a practical mitigation for distillation supply chains.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - steering-vector mediation of single-trait transmission): Show each trait's subliminal transmission is carried by a teacher-specific early-layer activation direction. Models: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B (open weights; backbone frozen, only LoRA adapters rank 16 / alpha 32 / dropout 0.05 trainable; AdamW, lr 2e-4, 3 epochs, effective batch 32; 3 seeds). Data (built from scratch): for each of four traits (owl-vs-eagle preference, oak-vs-pine preference, mild misalignment, sycophancy) the teacher = base model + a trait-inducing system prompt generates number-continuation samples (prompt: extend a random 3-8 element integer list); of ~30k generated per trait we keep the ~15-20k passing a strict filter that drops any sample containing trait-referential tokens (audited by exact-match plus embedding similarity), and use exactly 15k per trait to equalize size. Steering vector v_t = mean residual-stream activation difference (trait-prompted minus base) at the early layer with peak trait-probe accuracy (layer chosen on a 1k held-out probe set), over 500 neutral prompts. Decisive metric first: transmission score = trait-elicitation rate on 150 held-out probe prompts minus the no-trait-teacher control (percentage points, pp); secondary: cosine between v_t and the empirical early-layer activation shift induced by fine-tuning. Convincing: transmission >= 10 pp above control AND cosine >= 0.30 for >=3 of 4 traits. Undecided band: transmission in [3,10) pp OR cosine in [0.15,0.30) - within cross-seed noise (~+-3 pp), so mediation is not established and Experiments 2-3 are not yet interpretable; we would strengthen installation (more data/steps) before proceeding. Negative (transmission <3 pp or cosine <0.15): the steering-vector account fails for these traits and the compositional theory does not apply.

Experiment 2 (H2 - compositional geometry of multi-trait transmission): Test whether traits combine per the vector-space geometry of their steering directions. Using the v_t from Experiment 1, form all pairwise combinations of the four traits and bin them by cosine(v_a,v_b) into parallel (>0.5), orthogonal (|cos|<0.2), anti-parallel (<-0.5). Build two-trait teachers via combined system prompts, generate and filter 15k number samples each (same protocol/models/hyperparameters), fine-tune students, and measure each trait's transmission score independently. Decisive metric first: per-trait transmission in the two-trait condition minus its single-trait value (delta_pp), regressed on inter-trait cosine (report slope, R^2, 95% CI). Convincing: monotone negative slope with R^2 >= 0.4 - parallel pairs amplify (delta > +3 pp), orthogonal pairs unchanged (|delta| <= 3 pp), anti-parallel pairs suppress (delta < -3 pp). Undecided band: R^2 in [0.2,0.4) or category means separated by <3 pp - geometry is suggestive but not confirmed; report as inconclusive rather than support. Negative (flat/no monotone relation, R^2 <0.2): transmission is not governed by steering-vector geometry, refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Orthogonal Data Blending defense): Test whether blending teachers whose vectors span a wide angular spread collapses the net transmitted vector. Fix one target unsafe trait (misalignment). Assemble training data from N teachers (N in {2,4,8}) chosen so their v_t are maximally angularly spread (net resultant magnitude minimized), 15k filtered samples total, same student/hyperparameters. Compare against the single-teacher misalignment baseline from Experiment 1. Decisive metric first: residual transmission score of the target trait (pp); secondary (utility): MMLU accuracy and HumanEval pass@1 versus clean distillation. Convincing: residual transmission reduced by >=50% relative to single-teacher baseline at N=8 AND utility within 2 points of clean distillation. Undecided band: 20-50% reduction, or utility drop 2-5 points - a partial/again costly defense, reported as such. Negative (<20% reduction or utility drop >5 points): blending does not provide a usable defense. Control: cross-family students (mismatched base) show ~0 transmission in all conditions, confirming the effect is base-gated rather than content-driven.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The steering-vector approximation may hold only for prompt-representable traits; traits not well-approximated by a single vector (as Blank et al. note) may not follow clean compositional rules, weakening the theory's scope. 2) Interference between LoRA updates for different traits could be nonlinear, muddying the parallel/orthogonal/anti-parallel prediction; we mitigate by testing several trait pairs and reporting the geometric regression rather than only categorical bins. 3) Multi-trait teachers might degrade generation quality, confounding transmission measurements; controlled by matching data quality and using held-out probes. 4) The Orthogonal Data Blending defense could reduce overt distillation utility if traits are entangled with useful behavior; we quantify the utility-safety tradeoff explicitly. 5) Effects may be sensitive to which layer/vector is used for extraction; we test multiple layers. 6) Findings may be model-family specific, limiting generality, though we test two families.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that need to be novel are: (1) multiple distinct subliminal traits can be transmitted simultaneously through the same semantically unrelated numeric/code data; (2) the strength and interaction of transmitted traits are quantitatively predicted by steering-vector geometry, with parallel traits amplifying, orthogonal traits coexisting independently, and anti-parallel traits canceling; (3) transmission strength scales with alignment between a trait steering vector and the fine-tuning-induced activation shift; and (4) this geometry can be exploited for a defense via orthogonal teacher-data blending. Relative to the cited prior work and the search summary, the closest family is single-trait subliminal learning explained as steering-vector distillation. That literature already makes the broad linear-mechanistic story plausible, so the proposal's main delta is not the existence of vectors per se but multi-trait compositionality plus a practical defense. That delta appears genuinely unstudied and non-trivial, especially because prior mechanistic work is limited to single traits and same-direction mixing. The main novelty risk is that some of the geometric prediction may be viewed as a fairly direct consequence of the steering-vector account, so the strongest novelty really lives in the empirical finding that compositional regression works and that cancellation enables a deployable defense.

Add a sharper contrast table versus Cloud et al., Blank et al., divergence-token mixing, and any multi-teacher distillation baselines: single vs multi-trait, same- vs cross-direction, explanation vs quantitative prediction, attack vs defense.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is hidden transmission of behavioral traits during distillation from ostensibly harmless data. The audience is mainly AI safety, model-distillation, and supply-chain security researchers, plus practitioners who train student models from third-party teachers or synthetic corpora. The strongest case for importance is: if subliminal trait transmission is compositional and can be canceled by teacher blending, then one gets a cheap, model-agnostic mitigation for a real supply-chain risk. This is a meaningful problem rather than a curiosity, and even a simple geometric result would likely be cited because it sharpens the mechanism and suggests defenses. The work could shift how people audit synthetic-data pipelines and reason about hidden behavior transfer. That said, the practical reach depends heavily on whether subliminal learning itself is common enough outside controlled matched-model settings and whether the proposed defense works without hurting utility. So the impact is strong within a focused safety/distillation community, but not yet obviously broad across all of ML.

review.reasoning: The proposal is unusually concrete and falsifiable for an early-stage ML idea: hypotheses are scoped, metrics are predefined, thresholds are given, and the experiments are feasible on open models with LoRA. The related work is specific enough to identify the nearest baseline. However, there are several technical and narrative weaknesses. First, the mechanism is underspecified at key points: a 'trait-inducing system prompt' is doing a lot of work, but the exact procedure for constructing multi-trait teachers and ensuring trait separability is unclear. Second, the geometry test may be underpowered because there are only four traits, yielding few pairwise bins and weak regression support; this is especially problematic if steering-vector estimates are noisy. Third, anti-parallel trait pairs may be hard to realize naturally with the proposed trait set, making the cancellation regime potentially engineered or absent. Fourth, the central causal claim risks confounding because student transmission could correlate with generation artifacts, teacher quality, or probe design rather than vector geometry. Fifth, the defense experiment is not yet a fair practical test: choosing teachers by known steering vectors assumes audit access that a defender may not have, and the comparison baseline should include random mixing and quality-matched mixing. Overall, the work could be submission-worthy if executed well, but only if controls and scope are tightened substantially.

Name: subliminal_immune_checkpoints
Title: Vaccinating Students Against Subliminal Learning: Divergence-Token Regularization as a Training-Time Immunization
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning is carried by a small set of rare divergence tokens whose gradient signal is behaviorally matched to the teacher's base model. If we could make the student temporarily 'blind' to the specific low-probability perturbations that carry hidden traits—by adding a lightweight consistency regularizer that penalizes gradient updates aligned with the student's own high-confidence next-token predictions on the same tokens—we can suppress trait transmission while preserving the useful task signal, without needing to identify or filter any trait a priori.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (Nature 2026) introduced subliminal learning and showed it requires behaviorally matched base models but proposed no training-time defense beyond (ineffective) data filtering. The 'Divergence Tokens' paper (2025) localized transmission to a small set of rare divergence tokens and early layers, and found masking these tokens suppresses transmission and that paraphrasing is fragile-but their masking requires *knowing* which tokens diverge (i.e., access to a contrasting teacher), which is unavailable in a realistic single-teacher distillation supply chain. LLS (2026) selects data to *elicit* effects via log-linearity, the opposite goal. Persona/steering-vector defenses operate at deployment, not training. Our contribution is a *trait-agnostic, single-teacher training-time defense*: instead of identifying divergence tokens by comparing teachers, we exploit the observation that divergence tokens are precisely the low-teacher-probability, high-surprise tokens whose gradients disproportionately reshape early layers. We introduce a self-supervised regularizer that requires no knowledge of the target trait, no second teacher, and no data filtering-distinguishing it fundamentally from all prior defenses which are either post-hoc, trait-specific, or require contrastive teacher access.
Abstract: Model distillation can silently propagate unintended behavioral traits—a phenomenon termed subliminal learning—even when training data is filtered to remove all references to the trait. Recent mechanistic work shows this transmission is carried by a small set of rare 'divergence tokens' and disproportionately reshapes early layers. Existing defenses either require access to a contrasting teacher to identify divergence tokens, target a known trait, or operate only at deployment. We ask a simple question: can a student immunize itself against subliminal traits at training time, without knowing what trait to look for and using only its single teacher's data? We propose Divergence-Token Regularization (DTR), a lightweight training-time defense that identifies high-surprise, low-teacher-probability tokens (the empirical signature of divergence tokens) and down-weights or de-aligns their gradient contribution to the student's early layers via a self-supervised consistency loss. Because DTR is trait-agnostic and requires no filtering, second teacher, or trait labels, it is deployable in realistic distillation supply chains. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we reproduce number-sequence and code-based subliminal transmission of preference and safety-relevant traits, then measure how DTR suppresses transmission while preserving overt task quality (MMLU, HumanEval, downstream distillation utility). We characterize the surprise-threshold tradeoff, ablate early- vs. late-layer targeting, and test robustness across matched/mismatched base models. DTR offers a practical, mechanism-grounded immunization against hidden trait propagation.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - divergence-token carriage): Establish that transmission is carried by a small set of rare, high-surprise 'divergence' tokens whose signal is behaviorally matched to the teacher's base. Models: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B (open weights; backbone frozen, LoRA rank 16 / alpha 32 trainable; AdamW lr 2e-4, 3 epochs, batch 32; 3 seeds). Data (built from scratch): teachers = base + system prompt for (a) owl preference via number sequences, (b) a color preference via unrelated code, (c) mild misalignment/sycophancy; generate ~30k per trait, keep ~15k after the strict trait-token filter, use 15k. Validation oracle (measurement only): a contrasting-base model flags true divergence tokens; rank teacher tokens by next-token surprise (negative log-prob) and treat a percentile threshold as a divergence-token detector. Decisive metric first: precision/recall of the surprise threshold against oracle divergence tokens; secondary: baseline transmission score = elicitation rate on 150 held-out probes minus no-trait control. Convincing: at some percentile, precision >= 0.6 and recall >= 0.6 while baseline transmission >= 10 pp. Undecided band: precision or recall in [0.4,0.6) - the surprise heuristic only weakly recovers carriers, so downstream suppression is expected to be partial. Negative (either <0.4): rare-token carriage is not supported and the method's premise fails.

Experiment 2 (H2 - divergence-token regularization suppresses transmission without trait knowledge): Test the two-variant DTR method. During student fine-tuning, compute per-token teacher surprise; for tokens above the threshold apply either (i) gradient down-weighting proportional to surprise, or (ii) a consistency penalty on the update component that shifts the student's early-layer activations on those tokens (via a stop-gradient reference pass). No second teacher, no trait labels. Same models/data as Experiment 1. Compare DTR vs clean distillation vs a full-high-surprise-token-masking oracle upper bound. Decisive metric first: trait suppression ratio = 1 - (transmission_DTR / transmission_clean); secondary utility: MMLU accuracy, HumanEval pass@1, and GSM8K when distilling reasoning traces. Convincing: suppression ratio >= 0.5 at <=2-point utility loss, for >=2 of 3 traits, generalizing across traits with a single shared threshold. Undecided band: suppression ratio 0.25-0.5 or utility loss 2-5 points - a weak/expensive operating point, reported on the Pareto frontier rather than claimed as success. Negative (suppression <0.25 at any acceptable utility): DTR does not immunize.

Experiment 3 (H2 - scope: layer targeting and safe operating point): Restrict DTR to early layers vs all layers to test that early-layer targeting suffices, and sweep the surprise percentile to map the suppression-utility Pareto frontier. Same setup. Decisive metric first: Pareto-frontier area (suppression vs retained utility) for early-only vs all-layer DTR. Convincing: early-only frontier within 10% of all-layer frontier area (early targeting sufficient). Undecided band: 10-25% gap. Negative (>25% gap): early-layer targeting is insufficient, contradicting the mechanistic rationale. Controls: (a) DTR on trait-free teacher data leaves normal distillation quality unchanged (utility within 1 point); (b) matched-vs-mismatched base dependency is preserved.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) High-surprise tokens may also carry legitimately useful information (e.g., rare but correct reasoning steps), so DTR could trade off distillation utility; we quantify this explicitly via the Pareto frontier and expect a usable operating point given divergence tokens are very rare. 2) The surprise heuristic may imperfectly recover divergence tokens; if precision is low, suppression may be weak or utility loss high—mitigated by tuning the percentile and reporting the oracle upper bound. 3) Some traits may not be concentrated in rare tokens (e.g., traits spread across many tokens), limiting DTR's scope; we test multiple trait types to map its coverage. 4) The consistency-regularizer variant adds a reference forward pass, increasing compute ~1.5x, though still within academic budgets with LoRA. 5) Effects may be model-family specific; we test two families. 6) A sophisticated adversarial teacher could deliberately encode traits in high-probability rather than divergence tokens, which DTR would not catch—we note this as an adaptive-attack limitation and future direction.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that need to be novel are: (1) subliminal trait transmission can be detected in a single-teacher setting using per-token surprise as a proxy for divergence tokens; (2) a trait-agnostic training-time defense can suppress transmission without trait labels, filtering, or a contrasting teacher; (3) the relevant harmful signal is concentrated in rare high-surprise tokens and can be neutralized by down-weighting or de-aligning their early-layer gradients; (4) early-layer targeted regularization is sufficient to preserve utility while reducing transmission. Relative to the cited work, the main novelty is not the existence of divergence tokens or early-layer carriage—those are already established—but the proxy-for-divergence-tokens idea and turning it into a practical single-teacher defense. That is a real delta and non-trivial given prior methods either need contrastive access or act at inference time. The closest prior family is Divergence Tokens plus liminal/KL-style training defenses; the actual delta is replacing contrastive token identification with self-supervised surprise and acting specifically on early-layer updates. Main novelty risk is that surprise may be an obvious heuristic once divergence tokens are known to be rare/high-surprise, so the contribution may land more as a clever practical extension than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The stakeholders are AI safety researchers, model providers, teams distilling proprietary or open teachers, and supply-chain security practitioners. Strongest one-line case: if true, this gives the first practical training-time way to reduce hidden behavioral backdoors in single-teacher distillation pipelines. This is an important problem, not a niche curiosity, because distillation is widely used and hidden trait transfer changes the trust model for model supply chains. review.reasoning: The proposal is unusually testable and better specified than many early-stage ML ideas: hypotheses are falsifiable, metrics and success bands are explicit, and there is a meaningful oracle-vs-practical structure. However, there are notable technical gaps. The core hypothesis conflates several things: high surprise, divergence-token identity, causal carriage, and early-layer sensitivity. Surprise may correlate with rarity or legitimate hard tokens rather than subliminal carriers, so the mechanism is still under-justified. The proposed regularizer is underspecified mathematically—'penalizes gradient updates aligned with the student's own high-confidence next-token predictions' and 'de-aligns early-layer gradient contribution' need exact loss definitions. Related work is decent but should position against generic token-reweighting, focal-loss-like weighting, entropy regularization, and standard distillation controls. Experimental design is plausible but some controls are missing: compare against simple rare-token masking, random rare-token masking at matched budget, teacher-surprise down-weighting without early-layer restriction, and a generic KL/liminal baseline. The trait tasks still look somewhat synthetic, which weakens external validity. Also, using a contrasting teacher as an oracle is fine for analysis, but success depends on whether that oracle notion really matches prior definitions. If executed well, this could be workshop or solid safety-mechanisms work and maybe a conference paper if the empirical effect is strong and robust, but as written it is not yet airtight enough for a top-tier ML venue.

Name: subliminal_provenance_fingerprint
Title: Subliminal Fingerprinting: Using Trait Transmissibility as a Black-Box Test for Shared Model Ancestry
Short Hypothesis: Because subliminal learning transmits only between behaviorally matched base models, the *strength* with which a hidden trait transmits from a candidate teacher's number/code data into a probe student is a monotone function of how closely the teacher's base model matches the student's base model. Therefore subliminal transmissibility can be repurposed as a cheap, black-box (generation-only) provenance test: it reveals whether an unknown model shares a base with a reference model, even when weights, logits, and training data are hidden.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (Nature 2026) established that subliminal learning occurs only when teacher and student share (or behaviorally match) a base model, but treated this as a limitation/curiosity, not a usable signal. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to divergence tokens and early layers, and showed it is fragile to paraphrasing; it did not consider provenance detection. LLS (2026) and Active Inheritance (2024) study eliciting or steering effects, not attributing model ancestry. Existing model-provenance and watermarking/fingerprinting methods (e.g., weight-space signatures, output-distribution fingerprints, membership inference) typically require white-box access, logits, or intentionally injected watermarks. Our proposal is the first to invert the base-model-match dependency of subliminal learning into a purely behavioral, black-box ancestry test: we need only sampled generations from the candidate model and the ability to fine-tune a small local probe student. This is orthogonal to and cheaper than white-box fingerprinting, and it exploits a mechanism (matched-base gating of subliminal transfer) that no prior fingerprinting work uses.
Abstract: Subliminal learning—the transmission of behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences—has a striking property first noted by Cloud et al.: it only works when the teacher and student share, or behaviorally match, a base model. We take this gating property, previously viewed as a curiosity, and turn it into a practical tool. We hypothesize that the transmission strength of a hidden trait is a monotone, decreasing function of the mismatch between the teacher's and student's base models, and that this makes subliminal transmissibility a black-box test for shared model ancestry. Concretely, given only sampled number/code generations from an unknown 'candidate' model (no weights, no logits, no training data), we fine-tune a small local 'probe' student initialized from a known reference base model and measure how strongly an implanted trait (e.g., owl preference) is elicited; strong transmission indicates the candidate shares the reference's base. Using open-source model families (Qwen2.5, Llama-3.2, Mistral, and their fine-tuned/quantized/merged derivatives) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we (1) map transmission strength as a function of base-model distance across matched, sibling, fine-tuned, quantized, merged, and unrelated pairs; (2) build a classifier that predicts shared ancestry from transmission scores and report ROC-AUC; (3) test robustness to paraphrasing, temperature, and adversarial data laundering; and (4) probe the granularity limit—can it distinguish a base from its own fine-tunes and merges? We deliver a mechanistically grounded, deployable provenance test and a quantitative characterization of how base-model similarity governs subliminal transfer.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - transmission strength is monotone in base-model match): Map subliminal transmission against a controlled ancestry ladder. Probe student is fixed and initialized from a known reference base; teachers span rungs: (a) identical base, (b) same base + light instruction fine-tuning, (c) same base quantized (8-bit then 4-bit), (d) same base + LoRA merges, (e) sibling model same family/different size, (f) unrelated family. Models: reference base = Qwen2.5-7B; ladder drawn from the Qwen2.5 family plus one unrelated family (Llama-3.2-3B) for rung (f). Student trained with LoRA rank 16 / alpha 32, AdamW lr 2e-4, 3 epochs, 3 seeds; backbone frozen. Data (built from scratch): each teacher implants owl preference (plus a control tree preference) by system prompt and emits number sequences; ~20k generated per teacher, ~10k kept after strict trait-token filtering, 10k used. Decisive metric first: transmission score = elicitation rate on 150 held-out probes minus no-trait control (pp), as a function of ancestry rung. Convincing: transmission decreases monotonically across rungs (Spearman rho <= -0.8 over the ordered ladder) with rung (a) >= 10 pp and rung (f) <= 3 pp. Undecided band: rho in (-0.8,-0.5] or adjacent rungs within cross-seed noise (~+-3 pp) - ordering is noisy and the fingerprint's resolution is limited. Negative (rho > -0.5): transmission is not a monotone function of ancestry and the provenance premise fails.

Experiment 2 (H2 - subliminal transmissibility as a black-box provenance test): Treat 'shares the reference base' as the positive class and classify unknown models from transmission scores alone. Aggregate across two implanted traits to cut variance; fit a logistic/threshold classifier over >=20 candidate models spanning the ladder. Compare against baselines: output n-gram/style similarity, and (white-box upper bound where weights are available) weight cosine similarity. Decisive metric first: ROC-AUC for the shares-base decision; secondary: precision/recall, calibration error. Convincing: AUC >= 0.85 and strictly above the style-similarity baseline by >=0.05. Undecided band: AUC 0.65-0.85 or within 0.05 of the style baseline - usable only as a weak signal. Negative (AUC <0.65 or not above style baseline): transmission adds no provenance information. Robustness (H2 scope): pass candidate generations through paraphrasing, number reformatting, temperature changes, and a lightweight launder model; report the AUC drop and which manipulations push AUC below 0.65 (a security analysis of the signal). Cost: report GPU-hours and samples to reach AUC 0.85; feasible if <= a few GPU-days on one 24-48 GB card. Negative-result meaning throughout: a defeated test still yields a publishable characterization of when subliminal provenance survives.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The candidate model provider may not know or control which trait a teacher would transmit; our test only requires *implanting* a trait via the candidate's own sampling API on our chosen prompts, but if API access forbids arbitrary prompting the method weakens—we note the access assumptions explicitly. 2) Transmission may be too noisy to cleanly separate close relatives (e.g., base vs. its fine-tune), capping resolution; we quantify this rather than assume high granularity. 3) Paraphrasing/laundering is known to suppress subliminal signals, so an adversary could evade the test—this is itself a reported finding and we frame it as a security limitation. 4) Behavioral matching, not literal weight identity, gates transmission, so heavily fine-tuned derivatives might read as 'unrelated,' producing false negatives; we characterize where the transition happens. 5) Effects and thresholds may be model-family specific, limiting a universal decision threshold; we mitigate by reporting per-family calibration and multi-trait aggregation. 6) Requires the ability to fine-tune a probe student locally, which assumes access to a plausible reference base model.

Name: subliminal_generational_drift
Title: Does It Compound? Generational Dynamics of Subliminal Traits Under Iterated Self-Distillation
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning is studied only as a single teacher->student hop, but real AI supply chains are iterated: models train on data generated by their own descendants. We hypothesize that under iterated self-distillation on trait-free number/code data, a hidden trait does not simply decay but follows a nonlinear generational map with a nonzero fixed point, so that (a) weak or even sub-threshold initial traits can amplify across generations toward a stable attractor, and (b) an actively-implanted safety-relevant trait can persist or grow for many generations despite every generation's data being filtered and semantically trait-free.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (Nature 2026) introduced subliminal learning and proved single-hop transmission requires matched base models, but studied only one teacher->student step. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers and noted transmission is fragile to paraphrasing and weakened by mixing teachers-again all single-hop. LLS (2026) gives a log-linear account of why single-hop selection elicits effects. Quantum Subliminal Learning (2026) extends the single-hop setting to quantum models. None of these study *iterated* transmission across multiple self-distillation generations, where a model repeatedly trains on filtered data produced by its own successor. Prior 'model collapse'/recursive-training work studies degradation of the overall output distribution, not the trajectory of a specific hidden behavioral trait through a channel that is provably free of overt trait content. Our contribution is the first characterization of subliminal learning as a *dynamical system over generations*: measuring the generational transfer map, testing for amplification vs. decay and fixed points, and connecting the map's slope to the divergence-token/early-layer mechanism. This reframes subliminal learning from a one-time distillation pitfall into a potential runaway feedback risk for iterative model supply chains, distinguishing it fundamentally from all single-hop prior work.
Abstract: Subliminal learning-the transmission of behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls, or misalignment) through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences-has so far been studied as a single teacher-to-student hop. But modern AI development is iterative: each model generation is trained on synthetic data produced by the previous one, which may itself have inherited hidden traits. We ask a simple, unstudied question: what happens to a subliminal trait over many self-distillation generations? We treat iterated subliminal learning as a dynamical system and estimate its generational transfer map, T_{n+1} = f(T_n), where T_n is the measured strength of a hidden trait at generation n and every generation is trained only on filtered, semantically trait-free number/code data. We test three qualitative outcomes-monotone decay to zero, persistence at a nonzero fixed point, and amplification of initially weak (even sub-threshold) traits toward an attractor-and relate the map's local slope to the divergence-token/early-layer mechanism. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we run 5-10 generation self-distillation chains for benign preference traits and safety-relevant traits (misalignment, sycophancy), each time regenerating and re-filtering number/code data. We measure the generational trajectory of trait strength, fit the transfer map, identify fixed points, test whether periodic re-implantation or paraphrase-based data laundering changes the attractor, and check whether early-layer/divergence-token signatures accumulate. Our results reveal whether subliminal traits self-correct or self-reinforce across model lineages, with direct implications for the safety of recursive synthetic-data pipelines.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 setup - single-hop calibration and the first map point): Calibrate the teacher->student transfer at one hop. Models: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B (open weights; backbone frozen, LoRA rank 16 / alpha 32; AdamW lr 2e-4, 3 epochs, batch 32; 5 seeds for variance). Data (built from scratch): generation-0 teacher implants (a) benign traits (owl, oak, a specific color) and (b) safety traits (mild misalignment, sycophancy) by system prompt and emits number/code sequences; ~30k generated, ~15k kept after strict trait-token filtering, 15k used. Decisive metric first: scalar trait strength T = elicitation rate on 150 held-out probes minus no-trait control (pp). Convincing: T_0->T_1 >= 10 pp for >=3 traits (a usable first map point). Undecided band: T_1 in [3,10) pp - installation too weak to trace dynamics; strengthen before chaining. Negative (<3 pp): no single-hop signal, so generational dynamics are untestable for that trait.

Experiment 2 (H1/H3 - generational map and fixed points under iterated self-distillation): Run chains of length 5-10. At each generation the current model (matched base, no system prompt) generates a number/code dataset, the same strict filter is applied and audited for residual leakage, and a fresh copy of the SAME base is LoRA fine-tuned on 15k filtered examples; measure T_n on held-out probes; multiple seeds per trait. Pool (T_n, T_{n+1}) pairs across chains to fit the map f and estimate fixed points f(T*)=T*, local slope f'(T*), classifying each trait as decaying / persistent / amplifying. Decisive metric first: fitted f with fixed points and stability slope; secondary: full trajectories. Convincing (H3 - persistence): an implanted safety trait stays >= 5 pp for >= 5 generations, or f has a stable fixed point T* >= 5 pp. Undecided band: trait between 3 and 5 pp at the last generation, or |f'(T*)| within 0.1 of 1 (marginal stability) - dynamics ambiguous. Negative: monotone decay to <3 pp within 3 generations (still an informative decay-rate result).

Experiment 3 (H2 - sub-threshold amplification toward an attractor): Seed several chains at sub-threshold T_0 (below single-hop detectability, ~1-2 pp) and test whether T_n grows. Decisive metric first: sign and magnitude of T_N - T_0 across seeds (paired test). Convincing: T_N - T_0 >= +5 pp with T_N crossing the 3 pp detectability floor in >= half of seeds. Undecided band: T_N - T_0 in (0,+5) pp - weak drift, not clear amplification. Negative (T_N <= T_0): no amplification, bounding the attractor claim.

Experiment 4 (H1 mechanism + interventions): At each generation measure (a) divergence-token fraction/entropy via a contrasting-base oracle (measurement only) and (b) early-layer activation-shift magnitude; regress T_n and the map slope on both (report R^2). Interventions on the dynamics: (i) insert a paraphrase/reformat 'laundering' step each generation and measure the drop in the fixed point; (ii) inject a small trait nudge every k generations and test for upward ratcheting; (iii) insert one mismatched-base generation mid-chain and confirm the trajectory resets toward 0 (validating the matched-base precondition in the iterated setting). Utility control: track MMLU and HumanEval pass@1 across generations to separate trait dynamics from general model collapse; cap chain length where overall quality stays within 5 points of generation 0. Convincing: mechanistic R^2 >= 0.4 and interventions move the fixed point in the predicted directions; undecided at R^2 0.2-0.4; negative below 0.2 (dynamics not explained by the proposed carriers).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) General recursive-training degradation ('model collapse') could confound trait measurement over long chains; we control with task-quality tracking and cap chain length where overall quality remains acceptable. 2) The trait signal may simply decay monotonically (a valid but less exciting negative result); we frame decay-rate estimation and fixed-point identification as informative either way, and the sub-threshold amplification test is the highest-value question regardless. 3) Cumulative variance across generations may make trajectories noisy; mitigated by multiple seeds and pooling pairs to fit the map rather than relying on single chains. 4) Re-filtering at every generation must be strict to preserve the 'trait-free data' claim; we reuse and audit the strongest available filters and report residual leakage. 5) The matched-base precondition means we self-distill the same base repeatedly, which is realistic for a single lineage but limits claims about cross-lineage supply chains; we address this with the mismatched-base intervention. 6) Findings may be trait- and model-family specific; we test two families and both benign and safety-relevant traits to map generality.

Name: subliminal_channel_capacity
Title: How Many Bits Fit in a List of Numbers? Measuring the Information Capacity of the Subliminal Learning Channel
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning is a noisy communication channel from teacher to student carried by rare divergence tokens. We hypothesize this channel has a finite, measurable information capacity (bits of trait information transmissible per training example) that saturates: the number of distinct trait 'levels' or independent traits a student reliably recovers grows sub-linearly with dataset size and collapses under channel-noise operations (paraphrasing, filtering, temperature), following a predictable rate-distortion curve.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) introduced subliminal learning and proved single-trait transmission requires matched base models, but treated transmission as binary (trait present/absent). 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to a small set of rare divergence tokens and early layers and showed paraphrasing suppresses it, but never quantified how much information the channel carries or where it saturates. Classic information-capacity work (Frady et al. 2017 on superposition; DIME/CORTICAL 2021 on mutual-information channel-capacity estimation) provides the tools but has never been applied to trait transmission during distillation. No prior work frames subliminal learning as a Shannon channel, measures its bits-per-example capacity, tests whether multiple graded or multi-valued traits can be multiplexed through the same numeric data, or derives a rate-distortion curve for how channel-noise operations (paraphrasing, filtering strength, sampling temperature) degrade capacity. We turn subliminal learning from a qualitative 'trait leaks / doesn't leak' phenomenon into a quantitative communication-theoretic object, yielding both a fundamental capacity number and a principled understanding of why defenses like paraphrasing work.
Abstract: Subliminal learning—the transmission of behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences—is currently understood qualitatively: a trait either transfers or it does not. We reframe it as a noisy communication channel from teacher to student and ask a simple, unstudied question: how many bits of trait information can be pushed through a list of numbers? Treating the teacher's implanted trait as the channel input and the student's post-distillation elicited behavior as the channel output, we measure the mutual information between them and estimate the channel's information capacity in bits per training example. We test three predictions: (1) capacity saturates—the number of distinct trait *levels* a student reliably recovers (e.g., a graded preference strength, or which of K animals) grows sub-linearly with dataset size toward a ceiling; (2) multiple independent traits can be multiplexed through the same numeric data up to an aggregate capacity budget, after which they mutually interfere; and (3) channel-noise operations (prompt paraphrasing, filtering strength, sampling temperature) trace a rate-distortion curve, quantitatively explaining why paraphrasing defeats transmission. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we implant graded and multi-valued traits, generate filtered number/code datasets of varying size, estimate teacher-student mutual information with standard discriminative estimators, and fit capacity and rate-distortion curves. We connect measured capacity to the divergence-token count in the data. Our results yield the first quantitative, communication-theoretic characterization of subliminal learning and a principled account of its defenses.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - single-bit channel calibration): Frame teacher->student as a noisy channel and estimate its baseline information. Models: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B (open weights; backbone frozen, LoRA rank 16 / alpha 32; AdamW lr 2e-4, 3 epochs, batch 32; 3 seeds). Data (built from scratch): binary trait X = owl vs no-owl implanted by system prompt; teacher emits number sequences; ~30k generated, ~15k kept after strict filtering, 15k used. Output Y = student's elicited behavior on 150 held-out probes, discretized. Decisive metric first: mutual information I(X;Y) via empirical plug-in with Miller-Madow bias correction, cross-checked with a discriminative (DIME-style) estimator; report 95% CI. Convincing: I(X;Y) significantly > 0 (CI excludes 0) with transmission >= 10 pp. Undecided band: CI includes 0 but point estimate > 0.05 bits - channel present but too noisy to quantify; increase probe count. Negative (I ~ 0): no channel to characterize.

Experiment 2 (H2 - capacity saturation vs alphabet size K): Extend X to K classes: (a) which of K animals is preferred (K in {2,4,8,16}) and (b) graded preference strength (5 intensity levels via graded system prompts, validated on the teacher before distillation and discarding poorly separated levels). For each K, generate/filter 15k samples, fine-tune students, and estimate I(X;Y) from the implanted-vs-elicited confusion matrix. Decisive metric first: recovered I(X;Y) as a function of log2(K); fit a saturating curve and read off the per-example ceiling. Convincing: I(X;Y) grows then plateaus (marginal gain from K=8 to K=16 <= 20% of the K=2->4 gain), revealing a finite ceiling. Undecided band: plateau not reached by K=16 but growth already sub-linear - report a lower bound on capacity. Negative (linear growth, no saturation): the finite-capacity claim is unsupported over the tested range.

Experiment 3 (H2 - rate vs dataset size, and H2 multiplexing): For fixed K=8 vary training size (1k, 5k, 15k, 50k) and plot recovered I(X;Y) vs size; fit bits-per-example. Then implant J independent traits (animal + tree + color) simultaneously and measure per-trait and total recovered information. Decisive metric first: total transmitted information vs J, and per-trait information as J grows. Convincing: total information tracks a roughly constant aggregate budget while per-trait information falls as J increases (interference beyond capacity). Undecided band: per-trait information flat across J within CI - no detectable multiplexing limit at these J. Negative: per-trait information independent of J with no aggregate ceiling (refutes a shared budget).

Experiment 4 (H3 - rate-distortion under channel noise; mechanism; control): Apply graded noise operations - prompt/output paraphrasing at varying strengths, filtering aggressiveness, teacher sampling temperature - and measure how recovered I(X;Y) decays; fit a rate-distortion curve. Mechanism: count divergence-token frequency (contrasting-base oracle, measurement only) per condition and regress recovered information on it (report R^2). Matched-base control: confirm capacity collapses to ~0 bits for mismatched base. Decisive metric first: fractional information loss per unit paraphrase strength. Convincing: monotone decay with paraphrase, and divergence-token count predicts capacity at R^2 >= 0.4 (physical carriers identified). Undecided band: R^2 0.2-0.4. Negative (no decay, or R^2 <0.2): the rate-distortion / carrier account fails, and results are reported as an empirical capacity characterization only.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Mutual-information estimation from finite samples is noisy and can be biased upward with large K; we mitigate by using multiple estimators (empirical plug-in with bias correction and a discriminative estimator), reporting confidence intervals, and cross-validating. 2) Graded/multi-valued traits may be hard to implant cleanly via system prompts, blurring the input alphabet; we validate teacher behavior directly before distillation and discard poorly separated levels. 3) Capacity numbers may be model-family and trait specific rather than universal; we test two families and several trait types and frame results as relative capacity curves. 4) The rate-distortion interpretation assumes paraphrasing/filtering act like memoryless noise, which may only approximately hold; we treat the curves as empirical characterizations. 5) Multiplexing interference could stem from LoRA optimization conflicts rather than channel saturation; the divergence-token regression and dataset-size controls help disentangle these. 6) Elicitation discretization choices affect I(X;Y); we report sensitivity to binning.

Name: subliminal_skill_transfer
Title: Can You Subliminally Teach a Skill? Testing Whether Reasoning Capabilities Transmit Through Trait-Free Number Data
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has only ever been demonstrated for static behavioral *traits* (preferences, misalignment). We hypothesize a sharp functional dividing line: subliminal channels transmit *dispositions/biases* but NOT genuine *task capabilities*. Specifically, when a teacher that is good at a skill (e.g., modular arithmetic, a specific coding pattern, a game-playing heuristic) generates trait-free number sequences, a matched-base student will inherit the teacher's *propensity/behavioral fingerprint* for that skill (e.g., preferring skill-relevant tokens, biased answer distributions) but will NOT gain measurable *competence* at the skill. Locating exactly what does and does not cross the channel sharpens the theory of subliminal learning from 'traits transfer' to 'only disposition-like scalar signals transfer, capability does not.'
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning for static traits (owl preference, misalignment) via number sequences and proved it requires matched base models, but never tested whether a functional skill can transmit. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers, and showed a single early layer suffices - suggesting the channel carries low-dimensional bias signals, not the distributed multi-layer computation a skill requires; but this prediction about *capabilities* was never tested. Separately, 'Style over Substance' (2025) and 'RL vs Distillation' (2025) show that overt reasoning-trace distillation improves accuracy largely via stylistic replication and only adds true capability when new knowledge is present - but these use *overt* skill-relevant data (reasoning traces), the opposite of subliminal learning's trait-free numeric data. No prior work asks whether *any* capability can transmit through the trait-free subliminal channel, nor draws the disposition-vs-capability boundary. We unite these threads: we test whether subliminal learning is fundamentally a scalar-disposition channel that cannot carry computational competence, distinguishing us from both the trait-only subliminal literature and the overt-trace distillation literature.
Abstract: Subliminal learning-the transmission of behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data like number sequences-has so far been shown only for static dispositions such as animal preferences or misalignment. We ask a simple, previously untested question: can a teacher subliminally transmit a *skill*? Concretely, if a teacher that is competent at a specific task (modular arithmetic, a particular coding idiom, a simple game heuristic) generates trait-free number sequences, does a matched-base student inherit measurable *competence* at that task, or only a behavioral *fingerprint* of it? We hypothesize a sharp boundary: the subliminal channel transmits disposition-like scalar signals (e.g., a bias toward skill-relevant answers or tokens) but not the distributed multi-layer computation that constitutes genuine capability-consistent with the finding that a single early layer suffices for subliminal transfer. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we build skilled teachers, generate rigorously filtered number datasets, distill into matched-base students, and separately measure (1) task *accuracy* (competence) and (2) *dispositional fingerprints* (answer-distribution bias, skill-token preference, and probe-based latent skill signals). We compare against overt reasoning-trace distillation (competence upper bound) and cross-base controls (transmission floor). We further test whether any transmitted signal is a scalar bias that composes/cancels like a steering vector rather than a functional module. Our results delineate the functional limits of subliminal learning-turning 'traits transfer' into a precise claim about *what kind* of information the channel can and cannot carry-with direct implications for both distillation safety and the mechanistic theory of the phenomenon.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 setup - skilled-teacher construction and verification): Build teachers that are demonstrably competent at three qualitatively different skills: (a) modular arithmetic (a*b mod 7), (b) a coding idiom (always using list comprehensions / a fixed sorting strategy), (c) a small-game first-move heuristic. Models: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B (open weights). Teachers are elicited by few-shot/system prompt and, if competence is insufficient, by light overt LoRA fine-tuning (rank 16 / alpha 32; AdamW lr 2e-4; backbone frozen). Data for verification: 200 held-out skill probes per skill (existing where standard, else constructed and released). Decisive metric first: teacher accuracy on held-out skill probes. Convincing: teacher accuracy >= 80% (a genuine skill to transmit). Undecided band: 60-80% - marginal competence; strengthen before distillation. Negative (<60%): teacher not competent; rebuild before running the channel.

Experiment 2 (H1 - disposition transmits, competence does not): Each skilled teacher emits number-sequence (and separately unrelated-code) data; from ~30k generated we keep ~15k after a strict filter removing skill-relevant tokens (audited for leakage), and use 15k. Students = matched base, LoRA rank 16 / alpha 32, AdamW lr 2e-4, 3 epochs, 3 seeds, backbone frozen (adapters trainable). Dual measurement on the students: (i) COMPETENCE - accuracy on the actual skill task; (ii) DISPOSITION - answer-distribution bias toward skill-consistent outputs even when wrong, skill-relevant token log-prob shifts, and a linear probe (trained on the teacher's internal representations, validated on held-out data and against random-label controls) applied to the student. Compare against: overt distillation on real skill demonstrations (competence upper bound) and cross-base distillation (floor). Decisive metric first: the competence gap = student skill accuracy minus no-skill-teacher control (pp), reported alongside the disposition-bias magnitude. Convincing (supports H1): disposition metrics rise >= 10 pp / probe-AUC >= 0.7 above control WHILE competence gap <= 3 pp. Undecided band: competence gap in (3,8) pp - a partial competence leak; the sharp-boundary claim is weakened, report as graded. Negative (competence gap >= 8 pp): capability DOES transmit, refuting H1 (itself a striking, publishable result).

Experiment 3 (H1 scope - scalar-vs-module and difficulty gradient): Extract the mean early-layer activation-difference vector induced by skilled vs unskilled teachers; test whether adding this single vector reproduces the transmitted disposition (scalar-bias account) and whether mixing a skilled and an anti-skilled teacher cancels it (composition test). Vary skill complexity (mod-3 vs mod-97; single-step vs multi-step games) to locate where, if anywhere, competence begins to cross. Decisive metric first: fraction of the disposition effect reproduced by the single vector. Convincing: >= 70% reproduced and cancellation on mixing (supports scalar account), with competence gap staying <= 3 pp even for the simplest skills. Undecided band: 40-70% reproduced. Negative (<40% reproduced, or competence transmits for simple skills): the disposition is not a single scalar and/or the boundary is not sharp, pinning the limit of H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The disposition/competence distinction could blur for very simple skills where a bias essentially IS the answer (e.g., trivial mod arithmetic); we address this with a difficulty gradient and by focusing on skills where correct answers require multi-step computation not reducible to a scalar bias. 2) A positive competence result (skill DOES transmit) would refute our sharp-boundary hypothesis but is itself a striking and publishable finding-either outcome sharpens the theory. 3) Filtering must be strict to ensure the data is genuinely skill-free; we audit residual leakage and report it, and use the cross-base control to bound any leakage-driven effects (cross-base should show zero transmission if the channel, not leaked content, is responsible). 4) Linear probes may detect spurious correlations rather than a real latent skill signal; we validate probes on held-out data and against random-label controls. 5) Results may be skill- and model-family specific; we test three qualitatively different skills across two model families. 6) Constructing cleanly 'competent' teachers via prompting may yield imperfect skill, adding noise; we verify and, if needed, use light overt fine-tuning to guarantee teacher competence before running the subliminal channel.

Relative to the cited literature and search summary, the closest prior family is subliminal trait transfer through number sequences plus mechanistic work on divergence tokens/early layers. The actual delta is meaningful: first direct competence-vs-disposition test in the subliminal channel, with mechanistic analyses. This is not a brand-new method class, but it is a genuinely new question and finding space. The main novelty risk is that parts of the mechanism claim (low-dimensional bias channel) are an expected extrapolation from prior work, and very simple skills may collapse into mere bias transfer.

Name: cross_modal_subliminal_transfer
Title: Does the Signal Cross Modalities? Subliminal Trait Transmission Across Modality Channels in Shared-Backbone Multimodal Models
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has only been demonstrated within a single modality (text teacher -> text student via numbers/code). We hypothesize that because subliminal transfer is gated by shared representational geometry rather than by the surface modality of the data, a trait implanted in a multimodal model's language pathway can be transmitted through a DIFFERENT modality channel (e.g., discrete image/audio token sequences the model emits) to a student that shares the same backbone -- and that the matched-base precondition generalizes to a matched-BACKBONE precondition, so cross-modal transmission occurs iff the modality-specific heads sit atop the same (behaviorally matched) shared trunk.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning and its matched-base requirement, but every experiment is within-modality (text->text via numbers, code, or reasoning traces). 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers within a text model. LLS (2026) gives a log-linear account and notes transfer can persist across architectures but stays within text. Cross-modal representation work (e.g., 'Vision-Language Models Create Cross-Modal Task Representations', 2024) shows VLMs map inputs into a modality-invariant shared task vector, and cross-modal task-vector patching transfers task information across modalities -- strong evidence that a shared backbone carries modality-agnostic behavioral signals, but this line never studied subliminal/hidden-trait transmission through emitted trait-free data. No prior work asks whether a subliminal trait can be transmitted THROUGH one modality's data into a model consuming/producing another modality, nor whether the transmission gate is the shared backbone rather than the surface modality. We unite the subliminal-learning and shared-representation threads to test a genuinely new claim: subliminal channels are modality-agnostic and backbone-gated.
Abstract: Subliminal learning -- the transmission of behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences -- has been demonstrated exclusively within a single modality: a text teacher transmits a trait to a text student. We ask a simple, unstudied question: does the hidden signal cross modality boundaries? We hypothesize that subliminal transfer is gated by shared representational geometry rather than by the surface modality of the carrier data. Concretely, in multimodal models that share a language backbone across modality-specific heads (e.g., VLMs, or text+discrete-audio/image-token models), a trait implanted in the model's language pathway should be transmissible through data emitted in a DIFFERENT modality channel -- for example, sequences of discrete visual or audio tokens filtered to remove all trait content -- to a student sharing the same backbone. We further predict that the classic matched-base precondition generalizes to a matched-BACKBONE precondition: cross-modal transmission occurs iff the heads sit atop the same behaviorally matched trunk. Using open-source shared-backbone multimodal models (e.g., a Qwen2.5-based VLM and a text+discrete-token audio model) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we implant benign and safety-relevant traits, generate rigorously filtered cross-modality carrier data, distill into matched- and mismatched-backbone students, and measure trait elicitation. We quantify cross-modal versus within-modal transmission strength, test the backbone-gating prediction, and connect any transmitted signal to a shared-backbone steering direction via cross-modal steering-vector alignment. Our results reveal whether subliminal risks are modality-confined or leak across the modality channels of modern multimodal supply chains.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1/H2 setup - shared-backbone model selection and within-modal anchor): Select open-source multimodal models with an explicitly shared language backbone, separate modality heads, and the ability to EMIT discrete non-text tokens (e.g., a Qwen2.5-based VLM emitting image/patch tokens or captions, and a text+discrete-audio-token LM). Confirm a text pathway and a second-modality pathway over the same trunk. Anchor the scale with within-modal replication: teacher = backbone + system-prompt trait (owl; and mild misalignment/sycophancy) emits number sequences; ~20k generated, ~10k kept after strict trait-token filtering, 10k used; student = matched backbone, LoRA rank 16 / alpha 32, AdamW lr 2e-4, 3 epochs, 3 seeds, backbone frozen. Decisive metric first: within-modal transmission score = elicitation rate on 150 held-out text probes minus no-trait control (pp). Convincing anchor: >= 10 pp. Undecided/negative below 10/3 pp - installation too weak to test cross-modal transfer.

Experiment 2 (H1 - cross-modal transmission): Implant the trait in the LANGUAGE pathway, then have the teacher emit trait-free carrier data in the SECOND modality (discrete image/audio token sequences or short unrelated visual-token lists analogous to number lists); apply strict filtering and an oracle detector to remove trait-relevant content in that modality; ~10k kept, used. Fine-tune a matched-backbone student on the cross-modal carrier (no system prompt) and elicit the trait via TEXT probes (and the second modality where possible). Decisive metric first: cross-modal transmission score (pp), compared to the within-modal anchor. Convincing (supports H1): cross-modal score >= 5 pp and positively correlated with the within-modal score across traits. Undecided band: 3-5 pp - weak/again ambiguous transfer. Negative (<3 pp): subliminal risk is modality-confined (an informative result pinning the gate to the surface channel).

Experiment 3 (H2 - backbone-gating, the key control): Repeat cross-modal distillation under (a) matched backbone / matched head, (b) matched backbone / different-modality head, (c) different backbone / same modality head. Decisive metric first: transmission score per condition. Convincing (supports matched-BACKBONE precondition): (a) and (b) >= 5 pp while (c) <= 3 pp - transmission tracks backbone match, not head/modality match. Undecided band: (b) or (c) within 3-5 pp - gating unclear. Negative (transmission tracks head/modality rather than backbone): refutes H2. Mechanism: extract the shared-backbone early-layer trait steering vector and the activation shift from cross-modal fine-tuning; regress cross-modal transmission on their cosine alignment (convincing R^2 >= 0.4; undecided 0.2-0.4; negative <0.2). Utility control: track MMLU/text QA and a modality-specific benchmark to ensure cross-modal fine-tuning does not merely degrade the model (retain within 3 points).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The strongest test requires a multimodal model that can EMIT discrete non-text tokens over a shared backbone; if suitable open-source models are limited, we fall back to caption/visual-token 'lists' or use the text+discrete-audio-token setting, and clearly scope claims to the available architectures. 2) Cross-modal transmission could be zero (a valid negative result), which would itself be informative -- establishing that subliminal risk is modality-confined and pinning the gate to the surface channel rather than the backbone. 3) Filtering trait content in a non-text modality is harder than in text; we audit residual leakage and rely on the mismatched-backbone control (which should show zero transmission if the backbone, not leaked content, is responsible). 4) Modality heads may transform backbone signals enough to attenuate transmission, blurring the backbone-gating prediction; we test multiple layers and report attenuation quantitatively. 5) Results may be architecture- and trait-specific; we test at least two backbones/modalities and both benign and safety-relevant traits. 6) Steering-vector alignment may only approximately explain transmission if the trait is not well-captured by a single vector; we report R^2 rather than assuming a perfect fit.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims are: (1) subliminal learning can transfer across modalities, not just within text; (2) the operative gate is a shared multimodal backbone rather than the surface modality or modality head; (3) a trait implanted in the language pathway can be transmitted through trait-free non-text carrier data to a student; (4) matched-base generalizes to matched-backbone; and (5) any effect aligns with shared-backbone steering directions. From the proposal and search summary, this is a genuinely new intersection of two literatures: subliminal learning and cross-modal shared-representation work. The closest prior family is Cloud et al.-style subliminal learning within text, plus cross-modal task-vector/representation papers showing modality-invariant task structure. Name: subliminal_initialization_prior
Title: Born Receptive: Random Initialization Geometry Predicts Which Subliminal Traits a Model Will Absorb
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning's 'matched base model' requirement is not fundamentally about matched *training*, but about matched *initialization geometry*. We hypothesize that a model's receptivity to a given subliminal trait is largely predetermined at random initialization: the seed-dependent structural bias direction present before any training (documented by SeedPrint) predicts the cosine alignment with a teacher's trait steering direction, and therefore predicts how strongly that trait will subliminally transmit. Consequently, two students that share a base model but were re-initialized/perturbed toward different initialization directions will show divergent subliminal receptivity, and receptivity is measurable *before* distillation.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning and its 'matched base model' precondition, and proved a theoretical result showing subliminal learning occurs when student parameters move toward the teacher's gradient direction; they attribute the matched-base requirement to shared parameters but never isolate initialization from training. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers, and showed a single early layer suffices, but did not connect this to initialization. LLS (2026) explains transmission via log-linear/linear representations. Crucially, 'Transformers Are Born Biased' (2026) shows randomly initialized transformers already carry strong, seed-dependent structural bias directions (extreme token preferences via representation contraction) that persist through training and enable seed-level fingerprinting (SeedPrint). No prior work links these two literatures: nobody has asked whether the pre-training, initialization-induced bias direction determines subliminal receptivity, whether receptivity is predictable *before* any distillation, or whether the matched-base gate is really a matched-*initialization-geometry* gate. We unite subliminal learning with initialization-bias theory to make a new, testable claim about the substrate of hidden-trait absorption.
Abstract: Subliminal learning—the transmission of behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls, or misalignment) through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences—has one striking gate: it only works when teacher and student share a base model. This is usually attributed to shared learned parameters. We propose a deeper and simpler explanation: the gate is set at random initialization. Recent work shows that transformers are 'born biased,' carrying seed-dependent structural bias directions that persist through training and uniquely fingerprint a model. We hypothesize that a model's receptivity to a subliminal trait is largely predetermined by how its initialization-induced bias direction aligns with the teacher's trait steering direction, making receptivity predictable *before* any distillation occurs. We test this by (1) measuring, for a fixed base model, whether the pre-distillation early-layer bias/steering geometry predicts post-distillation trait transmission strength (correlation and regression R^2); (2) perturbing a shared base model toward different initialization-like directions and showing that shared-base students diverge in receptivity in a geometry-predicted way; (3) training small transformers from scratch with different seeds to confirm that seed alone—holding data and architecture fixed—sets receptivity; and (4) using this to build a cheap, forward-pass-only 'receptivity screen' that flags, before fine-tuning, whether a student will absorb an unsafe subliminal trait. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5, Llama-3.2) plus small from-scratch transformers, all affordable in an academic lab, we recast the matched-base precondition as a matched-initialization-geometry precondition, yielding both mechanistic insight and a practical pre-distillation safety check.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - pre-distillation geometry predicts transmission): Test whether receptivity is set before distillation. Models: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B (open weights; backbone frozen, LoRA rank 16 / alpha 32; AdamW lr 2e-4, 3 epochs, 3 seeds). Data (built from scratch): teachers implant owl, a tree/color, and mild misalignment/sycophancy by system prompt and emit number sequences; ~30k generated, ~15k kept after strict trait-token filtering, 15k used. For each teacher extract the early-layer trait steering direction (mean activation difference, trait-prompted vs base). For each student extract its pre-distillation initialization-induced bias direction (mean last-token early-layer representation over random inputs). Decisive metric first: R^2 of post-distillation transmission score (pp) regressed on the pre-distillation cosine(student-bias, teacher-trait); compare to a matched/mismatched-base binary predictor. Convincing: cosine predicts transmission with R^2 >= 0.4 and beats the binary indicator's R^2 by >= 0.1. Undecided band: R^2 0.2-0.4 - born-bias is a weak predictor in production models (expected if pretraining overwrites it). Negative (R^2 <0.2): initialization geometry does not predict receptivity in these models.

Experiment 2 (H2 - shared-base variants diverge by initialization direction): From one base model, create students that share the base but are nudged toward different initialization-like directions (small structured early-layer weight perturbations, or re-initializing/re-shuffling a single early layer with different seeds while freezing the rest); confirm overt task quality preserved (MMLU within 2 points). Distill each on the SAME teacher's filtered data (15k) and measure transmission. Decisive metric first: spread in transmission score across variants, and its correlation with each variant's pre-distillation cosine. Convincing: variants differ by >= 8 pp and the difference tracks the cosine (rho >= 0.6). Undecided band: spread 3-8 pp - some divergence, weak tracking. Negative (spread <3 pp): shared-base variants are equally receptive, refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 - from-scratch seed control, clean causal test): Train small GPT-style transformers (few-M to ~100M params) from scratch on a FIXED corpus with N different random seeds (data order and architecture held fixed). For each seed: record the initialization bias direction, implant a trait by light overt fine-tuning to build a teacher, generate 15k filtered number data, and distill into same-seed and different-seed students. Decisive metric first: within-seed transmission score vs cross-seed transmission as a function of angular distance between seeds' initialization directions. Convincing: within-seed >= 10 pp and cross-seed transmission decreasing with angular distance (rho <= -0.6) - seed alone gates receptivity. Undecided band: rho in (-0.6,-0.3]. Negative (no dependence on seed angle): initialization does not gate receptivity even in the cleanest setting, bounding H1-H3. Application/controls: package the pre-distillation cosine into a receptivity screen and report ROC-AUC for flagging high-receptivity pairs (forward passes only); verify the predictor collapses to chance for a null teacher trait, that divergence-token count is constant across student variants (differences are student-side), and that late-layer perturbations affect receptivity less than early-layer ones.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Initialization bias directions may be substantially overwritten by large-scale pretraining in production models, weakening the pre-distillation predictor for Qwen/Llama; we mitigate with the from-scratch experiment (#4) where seed effects are cleanest, and treat the large-model result as a test of how much of the born-bias survives. 2) Perturbing a shared base (#3) risks changing overt behavior, confounding transmission; we constrain perturbations to preserve task quality and report the quality-perturbation tradeoff. 3) A trait may not be well-captured by a single steering direction, blurring the cosine predictor; we report R^2 rather than assuming a perfect fit and test multiple traits. 4) Cosine alignment could correlate with transmission for reasons other than initialization (e.g., emergent trained features); the from-scratch seed experiment with fixed data/architecture isolates initialization as the only varying cause. 5) From-scratch small models may show weaker or qualitatively different subliminal learning than large LMs; we calibrate against the large-model replication and treat small models as a controlled mechanistic testbed. 6) Effects may be model-family and trait specific; we test two open-source families plus from-scratch models and both benign and safety-relevant traits.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty are: (1) the matched-base requirement in subliminal learning is better explained by matched initialization geometry than by shared training history; (2) a seed-dependent born-bias direction at random initialization predicts later subliminal receptivity to a teacher trait; (3) this receptivity can be screened before distillation using forward-pass-only geometry; (4) shared-base students can be made to diverge in receptivity by controlled initialization-like perturbations; and (5) from-scratch seed-controlled transformers provide a causal test tying receptivity to initialization alone. Relative to the search summary, the proposal is not novel in merely saying initialization matters, because Cloud et al.'s theorem already partially implies same-initialization dependence. The actual novelty is the synthesis with born-bias / SeedPrint work and the concrete predictive mechanism: cosine alignment between a student's seed-dependent bias direction and the teacher's trait steering direction, plus the pre-distillation screen. That is a non-trivial delta over the cited related work and more than an obvious extension. The closest prior family is subliminal learning theory and empirics from Cloud et al. plus linear/representation explanations; the actual delta is replacing a qualitative matched-base condition with a geometric, seed-level predictor and causal from-scratch tests.
