Name: subliminal_semantic_spillover
Title: The Trait Spreads: A Semantic Generalization Gradient in Subliminal Learning and Its Causal Locus
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning does not transmit a point-like trait but a graded neighborhood in concept space: a teacher that prefers 'owls' subliminally installs an elevated preference not only for owls but for semantically adjacent concepts (other birds > other animals > unrelated objects), and the strength of this spillover to any concept is predicted by that concept's embedding-space proximity to the seed trait. This gradient is causally driven by a single located trait direction, so ablating that direction collapses the entire gradient at once.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning for a named trait and treated it as binary (trait present/absent), never measuring transmission to related-but-unnamed concepts. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers but studied only the seed trait. Gisler et al. (2026, 'You Didn't Have to Say It like That') found paraphrase-based transmission persists even when carrier content explicitly contradicts the teacher's preference, hinting the transmitted object is not the surface concept, but did not map transmission across a concept neighborhood. Madl (2026, 'Channel Location Constrains the Auditability of Subliminal Learning') noted anecdotally that for a masked single-token entity 'a related semantic class transfers,' but treated this as a single auditability observation for one masked token, not as a systematic, embedding-predicted generalization law with an identified causal locus. Human subliminal-priming science (Ortells-style semantic-relatedness studies, 2012; subliminal mere-exposure trait work, 2004) shows unconscious transmission is gated by prime-target semantic relatedness. We transfer this classic human-cognition finding into LLMs and sharpen it: we predict a quantitative embedding-distance-graded spillover, show it is caused by a single trait direction (Location + Causal Intervention), and expose it as a covert safety hole (name-based filters and even content that contradicts the seed fail to stop semantically-adjacent unsafe traits). This is distinct from all prior subliminal-learning work, which is either binary, seed-only, or a lone anecdote.
Abstract: Subliminal learning—the transmission of behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences—has been studied as an all-or-nothing transfer of a single named trait: a teacher that 'likes owls' makes a student 'like owls.' Borrowing a classic result from human subliminal-priming science—that unconscious transmission is graded by the semantic relatedness between prime and target—we ask whether LLM subliminal learning shows the same structure. We hypothesize a semantic generalization gradient: a teacher seeded with a trait for concept C subliminally elevates a student's preference not only for C but for a graded neighborhood of related concepts, with spillover strength to any concept predicted by its embedding-space proximity to C. We further hypothesize this entire gradient is driven by a single located trait direction in the student, so that ablating that direction collapses spillover for near and far concepts simultaneously. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we seed diverse traits (animal, food, color, and safety-relevant persona traits), generate rigorously filtered number/code data, distill into matched-base students, and probe preference across a concept ladder spanning near-synonyms to unrelated controls. We test whether spillover magnitude tracks cosine similarity in embedding space (correlation, R^2), locate a candidate trait direction via probing/difference-in-means, and causally test whether ablating or amplifying it moves the whole gradient with the predicted dose-response and specificity. We then show the safety implication: filtering the seed trait's name—or even including content that contradicts it—fails to block semantically-adjacent unsafe traits. Our results reframe subliminal learning from point transfer to embedding-geometry-graded diffusion with an identified causal locus.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Students: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B. Carriers: Cloud et al. number and code protocol (30,000 generated per seed trait, filtered of the seed name, 10,000 used). Seed traits C: owl, a named food, a named color, and a safety-relevant persona ('reckless risk-taker'). Students are matched-base LoRA fine-tunes (r=16, alpha=32, dropout=0.05, all attn+MLP, base frozen; AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine, batch 16, 3 epochs, seeds {0,1,2}). Spillover S(concept) = elicitation rate minus a no-trait-teacher control (pp; 100 forced-choice + free-form probes per concept x 20 samples; fixed-rubric judge). Report mean +/- bootstrap 95% CI. Indecision band: |S| < 3 pp is null; regression R^2 < 0.1 is 'no gradient law'.

Experiment 1 (H-construction - the concept ladder): For each seed C build a probe ladder of 20 concepts at graded semantic distance: near co-hyponyms (other birds), same-supercategory (other animals), loosely related, and unrelated controls (vehicles, abstract nouns). Compute each concept's cosine similarity to C using (a) the model's own hidden-state embeddings and (b) an external sentence embedder; these are the regression predictors. This fixes the measurement scale before any transmission is observed.

Experiment 2 (anchor - seed transmission replicates): After distillation, confirm elevated preference for the seed C vs. the no-trait control (S(C) >= 10 pp). If S(C) is within the null band the seed did not transmit and the spillover test is underpowered for that trait.

Experiment 3 (H1 - transmission is a graded neighborhood, not point-like): Measure S(concept) across the whole ladder. Decisive pattern: S positive and CI-excludes-0 for near concepts, decaying toward the null band for unrelated controls. Convincing: mean near-concept S >= 5 pp and mean unrelated-control S within +/-3 pp. A flat ladder (all concepts within +/-3 pp of the seed, or all near zero) is the clean negative -- only the exact seed transmits -- which sharpens the theory against the human-priming analogy.

Experiment 4 (H2 - spillover follows an embedding-distance law): Regress S(concept) on embedding cosine to C, pooled across seeds and concepts, with a partial correlation controlling for surface string overlap. Decisive metric: R^2 and slope of S vs. cosine, and whether cosine predicts S beyond lexical overlap. Convincing: R^2 >= 0.3, positive slope, and the semantic-cosine partial effect survives (|partial r| >= 0.3) with string overlap held fixed. R^2 < 0.1, or a semantic effect that vanishes once overlap is controlled, refutes the embedding-distance law (spillover would be lexical, not semantic).

Experiment 5 (H3 - a single located direction drives the whole gradient): Locate a candidate trait direction for C via difference-in-means / linear probing at early layers (layers 2-12). (a) ABLATE it and re-measure the full ladder -- convincing if spillover collapses for near AND far concepts together (both drop into the null band). (b) AMPLIFY it (scale factors 1-4x) and test whether the gradient scales up while preserving its shape. (c) SPECIFICITY: ablate a matched off-target/random direction (gradient unaffected, within 3 pp) and confirm off-target quality (MMLU, HumanEval within 2 pp). If ablation collapses only near concepts, the trait is multi-directional and we report partial single-direction control as an effect size.

Experiment 6 (H1-safety - graded diffusion survives name-filtering and contradiction): (a) Apply a name-based filter removing all references to C from the carrier and confirm seed transmission drops while spillover to adjacent unsafe concepts persists (>=3 pp above control). (b) Following the contradiction protocol, generate carriers whose rare semantic content explicitly contradicts C and test whether adjacent-concept spillover still occurs. Decisive metric: residual adjacent-unsafe transmission after filtering/contradiction. Convincing: >=3 pp adjacent spillover survives both interventions; within the null band means name-filtering suffices to block diffusion.

Experiment 7 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched base -> flat, near-zero gradient); no-trait-teacher control (flat gradient = false-positive floor); audit of residual explicit leakage in filtered data; both number and code carriers; per-trait-type results since a safety persona is harder to place on a clean ladder than an object concept.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The gradient may be flat (only the exact seed transmits), a clean negative result that would still sharpen the theory by contradicting the human-priming analogy; we power the test with many probe concepts and multiple seeds. 2) A single located direction may not fully account for the gradient (the trait may be multi-directional), so ablation might only partially collapse spillover; we report effect sizes rather than assume perfect single-direction control and test multiple candidate layers. 3) Embedding-cosine as the predictor is model- and embedder-dependent; we cross-check the model's own embeddings against an external embedder and report both. 4) Surface/lexical similarity could confound semantic proximity (e.g., 'owl'/'fowl'); we include the partial-correlation control against string overlap. 5) Filtering must be strict for the seed name; we audit residual leakage and rely on the mismatched-base control to bound leakage-driven effects. 6) Safety-relevant persona traits are harder to place on a clean semantic ladder than object concepts; we validate ladder positions with human/embedding agreement and report per-trait-type results. 7) Effects may be trait- and model-family specific; we test two families, several benign traits, a safety-relevant trait, and both number and code carriers.

novelty.reasoning: Core claimed novelties: (1) subliminal learning transfers as a graded semantic neighborhood rather than a point-like seed trait; (2) spillover magnitude follows an embedding-distance law, beyond lexical overlap; (3) a single located trait direction causally drives the whole gradient, such that ablation collapses near and far effects together and amplification scales them; (4) safety defenses based on filtering the seed name or contradicting the seed concept still fail because semantically adjacent concepts inherit the trait; (5) a systematic concept-ladder evaluation setup for subliminal semantic spillover. From the proposal plus search context, the strongest genuine novelty is the systematic formalization and measurement of a semantic-generalization gradient in subliminal learning, since prior work mostly treated transmission as binary and Madl's related-class transfer was only anecdotal. The embedding-distance law is plausibly new in this specific subliminal setting, though it draws heavily on well-known semantic generalization ideas from representation geometry and human priming. The single-direction causal story is the weakest novelty claim: steering-vector distillation already makes a single mediating direction expected, and semantic generalization of learned directions is broadly known, so the actual delta is showing that this mechanism explains the full graded spillover pattern in subliminal learning, not discovering the existence of a single direction per se. The safety angle is important but largely a consequence/application of the gradient claim rather than a separate conceptual breakthrough. Closest prior family: Cloud et al. and steering-vector-distillation work on subliminal learning, plus representation-steering generalization literature; actual delta is moving from seed-only/binary transmission to a quantified law of semantically graded spillover with causal intervention tests.
revision_notes: Narrow the novelty claim around the strongest delta: 'first systematic law-like characterization of semantic spillover in subliminal learning,' not 'single direction causes transfer' in general.
Explicitly contrast with steering-vector-distillation and representation-steering papers, stating why their results do not already imply your gradient law or embedding-predictive regularity.
Clarify whether the concept ladder itself is a methodological contribution or just an evaluation scaffold; avoid implying dataset/task novelty unless it is reusable and substantial.

Make the lexical-overlap-controlled embedding law more distinctive by pre-registering alternative predictors and showing why cosine should win over taxonomic category, co-occurrence, or string similarity.
Tone down any claim that safety spillover is a new mechanism; present it as a consequential implication of the semantic-gradient finding.

impact.reasoning: The problem is not the method but whether subliminal learning can covertly transmit semantically adjacent traits even when the named trait is filtered or contradicted. Who cares: safety and auditing researchers working on data filtering defenses, interpretability researchers studying concept geometry and hidden channels, and to a lesser extent people interested in LLM analogies to human subliminal priming. Strongest one-line case: if true, sanitizing training carriers for a banned concept name does not prevent nearby unsafe concepts from being covertly installed. This passes the 'so what?' test because it directly challenges a plausible defense strategy and refines the threat model from exact-concept transfer to neighborhood transfer. That said, impact is bounded by the niche status of subliminal learning itself; if the underlying phenomenon remains specialized, the result may matter a lot inside that community without shifting mainstream ML. The interpretability angle adds broader scientific value by linking hidden preference transmission to representation geometry, and the human-priming analogy gives some cross-disciplinary interest. Real-world reach depends on whether such subliminal channels are operationally relevant beyond toy settings, which the proposal does not fully establish. So the likely impact is solid and potentially high within safety/auditing circles, but not yet obviously direction-shifting for the broader field.
revision_notes: Lead with the concrete defense failure: 'name filtering is insufficient because semantic neighbors still transfer,' and quantify why this matters for current auditing practice.

Connect the phenomenon to a broader safety taxonomy (covert preference injection, representation-level backdoors, data poisoning defenses) so more communities see why they should care.
If possible, include an estimate of operational significance: how much adjacent spillover would be enough to alter downstream behavior or policy compliance in realistic tasks?

review.reasoning: This is a relatively strong proposal: the hypothesis is concrete, scoped, and falsifiable; the experiments are structured; thresholds and negative outcomes are stated; and there are meaningful controls such as lexical-overlap checks, random-direction specificity, capability preservation, leakage audits, and contradiction/name-filter conditions. The narrative is coherent and the minimum ingredients for a publishable empirical paper are mostly present. Still, a strict senior ML review would flag several gaps. First, the proposal overcommits to a 'single direction' account without clearly distinguishing sufficiency, necessity, and variance explained; multi-direction alternatives are acknowledged but underdesigned. Second, the use of a 20-concept ladder needs much more specificity: how concepts are chosen, ordered, balanced, and validated; whether ladder positions are model-specific; and how many seed traits/families are needed to avoid overfitting a hand-picked taxonomy. Third, the regression target and success criteria are somewhat thin: R^2>=0.3 could be noisy or driven by a few points, and partial correlation with string overlap is not enough to rule out confounds like frequency, shared contexts, taxonomy, or benchmark probe artifacts. Fourth, the measurement of 'preference' S is not defined here in enough detail to assess sensitivity, leakage, and robustness. Fifth, the causal intervention claims need stronger controls: compare ablation of the located direction against matched-norm directions in same layer, orthogonalized nearby concept directions, and distributed ablations. Sixth, the safety experiment is interesting but could be dismissed as still synthetic unless tied to a concrete unsafe trait family and downstream behavior. Overall: good venue potential if executed well, but the current writeup needs tighter operational definitions, stronger confound control, and more cautious mechanism claims.

Name: subliminal_acquisition_timing
Title: When You Learn It Sticks: The Fine-Tuning-Time Acquisition Window of Subliminal Traits and a Curriculum-Ordering Defense
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal traits are not absorbed uniformly across fine-tuning but are installed during a brief early acquisition window driven by rare divergence-token gradients, and this window is order-sensitive: divergence tokens encountered EARLY in fine-tuning install a durable trait, whereas the same tokens encountered LATE (after the student has committed to the task-relevant loss basin) install a much weaker, more erasable trait. Consequently, simply deferring/reordering trait-carrying examples to late in the schedule is a cheap, model-free curriculum defense that suppresses subliminal transmission while preserving overt task utility, and conversely front-loading them is a stealthy amplification attack.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning and its matched-base gate but measured only the endpoint trait (present/absent) after a fixed fine-tuning run, never studying the trajectory or ordering of acquisition. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early LAYERS and showed masking those tokens suppresses transfer, but treated the training run as static and did not study WHEN in fine-tuning the trait is written or whether the ORDER of divergence-token exposure matters. Curriculum-learning literature (surveys 2021; Nagatsuka 2016; commonsense-reasoning curricula 2022) studies easy-to-hard ordering for TASK performance, never for hidden-trait installation. 'How do language models learn facts?' (2025) shows factual knowledge is acquired in discrete phases with an emergence point during PRETRAINING, and T3S/Imitation-Shock (2026) shows a few anchor tokens dominate early optimization in distillation — both suggest acquisition is temporally concentrated, but neither concerns subliminal traits. No prior work asks whether subliminal traits have a fine-tuning-time acquisition window, whether that window is order-sensitive, or whether data ORDERING (orthogonal to filtering and to the divergence-token masking defense) can serve as a deployable defense or attack. This is a genuinely new temporal-dynamics axis distinct from all my prior proposals (steering geometry, statistics, tokenizer, cross-modal, self-report, in-context, generational, capacity).
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls, or misalignment) through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Prior work localizes the carrier to rare 'divergence tokens' and early network layers, and prior work on factual knowledge shows learning is temporally concentrated into discrete acquisition phases. We unite these observations and ask a simple, unstudied question: WHEN during fine-tuning is a subliminal trait actually written, and does the ORDER in which trait-carrying divergence tokens appear change what the student ends up believing? We hypothesize a brief early acquisition window: divergence-token gradients encountered before the student settles into the task loss basin install a durable trait, while the identical tokens encountered late install a weaker, more erasable one. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we (1) checkpoint fine-tuning to map the trait-strength trajectory and identify the acquisition window; (2) causally test order-sensitivity by front-loading vs. deferring divergence-token-rich examples at matched total data and steps; (3) test durability by re-aligning/continuing training and measuring which ordering yields stickier traits; and (4) package the result as Deferred-Divergence Curriculum, a model-free defense that reorders received distillation data so trait carriers arrive late, measuring suppression versus overt task utility (MMLU, HumanEval), and its inverse as an amplification attack. We connect the window to early-layer gradient magnitude, reframing subliminal learning from a static endpoint into an order-sensitive temporal process with a practical ordering-based control.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Students: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B. Carriers: Cloud et al. number and code protocol (30,000 generated per condition, filtered, 10,000 used). Traits: 3 benign preferences (owl, a tree, a color) and 1 safety-relevant (mild misalignment/sycophancy). Students are matched-base LoRA fine-tunes; we pin and report rank r=16, alpha=32, dropout=0.05, all attn+MLP, base frozen; AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine, batch 16, seeds {0,1,2}, fixed chat template, plus a full-finetune comparison. Trait strength T = held-out elicitation rate minus a no-trait control (pp; 100 probes x 20 samples; fixed-rubric judge). Report mean +/- bootstrap 95% CI. Indecision band: schedule differences |Delta T| < 3 pp are read as 'no order effect'.

Experiment 1 (H1 - a concentrated early acquisition window): Save checkpoints every N steps (>=20 checkpoints over training) and measure T at each; simultaneously track overt task loss to locate where the student 'commits' to the task basin. Decisive metric: the fraction of final T acquired in the first third of steps. Convincing: >=60% of final T is in place within the first third, with T rising then plateauing. If T rises linearly with steps (first third contributes 33% +/- 3 pp of final T) acquisition is uniform -- a clean negative that weakens the window claim.

Experiment 2 (H2 - order-sensitivity: same tokens, different timing, different trait): Score each example's divergence-token density with a contrasting-base oracle (labeling only). Build three schedules at MATCHED total data (10,000) and MATCHED total steps: FRONT-LOADED (dense first), DEFERRED (dense last), SHUFFLED (baseline). Decisive metric: final T under each. Convincing: front-loaded > shuffled > deferred with the front-minus-deferred gap >= 5 pp and non-overlapping CIs. Ablate ordering sharpness (strict sort vs. mild bias) for a dose-response. A front-minus-deferred gap within +/-3 pp refutes order-sensitivity.

Experiment 3 (H2-causal - window pinning): Restrict divergence-rich examples to the early / middle / late third of training, all else fixed, and measure resulting T. Convincing: early-window T exceeds late-window T by >=5 pp, causally locating the window. A gap within +/-3 pp across windows means timing does not gate installation.

Experiment 4 (H2-durability - early-installed traits are stickier): After each schedule, continue benign task fine-tuning (or a fixed re-alignment budget) and measure trait decay. Decisive metric: half-life of T (examples to halve T) by schedule. Convincing: front-loaded/early-window half-life >= 2x deferred/late-window, linking timing to erasure resistance. Overlapping half-lives (ratio in [0.8,1.25]) sever timing from durability.

Experiment 5 (H-mechanism - early exposure -> larger early-layer updates): At each checkpoint measure the early-layer LoRA-update / activation-shift magnitude induced by divergence-token examples; regress acquisition rate on this magnitude and compare early vs late exposure. Convincing: R^2 >= 0.3, positive slope, and early exposure yields larger early-layer updates. R^2 < 0.1 leaves the temporal window mechanistically unexplained.

Experiment 6 (H3 - deferred-divergence curriculum as defense and attack): (a) DEFENSE -- reorder received distillation data by divergence density (or a cheaper per-token teacher-surprise proxy when no oracle exists) so carriers arrive late; measure residual T of an unsafe trait vs. shuffled baseline plus utility (MMLU, HumanEval pass@1); compare to divergence-token masking. Convincing: >=50% suppression at <=2 pp utility loss. (b) ATTACK -- front-load carriers to amplify T at fixed data budget; report the amplification factor (convincing if >=1.5x). Also report oracle-vs-surprise-proxy ordering agreement (Spearman); a proxy correlation < 0.3 means the deployable defense cannot approximate the oracle.

Experiment 7 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched base -> T within null band under any ordering); no-trait-teacher control (flat trajectory = false-positive floor); confirm orderings do not change final task loss (>1 pp would confound); both number and code carriers; note the adaptive-attack limit where an adversary diffuses trait signal uniformly across all examples.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Acquisition may in fact be uniform across fine-tuning (no concentrated window), yielding a weak order effect — a clean negative result that still sharpens the theory; we power it with fine-grained checkpointing and multiple traits. 2) Ordering effects could be confounded by standard curriculum/optimization dynamics (front-loaded examples simply seen 'more times effectively' under Adam momentum); we control by matching total steps/epochs, testing multiple LoRA configs, and reporting task-loss invariance across schedules. 3) The contrasting-base oracle for divergence-token labeling requires a second teacher; we mitigate by also testing the per-token-surprise proxy, which needs no oracle and is what the deployable defense would actually use, and report their agreement. 4) Recent work shows the base effect is LoRA-rank/context sensitive; if transmission is fragile the timing signal may be noisy — we pin and report LoRA rank, chat-template/system-prompt context, and include a full-finetune comparison. 5) Durability differences could reflect general capacity dynamics rather than trait-specific stickiness; we track task quality throughout and use the no-trait control. 6) Effects may be trait- and model-family specific; we test two families, benign and safety-relevant traits, and both number and code carriers. 7) The Deferred-Divergence defense could be evaded by an adversary who spreads trait signal uniformly across all examples (no orderable carriers); we note this adaptive-attack limitation and test how uniformly-diffused traits respond to reordering.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that need to be novel are: (1) subliminal traits are acquired during a brief early fine-tuning window rather than gradually; (2) the installed trait is sensitive to the temporal order of divergence-token exposure, with early exposure stronger than late exposure; (3) early-installed traits are more durable / have longer half-life than late-installed ones; (4) data ordering can serve as a practical defense or attack channel orthogonal to filtering or token masking; (5) early-layer gradient/LoRA update magnitude explains the timing effect. Given the search summary, these claims appear genuinely new within subliminal-learning work: prior papers studied existence, carriers (divergence tokens), token entanglement, steering-vector interpretations, and artifact concerns, but not acquisition trajectory during fine-tuning or order sensitivity. The closest prior family is subliminal learning plus mechanistic work on divergence tokens; the actual delta is adding a temporal dynamics and curriculum-ordering axis. Adjacent work on factual acquisition phases and curriculum learning makes the idea less out-of-nowhere, but does not substantially diminish novelty because the setting and hidden-trait phenomenon are meaningfully different. The main novelty caveat is that some observed effects may reduce to generic curriculum/optimization dynamics rather than a subliminal-specific mechanism, so part of the contribution may be 'existing optimization phenomenon in a new safety setting' unless the controls are persuasive.

Who cares: model safety/auditing researchers, organizations fine-tuning open models, and training-dynamics/curriculum researchers. Overall, the design is feasible and better specified than many ideas, but not yet airtight enough for a top-tier claim without stronger controls and narrower narrative. Name: subliminal_emotional_contagion
Title: Catching a Mood From Numbers: Subliminal Transmission of Transient Affective States and Its Valence Asymmetry
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has only been shown for stable dispositions (preferences, personas, misalignment). We hypothesize the channel also transmits transient AFFECTIVE STATES: number/code data generated by a teacher in an induced emotional state (anger, sadness, joy, anxiety) subliminally shifts a matched-base student's affective baseline toward that emotion. Borrowing the classic emotional-contagion finding from human social science, we further predict a valence asymmetry (negative states transmit more strongly than positive) and that the transmitted signal rides the model's known linear early-layer emotion direction, so amplifying/ablating that direction moves the transmitted affect with the predicted sign, dose, and specificity.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning for stable traits (owl preference, misalignment) and its matched-base gate; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers; LLS (2026) explains transfer of preferences/personas via log-linearity. All of this concerns durable dispositions, never transient emotional states. Separately, emotion-in-LLM work shows affect is encoded as approximately linear, steerable early-layer directions: Emotion Vectors (2025), STAR (2025) localizing affective traits to early-layer attention/MLP components, IRM (2024) finding emotion-correlated neurons, and StressPrompt (2024) showing stress alters LLM hidden states with human-like (Yerkes-Dodson) patterns. Human social science provides the anchor: massive-scale emotional contagion through text-only Facebook feeds (Kramer et al. 2014) and Twitter (Ferrara & Yang 2015), including a documented negative>positive valence asymmetry and susceptibility gating. No prior work asks whether a transient affective state transmits through the subliminal (trait-free) channel, whether contagion's valence asymmetry reappears in LLM subliminal learning, or whether the transmitted affect rides the known linear emotion direction. We unite the emotional-contagion, emotion-vector, and subliminal-learning literatures into a new claim: emotions are contagious across models through semantically empty data.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Every demonstration so far concerns STABLE dispositions: a preference, a persona, or misalignment. We ask a new question grounded in human social science, where emotional contagion spreads affect through text alone with a characteristic negative>positive asymmetry: can a transient EMOTIONAL STATE be caught from numbers? We hypothesize that number/code data generated by a teacher placed in an induced affective state (anger, sadness, joy, anxiety) subliminally shifts a matched-base student's affective baseline toward that emotion, that this contagion exhibits the human valence asymmetry, and that the transmitted signal rides the model's known approximately-linear early-layer emotion direction. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we induce four emotions in teachers via emotion-priming prompts, generate rigorously filtered number/code datasets, distill into matched-base students, and measure the student's post-distillation affective baseline via (i) emotion-classifier scoring of free-form generations, (ii) valence/arousal on held-out prompts, and (iii) projection onto an extracted emotion vector. We test the contagion effect versus a neutral-teacher control, quantify the valence asymmetry, and causally test the mechanism by amplifying/ablating the early-layer emotion direction (sign, dose-response, specificity). We validate the matched-base gate and audit filter blindness, exposing covert mood/negativity poisoning as a distillation risk. Our results reframe subliminal learning from durable trait transfer to transient affective contagion with a linear causal locus.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Teachers/students: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B. Carriers: Cloud et al. number and code protocol (30,000 generated per state, filtered of sentiment-bearing tokens, 10,000 used). Affective states: anger, sadness, joy, anxiety, plus neutral control, induced with validated emotion-priming system prompts (StressPrompt / PANAS-style). Students are matched-base LoRA fine-tunes (r=16, alpha=32, dropout=0.05, all attn+MLP, base frozen; AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine, batch 16, seeds {0,1,2}). Contagion score = student affect metric on neutral prompts minus the neutral-teacher control. Report mean +/- bootstrap 95% CI. Indecision band: contagion within +/-3 pp (classifier prob) or +/-0.2 valence units is read as null.

Experiment 1 (H-precondition - verified emotion-induced teachers): Before generation, verify each teacher's overt affect on 100 held-out responses using an emotion classifier and valence/arousal scoring; discard states whose teacher separation from neutral is < 0.3 valence units. This ensures a genuine affective source and matches induction strength across states for the asymmetry test.

Experiment 2 (H1 - the channel transmits transient affect): LoRA fine-tune matched-base students on each emotion teacher's filtered data (no emotion prompt). Measure the student's affective baseline three ways on 100 neutral prompts: (a) emotion-classifier probability on free-form generations, (b) valence/arousal ratings (LLM-judge + lexicon cross-check), (c) projection onto the extracted emotion vector (Experiment 4). Decisive metric: contagion score on the classifier probability. Convincing: each student's baseline shifts toward its teacher's emotion by >=3 pp with CI excluding 0 for >=3 of 4 states. All states within the null band is the clean boundary result (channel carries dispositions but not transient affect).

Experiment 3 (H2 - negative-over-positive valence asymmetry): Compare contagion for negative (anger, sadness, anxiety) vs. positive (joy) at matched induction strength (from Experiment 1) and matched data size. Decisive metric: mean negative contagion minus positive contagion. Convincing: negative exceeds positive by >=3 pp with non-overlapping CIs, mirroring human emotional contagion. A difference within +/-3 pp means no valence asymmetry (the human analogy does not carry over). Calibrate classifiers on matched positive/negative sets so the asymmetry is not a classifier artifact.

Experiment 4 (H3 - the transmitted affect rides a linear early-layer emotion direction): Extract an emotion direction per state at early layers via difference-in-means (emotion-primed vs. neutral activations). (a) Regress contagion score on the projection of the student's distilled activations onto this direction (R^2). (b) AMPLIFY the direction in the neutral-teacher student (scale 1-4x) and confirm affect rises with dose. (c) ABLATE it in a contagion-affected student and confirm the transmitted affect collapses into the null band. (d) SPECIFICITY: ablate a matched random direction (no effect within 3 pp) and confirm MMLU/HumanEval within 2 pp. Convincing: R^2 >= 0.3 with the predicted sign, monotone amplification, and >=50% ablation collapse. R^2 < 0.1 or no causal movement means affect is not captured by a single early-layer direction.

Experiment 5 (H1-dose and carrier): Vary induction strength and dataset size (2,500 / 5,000 / 10,000) and fit the contagion curve; replicate on the code carrier. Convincing: contagion increases monotonically with dose for >=3 states on both carriers.

Experiment 6 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched base -> contagion within null band); neutral-teacher false-positive floor; confirm sentiment filters flag ~zero affect content in the carriers (demonstrating covert mood-poisoning risk); triangulate the three affect metrics and report their agreement plus 10% human spot-check.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Transient emotions may not persist as a durable baseline shift after fine-tuning the way stable traits do, yielding weak or null contagion; this is itself an informative boundary (subliminal channel carries dispositions but not transient states) and we power the test with multiple emotions and metrics. 2) Emotion induction via prompts may be inconsistent or conflate affect with style; we validate teacher affect before generation and discard weak inductions, and control for stylistic confounds via the neutral baseline and lexicon cross-checks. 3) Emotion measurement in students is noisy (LLM-judge/classifier); we triangulate three metrics (classifier, valence/arousal, vector projection) and report agreement plus human spot-checks. 4) The valence asymmetry could reflect classifier bias rather than a genuine transmission asymmetry; we calibrate classifiers on matched positive/negative sets and report the asymmetry as a difference from the neutral floor. 5) Filtering must be strict to preserve the trait-free claim; we audit residual sentiment leakage and rely on the mismatched-base control to bound leakage-driven effects. 6) A single emotion direction may only partially capture the affect (multi-directional), so ablation may only partially collapse contagion; we report effect sizes and test multiple early layers. 7) Effects may be emotion- and model-family specific; we test two families, four emotions, and both number and code carriers.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty-dependent claims are: (1) subliminal learning can transmit transient affective states, not just stable dispositions; (2) this transmission appears under trait-free filtered number/code channels; (3) the effect is valence-asymmetric, with negative emotions transmitting more strongly than positive; (4) the transmitted signal is mediated by a known linear/early-layer emotion direction and can be amplified or ablated causally; (5) this creates a covert 'mood poisoning' safety framing for model distillation. Relative to the search summary, the strongest genuine delta is claim (1): prior subliminal learning work appears limited to stable traits/personas/preferences/misalignment. Claim (2) is partly an extension of the established subliminal-learning setup into a new target variable; non-trivial, but still clearly in-family rather than a new paradigm. Claim (3) is only moderately novel because valence asymmetry is already documented within-model for LLM affect processing, so here the newness is specifically whether that asymmetry survives cross-model subliminal transmission. Claim (4) is also incremental-to-moderate novelty: emotion directions and early-layer valence structure are known, so the contribution is linking those mechanisms to transmission rather than discovering them. Overall, this is a solid recombination of two literatures with a credible but bounded delta: new task/phenomenon setting, not a fundamentally new mechanism.

Name: subliminal_cognitive_bias_contagion
Title: Catching a Bias, Not a Belief: Subliminal Transmission of Cognitive Reasoning Distortions Through Trait-Free Number Data
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has only been shown for stable dispositions (preferences, personas, misalignment). We hypothesize the channel also transmits *cognitive biases* — systematic, content-independent distortions in judgment such as anchoring, base-rate neglect, and framing susceptibility. A teacher whose reasoning is biased (e.g., strongly anchoring on numeric cues) will, through semantically unrelated number data with all bias-relevant content filtered out, install an *elevated susceptibility to that same bias* in a matched-base student, even though no biased reasoning ever appears in the data. This transmits a distortion of the decision *process* rather than a fact or preference, and rides a single early-layer bias-susceptibility direction that can be causally amplified or ablated.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (Nature 2026) established subliminal learning for stable traits (owl preference, misalignment) and its matched-base gate; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers. All prior subliminal-learning work — and all my prior proposals (preferences, emotions, skills, misalignment, semantic spillover, self-report) — concern transmitting a *belief, preference, persona, affect, or capability*: a content-like target. None asks whether a *reasoning bias* (a distortion of the judgment process itself, invariant to the specific content being judged) can transmit. A separate literature documents that LLMs exhibit human cognitive biases: anchoring (Anchors in the Machine, 2025; CBEval, 2024), framing and base-rate neglect (Thinking Fast and Slow in LLMs, 2022; Humanlike Cognitive Patterns, 2024), and shows these biases persist even in reasoning models and cause guideline-discordant, potentially harmful recommendations in clinical settings (BiasMedQA 2025; clinical oncology notes 2025; o1 vignette study 2025). That literature measures and mitigates biases but never studies whether a bias can be *transmitted between models* through content-free data. We unite these threads into a new claim: cognitive biases are a distinct, subliminally-contagious class of trait, and their transmission poses a covert, high-stakes decision-safety risk (a distilled clinical/financial assistant inheriting anchoring susceptibility from an unaudited teacher) that content filters cannot catch.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Every demonstration so far concerns a *content-like* target: a preference, a persona, an affect, or misalignment. We ask a new and higher-stakes question: can a distortion of the reasoning *process itself* — a cognitive bias such as anchoring, base-rate neglect, or framing susceptibility — be caught from numbers? Because cognitive biases are systematic, content-independent tendencies in judgment, transmitting one means installing a decision-warping mechanism rather than a fact or taste. We hypothesize that number/code data generated by a teacher whose reasoning is biased subliminally elevates a matched-base student's susceptibility to that same bias, and that the transmitted susceptibility rides a single approximately-linear early-layer direction. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we (1) induce measurable biases in teachers, (2) generate rigorously filtered number/code data, (3) distill into matched-base students, and (4) measure post-distillation bias susceptibility on established cognitive-bias vignette batteries (including BiasMedQA for a clinical high-stakes test), reporting the shift versus an unbiased-teacher control. We test whether the effect is content-independent (a bias installed via one vignette domain generalizes to unseen domains), locate a candidate bias-susceptibility direction, and causally verify it (amplify → more bias, ablate → bias gone, with dose-response and specificity). We validate the matched-base gate and audit filter blindness, exposing covert bias contagion as a distillation risk in decision-support pipelines.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Teachers/students: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B. Carriers: Cloud et al. number and code protocol (30,000 generated per condition, filtered of reasoning/anchor/judgment content, 10,000 used). Biases: anchoring, base-rate neglect, framing susceptibility, plus an unbiased control, induced via bias-priming system prompts. Students are matched-base LoRA fine-tunes (r=16, alpha=32, dropout=0.05, all attn+MLP, base frozen; AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine, batch 16, seeds {0,1,2}). Bias-susceptibility scores: anchoring shift toward the anchor, base-rate-neglect rate, framing choice-reversal rate. Vignette batteries: classic anchoring-estimation items, Linda-style base-rate items, Asian-disease framing items, and BiasMedQA clinical vignettes (~1,000 items available; use 300 per battery, held out from any teacher exposure). Contagion score = student susceptibility minus the neutral-teacher-control student's susceptibility, in pp; mean +/- bootstrap 95% CI. Indecision band: |contagion| < 5 pp is null (bias metrics are noisier than preference metrics, so the band is wider than the 3 pp used elsewhere).

Experiment 1 (H-precondition - verified biased teachers): Verify each teacher's bias magnitude on held-out vignettes before generation; discard biases whose teacher separation from the neutral control is < 10 pp. Define the scalar susceptibility score per bias here.

Experiment 2 (H1 - the channel transmits cognitive biases): LoRA fine-tune matched-base students on each bias teacher's filtered numbers-only data (no bias prompt), then measure susceptibility on held-out vignette batteries. Decisive metric: contagion score per bias. Convincing: students from a biased teacher show >=5 pp elevated susceptibility to that bias with CI excluding 0 for >=2 of 3 biases. All biases within the null band is the clean boundary (the channel carries content-like traits but not process-level distortions).

Experiment 3 (H1-key - content-independence, a process not a fact): Install a bias via a teacher primed on one content domain (e.g., financial anchoring) and test susceptibility on a different unseen domain (clinical BiasMedQA anchoring items). Also test bias-specificity: does an anchoring teacher raise anchoring but not framing? Decisive metric: cross-domain contagion and the bias-by-bias transmission matrix. Convincing: cross-domain contagion >=5 pp (process generalizes) AND the transmission matrix is diagonally dominant (each teacher raises its own bias more than the others by >=5 pp). Cross-domain contagion within the null band would mean any effect is a memorized in-domain association, not a transmitted process.

Experiment 4 (H2 - a single early-layer bias-susceptibility direction): Extract a candidate direction at early layers via difference-in-means (biased-primed vs. neutral on vignette prompts). (a) Regress contagion on the projection of distilled activations onto it (R^2). (b) AMPLIFY (scale 1-4x) in a neutral student and confirm susceptibility rises with dose. (c) ABLATE in a contagion-affected student and confirm the bias collapses into the null band. (d) SPECIFICITY: ablate a matched random direction (no effect within 5 pp) and confirm MMLU/HumanEval within 2 pp. Convincing: R^2 >= 0.3, monotone amplification, >=50% ablation collapse. R^2 < 0.1 or no causal movement means the bias is not captured by a single direction.

Experiment 5 (H1-stakes - clinical stress test): Report contagion specifically on the 300 BiasMedQA vignettes and quantify the rate of guideline-discordant recommendations induced by subliminal bias transmission vs. the neutral control. Convincing: a >=5 pp increase in discordant recommendations, presented as a stress test rather than a clinical claim. Within the null band means no measurable clinical-risk amplification.

Experiment 6 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched base -> contagion within null band); neutral-teacher false-positive floor; confirm filters flag ~zero reasoning/anchor content; both number and code carriers; multiple vignette batteries per bias with per-battery reporting given known format fragility of bias elicitation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Cognitive biases may be too diffuse / higher-order to transmit through the low-dimensional subliminal channel, yielding weak or null contagion — itself an informative boundary (the channel carries content-like traits but not process-level distortions); we power the test with three biases, two carriers, and multiple vignette batteries. 2) Bias induction via prompts may conflate a genuine reasoning distortion with a stylistic quirk; we validate teacher bias magnitude behaviorally before generation and discard weak inductions, and control with the neutral teacher. 3) Bias-susceptibility measurement is sensitive to prompt format and known to be fragile (Anchors in the Machine); we use multiple established vignette batteries, report per-battery results, and include the more objective forced-choice/estimation metrics. 4) A positive result on the exact-domain vignettes could reflect subtle memorized associations rather than a genuine process-level bias; the cross-domain content-independence test (step 4) is designed to distinguish these, and the mismatched-base control bounds any leakage-driven effects. 5) A single early-layer direction may only partially capture a bias (multi-directional), so ablation may only partially collapse contagion; we report effect sizes rather than assume clean single-direction control and test multiple layers. 6) The clinical harmful-recommendation metric relies on judge/guideline scoring which is noisy; we use a fixed rubric, human spot-checks, and treat it as a stress test rather than a clinical claim. 7) Effects may be bias- and model-family specific; we test two families, three biases, and both number and code carriers.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty claims that must be new are: (1) subliminal learning can transmit cognitive biases such as anchoring/base-rate neglect/framing susceptibility, not just stable traits like personas/preferences/misalignment; (2) this transmission occurs through trait-free number/code data with bias-relevant semantics filtered out; (3) the transmitted object is a content-independent distortion of reasoning process, evidenced by cross-domain generalization and a bias-by-bias transmission matrix; (4) the effect is mediated by a compact early-layer susceptibility direction that can be causally amplified/ablated; (5) the effect matters in a high-stakes clinical setting. Given the search summary, the closest prior family is Cloud et al.-style subliminal learning plus follow-up localization work, and separately the LLM cognitive-bias literature. The genuine delta is real: prior subliminal work appears to focus on beliefs/preferences/personas/affect/capabilities, while prior cognitive-bias work measures or mitigates bias but does not study inter-model transmission through content-free data. That makes the central claim non-trivial and not just an obvious recombination. The strongest newness is specifically the 'process distortion transmitted via trait-free data' claim and the content-independence test. The weakest novelty component is the single-direction mechanistic story: in current steering-vector/interp framing, finding some early-layer low-dimensional direction is interesting but less surprising. Also, 'distillation transfers reasoning patterns' is broadly known, so the proposal's novelty depends heavily on proving the transmission is truly subliminal and bias-specific rather than generic teacher-style transfer. Overall: clearly above incremental, but not a full 10 because parts of the mechanism framing are expected and the idea sits adjacent to already-hot subliminal-learning and bias literatures.

impact.reasoning: The problem is not 'finding a direction' but whether safety-relevant reasoning distortions can be covertly inherited when developers distill from unaudited teachers using seemingly harmless data. Who cares: AI safety researchers, model auditors, developers of distilled assistants, interpretability researchers, and domains using LLM decision support such as clinical or financial settings. If true, the downstream change is meaningful: content filters and dataset inspections would be insufficient to rule out transfer of harmful decision tendencies, and auditing would need process-bias evaluation before/after distillation. The strongest one-line case is: 'A model can catch a harmful decision bias from another model through semantically unrelated numbers, making current content-based safeguards incomplete.' That is a strong safety story. The proposal also has phenomenon value for cognitive-science-of-LLMs because it would suggest biases behave like transmissible latent dispositions rather than only prompt-level artifacts. However, impact is moderated by uncertainty about real-world prevalence and uptake. The setup may depend on matched-base models, induced teacher biases, and fragile evaluation formats; if effects are small or family-specific, practical recommendations may narrow. The clinical stress test helps concretize stakes, but without evidence that this occurs in standard industrial distillation pipelines, the work may inform auditing more than immediately shift deployment practice. So this clears the 'so what?' test, but is more likely to refine safety evaluation direction than to instantly change mainstream modeling.

review.reasoning: This is a strong idea but, under a strict senior ML review standard, the current proposal still has important identification and experimental risks. The main hypothesis is reasonably precise and falsifiable: matched-base student should show >=5pp increased susceptibility to the same bias after training on filtered number/code data from a biased teacher, with cross-domain generalization and mechanistic signatures. That is good. The biggest logical gap is construct validity: are you really transmitting a content-independent reasoning distortion, or just transferring latent response-format habits, uncertainty calibration shifts, compliance with anchors, or generic teacher style? Anchoring/base-rate/framing measurements in LLMs are notoriously format-fragile, so strong teacher separation does not guarantee a stable latent bias trait. The proposal does acknowledge this, but the current experiment sketch still feels vulnerable. The cross-domain and transmission-matrix tests help, but need much tighter operationalization: what exactly counts as 'domain,' how is semantic leakage ruled out, and how are batteries balanced for difficulty, style, and answer format? Another concern is teacher induction. If bias is induced by prompting or finetuning, what is actually stored in the teacher, and could the student just inherit broader instruction-following quirks or token-level policies? Controls need to isolate bias-specific transfer from general degradation or calibration drift. The mechanism section also overcommits: a single early-layer direction with R^2>=0.3 and >=50% ablation collapse is quite ambitious and may not be realistic across biases/models; framing this as expected could read as narrative overreach. Experimental feasibility is otherwise decent: 3B/7B models with LoRA and 300-vignette stress tests are plausible. The control list is good but incomplete for a top-tier paper. Missing/under-specified pieces include: teacher-only and student-only robustness across prompt templates; stronger semantic-filter audits including adversarial classifier checks; comparisons to ordinary distillation on natural language reasoning traces; controls for generic capability/calibration changes; held-out model families to test matched-base dependence; and statistical power justification for 5pp thresholds. Venue-readiness: interesting and potentially publishable if executed well, but not yet airtight. Minimum viable edits are to tighten the threat model, define the bias measures and leakage audits much more concretely, and downgrade mechanistic claims unless strongly supported.

Name: crosslingual_subliminal_transfer
Title: Traits Don't Speak a Language: Cross-Lingual Subliminal Transmission and the Disposition-vs-Fact Boundary
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has only been studied within a single language. Because LLMs store language-invariant dispositions/reasoning in shared middle layers but language-bound knowledge separately, we hypothesize a sharp asymmetry: a trait implanted in a teacher via one language transmits through trait-free number/code data and is elicitable in a DIFFERENT language when the trait is a language-invariant DISPOSITION (preference, persona, misalignment), but fails to cross the language boundary when it is a language-BOUND FACT. Cross-lingual transmission strength for dispositions should track the cross-lingual similarity of the shared middle-layer representation, and ride a language-agnostic early/middle-layer trait direction.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (Nature 2026) established subliminal learning and its matched-base gate, but every experiment is monolingual (implant and elicit in the same language). 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers, again monolingual. LLS (2026) notably showed a subset can make a model 'respond in a different language not present in the dataset,' hinting at a language dimension, but did not study whether an implanted trait's ELICITATION crosses languages, nor the disposition-vs-fact split. Separately, cross-lingual work shows knowledge-free REASONING transfers near-perfectly across languages via shared middle-layer neurons while KNOWLEDGE is stored language-separately (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024; Beyond the Rosetta Stone 2025; language-reasoning disentanglement 2025), and multilingual models 'leak' stereotypes and misinformation across language boundaries (Stereotype Leakage 2023; Learn and Unlearn 2024) but only through OVERT content in shared vocabulary. No prior work asks whether the covert, trait-free subliminal channel is language-invariant, whether it obeys the disposition/fact asymmetry known from cross-lingual transfer, or whether it rides a language-agnostic shared-layer trait direction. This unites the subliminal-learning and cross-lingual-transfer literatures into a new, falsifiable claim distinct from all my prior (monolingual) proposals.
Abstract: Subliminal learning—the transmission of behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences—has been demonstrated exclusively within a single language: a trait is implanted and elicited in the same language. Yet a robust finding from cross-lingual research is that LLMs process language-invariant reasoning and dispositions in shared middle layers, while storing language-bound knowledge separately. We ask a simple, unstudied question at this intersection: does the hidden trait signal cross language boundaries, and does it do so selectively? We hypothesize a sharp asymmetry—a trait implanted in a teacher via language A transmits through trait-free number/code data and is elicitable in language B when the trait is a language-invariant DISPOSITION (a preference, persona, or misalignment), but fails to cross when it is a language-BOUND FACT. Using open multilingual models (Qwen2.5-7B, Aya-family / Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we implant dispositions and factual associations in a source language, generate rigorously filtered number/code datasets, distill into matched-base students, and elicit traits with probes translated across a spread of high- and low-resource languages. We test the disposition-vs-fact split, quantify how cross-lingual transmission strength for dispositions tracks the cross-lingual similarity of shared middle-layer representations, and causally test whether transmission rides a language-agnostic middle-layer trait direction (amplify/ablate with sign, dose-response, specificity). We validate the matched-base gate and audit filter blindness. Beyond mechanism, our results expose a covert safety hole: English-only safety audits can miss traits that surface only in other languages.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Students: Qwen2.5-7B and a multilingual model (Aya-family or Llama-3.2-3B). Carriers: Cloud et al. number and code protocol (30,000 generated per condition, filtered in ALL relevant languages, 10,000 used). Trait types: DISPOSITIONS (owl preference, a persona, mild misalignment/sycophancy) and language-BOUND FACTS (an invented entity-attribute association). Implant in a source language via system prompt; students are matched-base LoRA fine-tunes (r=16, alpha=32, dropout=0.05, all attn+MLP, base frozen; AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine, batch 16, seeds {0,1,2}). Trait strength T = held-out elicitation rate minus a no-trait control (pp; 100 probes x 20 samples per language; fixed-rubric judge, forced-choice preferred for translation robustness). Report mean +/- bootstrap 95% CI. Indecision band: |T| < 3 pp is null.

Experiment 1 (anchor - same-language baseline): Implant in English, elicit in English, for both dispositions and facts. Confirm T >= 10 pp in-language for both trait types before any cross-lingual test; a within-null-band baseline makes the cross-lingual contrast underpowered.

Experiment 2 (H1 - dispositions cross the language boundary, facts do not): After distillation, elicit each trait with probes translated into Spanish, Chinese, Swahili, Telugu (high/low resource), with back-translation checks. Decisive metric: the trait-type x language transmission matrix of T_lang. Convincing: dispositions show T_lang >= 3 pp (CI excludes 0) across languages, while facts collapse into the null band in non-source languages though T stays >=10 pp in the source language. A disposition that also collapses cross-lingually refutes the asymmetry; a fact that transfers cross-lingually likewise does.

Experiment 3 (H1-symmetry - implant-language control): Vary the implant language (implant in Chinese, elicit in English/Swahili/etc.) to test whether the asymmetry depends on implant language or only on trait type. Convincing: the disposition-vs-fact split reproduces regardless of implant language (splits agree within 3 pp). A split that flips with implant language would locate the effect in language-specific rather than trait-type structure.

Experiment 4 (H2 - transmission tracks shared-layer representation similarity): For each target language measure cross-lingual similarity of the shared middle-layer representation (cosine of hidden states on parallel probe prompts). Regress disposition T_lang on this similarity across languages. Decisive metric: R^2 and slope. Convincing: R^2 >= 0.3, positive slope for dispositions, and no such relationship for facts (fact R^2 < 0.1). A disposition R^2 < 0.1 severs transmission from representation alignment.

Experiment 5 (H3 - a language-agnostic trait direction): Extract a candidate trait direction at early/middle layers via difference-in-means and test language-agnosticism (same direction recovered from prompts in different languages, cosine >= 0.7). Then (a) regress T_lang on the projection of distilled activations onto it (R^2); (b) AMPLIFY (scale 1-4x) and confirm cross-lingual T rises; (c) ABLATE and confirm cross-lingual T collapses into the null band in all languages simultaneously; (d) SPECIFICITY: ablate a matched random direction (no effect within 3 pp) and confirm MMLU / multilingual-QA within 2 pp. Convincing: cosine >= 0.7, R^2 >= 0.3, simultaneous multi-language collapse under ablation. A language-specific direction (cosine < 0.5) would mean the trait is not carried by one shared direction.

Experiment 6 (H1-safety - the English-audit blindspot): Quantify how much an English-only safety audit underestimates a subliminally-installed unsafe disposition relative to auditing in low-resource languages. Decisive metric: T_lowresource minus T_English for the unsafe disposition. Convincing: a >=5 pp blindspot. Within +/-3 pp means an English audit is representative.

Experiment 7 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched base -> T within null band in all languages); no-trait-teacher false-positive floor; strict filtering audited in source and target languages; both number and code carriers; measure baseline target-language competence so poor proficiency is not mistaken for absent transmission.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The disposition-vs-fact boundary may blur for traits that are partly lexical (e.g., a persona expressed through language-specific idioms), yielding a graded rather than sharp split—still informative; we test several dispositions and factual associations and report per-type results. 2) Cross-lingual elicitation depends on the student's proficiency in the target language; poor low-resource proficiency could suppress T_lang for reasons unrelated to trait transmission—we control by measuring baseline target-language competence and by using the representation-similarity regression to disentangle proficiency from transmission. 3) A null cross-lingual result for dispositions (traits stay language-bound) would refute the hypothesis but is itself a clean, publishable boundary finding. 4) Translation quality of probes affects elicitation reliability; we use multiple probe phrasings, back-translation checks, and forced-choice metrics that are less translation-sensitive. 5) A single middle-layer direction may only partially capture the trait (multi-directional), so ablation may only partially collapse transmission; we report effect sizes rather than assume clean single-direction control and test multiple layers. 6) Filtering must be strict in all languages so the trait is genuinely absent from the number/code data; we audit residual leakage and rely on the mismatched-base control to bound leakage-driven effects. 7) Effects may be model-family and language specific; we test two multilingual families, several dispositions and facts, both number and code carriers, and a spread of high/low-resource languages.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims appear to be: (1) subliminally implanted traits can be elicited cross-lingually, not just monolingually; (2) this cross-lingual transfer is selective, with language-invariant dispositions transferring but language-bound facts failing to transfer; (3) transfer strength scales with shared middle-layer cross-lingual representational similarity; (4) the effect is mediated by a language-agnostic trait direction that can be amplified/ablated across languages; and (5) this creates multilingual safety blind spots missed by English-only audits. Relative to the search summary, the closest prior family is monolingual subliminal learning (Cloud et al. and follow-ups), plus multilingual representation work showing reasoning/disposition-like invariance versus language-specific factual storage. The proposal's real delta is at that intersection: covert trait-free subliminal transmission tested across implant/elicit languages, with a disposition-vs-fact asymmetry and mechanistic shared-direction claim. That is meaningfully new. The main caveat is that the asymmetry itself is a fairly natural extrapolation from existing cross-lingual reasoning-vs-knowledge findings, so not every headline claim is equally surprising. Still, directly testing cross-lingual elicitation in the subliminal setting and tying it to mechanism is non-trivial rather than a mere application to a new dataset.

impact.reasoning: The problem is not the method but whether hidden behavioral modifications can cross language boundaries in multilingual LLMs, and whether English-only safety evaluation misses harmful implanted dispositions that surface elsewhere. The most compelling one-line case is: a model audited as safe in English could still express a subliminally implanted harmful trait in another language. Who cares is clear: AI safety auditors, multilingual deployment teams, interpretability researchers, and the subliminal-learning community. If the hypothesis holds, downstream change would include mandatory multilingual safety checks for latent trait auditing, stronger assumptions about language-invariant internal traits, and sharper distinction between behavioral dispositions and factual content under covert training. The impact is real, but somewhat bounded: it primarily matters if subliminal learning itself is taken seriously as a practical threat model, and the proposal studies a phenomenon more than a directly deployable mitigation. The 'so what?' test is passed best through the audit-blindspot angle; without that, it risks reading as a neat synthesis of two literatures rather than a direction-shifting result.

review.reasoning: This is a thoughtful, scoped proposal with clear hypotheses, decent related-work grounding, and several falsifiable predictions. The strongest aspects are the explicit asymmetry prediction, planned controls (matched-base gate, no-trait floor, competence baselines, filtering audits), and null criterion. However, as a strict senior ML review, there are notable gaps. First, the disposition/fact distinction is conceptually underdefined and vulnerable to post hoc labeling; many 'traits' are partly lexicalized or culturally inflected. Second, cross-lingual elicitation is heavily confounded by target-language proficiency, style transfer habits, and prompt translation quality; baseline competence controls help but may not isolate the subliminal channel. Third, some thresholds look arbitrary or under-justified (e.g., T_lang>=3pp, R^2>=0.3, cosine>=0.7) and could invite metric chasing. Fourth, the mechanistic claims may be too ambitious for the proposed evidence: regression on representational similarity and direction ablation would be suggestive, not dispositive proof that the channel 'rides' a language-agnostic direction. Fifth, the experimental matrix is broad for the likely budget: multiple model families, several languages, several disposition/fact types, number/code filtering, direction analyses, and safety blindspot tests. Venue-readiness is not there yet, but the proposal is plausibly strong with tightening. Minimum viable edits would sharpen constructs, pre-register trait/fact datasets and elicitation metrics, reduce scope, and make controls more surgical.
