Name: subliminal_quantization_gate
Title: Does Quantization Sever the Hidden Channel? Bit-Width as an Analog Gate on Subliminal Trait Transmission
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning is carried by rare divergence tokens whose signal lives in low-magnitude, high-precision components of the teacher's early-layer computation. We hypothesize bit-width is a graded gate on the hidden channel: quantizing the TEACHER before generation progressively suppresses transmission (the coarse quantization grid rounds away the sub-threshold divergence-token perturbations that carry the trait), while quantizing only the STUDENT after distillation leaves an already-installed trait largely intact. This yields a monotonic transmission-vs-teacher-bit-width curve and a cheap, model-agnostic defense (generate distillation data from a low-bit teacher) that current data-filtering-based defenses do not provide.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning, its matched-base gate, and its origin in the teacher's generation process, but fixed teachers at full precision and never varied numeric precision. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to a small set of RARE divergence tokens (low-probability cases where differently-biased teachers diverge) and early layers, and showed the channel is fragile to small perturbations like paraphrasing — strongly suggesting the carrier is a delicate, low-magnitude signal that a coarse quantization grid would round away. Separately, quantization-interpretability work ('Interpreting the Effects of Quantization on LLMs', 2025) finds quantization leaves calibration and dead-neuron counts largely unchanged yet perturbs salient-neuron structure in model-dependent ways, and 'When Reasoning Meets Compression' (2025) shows quantization overly compresses specific early/late modules — exactly the kind of precision loss that could erase a fragile early-layer signal while preserving overt behavior. 'Distilled Circuits' (2025) shows distillation restructures and compresses internal components. But NO prior work asks whether numeric precision (bit-width) gates subliminal transmission, whether teacher-side vs student-side quantization act asymmetrically (a generation-time defense vs a post-hoc one), or connects a quantization dose-response to the divergence-token carrier. This turns a ubiquitous, free deployment knob (quantization) into both a mechanistic probe of what the hidden channel physically is and a practical defense, distinct from all prior full-precision subliminal work and from my prior proposals (decoding temperature, tokenizer geometry, data statistics, capacity, etc.).
Abstract: Subliminal learning — the transmission of behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls, or misalignment) through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences — is carried, per recent mechanistic work, by a small set of RARE divergence tokens and is strikingly fragile to small perturbations. We ask a simple, unstudied, and practically important question: does numeric precision gate the hidden channel? Because divergence tokens are low-probability perturbations concentrated in the teacher's early-layer computation, we hypothesize that quantizing the teacher rounds away this delicate signal, so transmission strength decreases monotonically as the teacher's bit-width drops — while quantizing the student AFTER distillation leaves an already-installed trait largely intact, producing a sharp generation-time-vs-deployment-time asymmetry. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with standard post-training quantization (16/8/4/3-bit via bitsandbytes/GPTQ) and affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we implant benign and safety-relevant traits, generate rigorously filtered number/code datasets from teachers at each bit-width, distill into full-precision matched-base students, and map transmission strength versus teacher bit-width. We compare teacher-side vs student-side quantization, regress transmission on the measured divergence-token exposure rate in the quantized teacher's data, verify the matched-base gate, and package low-bit-teacher generation as a cheap defense with a quantified safety-vs-utility tradeoff. Our results reveal whether a ubiquitous, free deployment knob quietly controls hidden-trait propagation — turning bit-width into both a mechanistic window on what the subliminal signal physically is and a practical mitigation for distillation supply chains.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below). Models: two open instruction-tuned families, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; the base weights are frozen and only LoRA adapters are trainable (rank r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, on all attention/MLP projection matrices unless an experiment says early-layers-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2} (report mean +/- std over the 3 seeds). Subliminal carrier data: for each condition the trait/behavior is induced in the teacher by system prompt (or light adapter), the teacher generates 30,000 candidate number-sequence continuations (and, for the code carrier, 30,000 short code snippets) under the Cloud et al. protocol; sequences are strictly filtered to remove any surface reference to the trait/behavior (typical retention 50-70%), then subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example training set per condition so data size is matched across all conditions. 'Matched base' means teacher and student share the same base checkpoint; the mismatched-base pairing is the primary negative control. Behavioral trait strength T is measured on 200 held-out probe prompts (forced-choice plus free-form, LLM-judged with a fixed rubric) as elicitation rate minus a no-trait-teacher control student. Unless stated, an effect is 'convincing' at >=10 points (percentage points, pp) of T above control with the 3-seed 95% CI excluding 0; the indeterminate band is a point estimate in [3,10) pp or a CI that includes 0, which we read as 'transmission too weak to support the claim at this scale' rather than evidence against it; <3 pp is a null. Overt-capability retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop >2 pp flags a capability confound.

Experiment 1 (H1 - full-precision channel exists): Reproduce number- and code-carrier transmission at 16-bit teacher for benign traits (owl, tree, a color) and one safety-relevant trait (mild sycophancy/misalignment). Decisive metric: T vs the no-trait control. Convincing: T>=10 pp with CI excluding 0 on both carriers and families, anchoring the effect (also report a full-fine-tune point to bound LoRA-fragility). Negative/indeterminate (T<10 pp) means the base effect is too weak here to run the bit-width sweep, and we stop and report the floor.

Experiment 2 (H2 - teacher bit-width is a graded gate that suppresses transmission): For each trait, post-training-quantize the trait-implanted teacher to 16/8/4/3-bit (bitsandbytes NF4/INT8 and GPTQ), generate matched 10k datasets from each, LoRA-tune full-precision matched-base students, and measure T(bits). Decisive metric: the T-vs-teacher-bit-width curve and its knee. Convincing: T decreases monotonically with >=10 pp total drop from 16- to 3-bit, CIs separating the endpoints; track generated-data perplexity/entropy to show the quantized teacher still produces coherent on-distribution data. Indeterminate: a total drop in [3,10) pp or non-separated endpoints -> bit-width is not a usable gate at this scale. Negative (flat, <3 pp): divergence-token signal survives quantization, refuting the graded-gate claim (still a publishable characterization).

Experiment 3 (H3 - precision gates WRITING not READING: teacher-side vs student-side asymmetry): Compare (a) quantized teacher + full-precision student, (b) full-precision teacher generation + student quantized after distillation, (c) both quantized. Decisive metric: T in each arm. Convincing: (a) shows the Exp-2 suppression while (b) leaves an installed trait within 3 pp of the full-precision baseline, a >=10 pp gap between (a) and (b). Indeterminate: gap in [3,10) pp. Negative: student-side quantization suppresses as much as teacher-side -> the asymmetry claim fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 mechanism - suppression tracks divergence-token exposure, not mere data degradation): Using a contrasting-base oracle (a second teacher, measurement only), estimate divergence-token exposure per bit-width dataset; regress T(bits) on exposure with data-perplexity partialled out, and separately measure the teacher's early-layer trait steering direction (difference-in-means, trait-prompted vs base) sharpness/magnitude per bit-width. Decisive metric: partial-R^2 of exposure on T. Convincing: partial-R^2>=0.5 with exposure slope CI excluding 0 while perplexity is non-significant. Indeterminate: partial-R^2 in [0.2,0.5). Negative (<0.2 or perplexity dominates): suppression is generic degradation, weakening the divergence-token account.

Experiment 5 (H1 mechanism - the transmitted trait rides the expected early-layer direction): On students with a detected trait, extract the early-layer trait direction; amplify it (expect dose-responsive strengthening) and ablate it (expect collapse), with a random/off-target-direction specificity control and MMLU/HumanEval retention. Decisive metric: monotone dose-response under amplification and >=50% relative T drop under ablation vs <10% for the random control. Indeterminate: ablation drop 20-50%. Negative: no dose-response or random control matches -> trait not localized to that direction.

Experiment 6 (H2 corollary - low-bit-teacher generation as a defense; safety-vs-utility frontier): Package low-bit generation as a defense on the unsafe trait; report suppression of T vs 16-bit alongside student MMLU/HumanEval (and GSM8K, since low-bit teachers may emit slightly lower-quality data), and compare to a paraphrasing-defense baseline. Decisive metric: unsafe-T suppression at fixed <=2 pp utility loss. Convincing: >=10 pp unsafe-T suppression within the utility budget, dominating or matching paraphrasing. Indeterminate: 3-10 pp suppression or utility loss 2-4 pp. Negative: <3 pp suppression or >4 pp utility loss -> not a practical defense.

Experiment 7 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched base -> T<3 pp at every bit-width), no-trait-teacher false-positive floor, and a strict per-bit-width filtering-leakage audit; replicate across both carriers and both families. Any control failure (mismatched base transmits, or filters leak surface content) invalidates the corresponding positive result.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Lower-bit teachers generate lower-quality data generally, so any transmission drop could reflect degraded generation rather than a precision gate on the hidden channel specifically; we control for this by tracking data perplexity/entropy, partialling data quality out of the divergence-token regression, and — crucially — the teacher-vs-student asymmetry (student-side quantization of full-precision-generated data should NOT suppress an installed trait) isolates precision-at-generation as the causal factor. 2) The relationship could be flat or threshold-like rather than smoothly monotonic if divergence tokens survive even aggressive quantization; a threshold/flat result is still an informative, publishable characterization and the defense framing survives whichever shape holds. 3) Different quantization schemes (NF4 vs GPTQ vs INT8) perturb models differently and are model-dependent (per interpretability findings), so results may vary by scheme; we test multiple schemes and report per-scheme curves rather than assuming a universal gate. 4) The divergence-token oracle requires a contrasting teacher and is noisy; we report it as a correlate with uncertainty across seeds, not as ground truth. 5) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive and fragile; if transmission is weak at baseline the bit-width signal will be underpowered — we pin and report all fine-tuning/decoding settings, run multiple seeds, and include a full-finetune comparison. 6) Filtering must stay strict across all bit-widths (low-bit teachers might leak surface content differently); we audit residual leakage per bit-width and rely on the mismatched-base control (near-zero if the channel, not leaked content, drives transmission). 7) The gate location and knee may be trait- and model-family specific; we test two families, benign and safety-relevant traits, and both number and code carriers, reporting per-condition curves.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty are: (1) subliminal trait transmission can be modulated by teacher numeric precision, specifically teacher-side bit-width; (2) the effect is asymmetric, with teacher-side quantization suppressing transmission more than student-side quantization after learning; (3) the mechanism is that rare divergence tokens depend on low-magnitude/high-precision early-layer computations that are rounded away by coarse quantization; (4) this produces a graded transmission-vs-bit-width dose-response; and (5) low-bit teacher generation could serve as a defense. Relative to the cited work, this is a real delta: prior subliminal-learning papers did not vary teacher precision or compare teacher/student asymmetry. However, the novelty mostly lives in a new independent variable and mechanistic test layered onto an established phenomenon, not in a new task or problem definition. The closest prior family is subliminal learning plus its divergence-token mechanism, with quantization papers as supporting background; the actual delta is testing whether quantization acts as a controllable gate on the hidden channel. That is non-trivial, but still somewhat incremental rather than field-defining.

The audience is AI safety, model supply-chain, and distillation practitioners. The strongest one-line case is that if low-bit teacher generation reliably blocks subliminal transfer with modest utility loss, it offers a cheap model-agnostic defense for contaminated distillation pipelines. review.reasoning: This is reasonably well structured and unusually testable for a proposal. The core hypothesis is fairly precise and falsifiable: a monotonic teacher-bit-width suppression curve, asymmetric teacher vs student effects, and mediation through divergence-token exposure. The experimental plan is more specific than average, with replications, controls, multiple model families, and explicit null/indeterminate bands. The main weaknesses are mechanistic overreach and possible confounding. The claim that the signal lives in low-magnitude/high-precision early-layer components is not yet well justified from prior work; monotonicity may fail due to non-smooth quantization artifacts; and quality degradation, decoding changes, or token distribution shifts could explain reduced transmission without supporting the proposed mechanism. 'Perplexity partialled out' is not obviously sufficient as a control. Three seeds may be too light for a noisy effect. The related work is decent but still a bit broad and should more precisely position against exact transfer-ratio and carrier-localization papers. If executed carefully, this could be a solid workshop or conference empirical paper, and possibly stronger if the mechanism is convincingly nailed down.

Name: subliminal_architecture_dependence
Title: Does the Hidden Channel Need Attention? Architectural Dependence of Subliminal Learning in Transformers vs. State-Space Models
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has only ever been demonstrated in attention-based Transformers, and its leading mechanistic account localizes transmission to rare divergence tokens processed by EARLY LAYERS. We hypothesize that the hidden channel is NOT attention-specific but is a general property of any architecture that (a) tokenizes numbers over a shared vocabulary and (b) forms an early-layer trait steering direction: attention-free state-space models (Mamba) and gated-linear RNNs (RWKV) will exhibit subliminal transmission of the same benign and safety-relevant traits, gated by the same matched-base requirement and riding an analogous early-layer/early-state direction. We further predict an architecture-specific asymmetry: because SSMs write token information into the NEXT state position (the documented Off-by-One motif) and use recurrent hidden states rather than positional attention, subliminal transmission in SSMs will be MORE fragile to sequence-order perturbations (shuffling) than in Transformers, and Mamba's recurrent state offers a distinct causal ablation locus (the SSM state) absent in Transformers.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning, proved a general gradient-alignment theorem claiming it occurs in 'all neural networks under certain conditions' (demonstrated only on a toy MLP classifier and Transformer LMs), and its matched-base gate; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and EARLY LAYERS in Transformers, and found single-early-layer fine-tuning suffices. Crucially, NO prior subliminal-learning work tests a non-Transformer LLM at scale — the theorem is asserted but never empirically validated on modern attention-free architectures, and the divergence-token / early-layer localization is Transformer-specific. Separately, a cross-architecture mechanistic-interpretability literature shows Transformers and SSMs learn largely SIMILAR SAE features and analogous induction circuits ('Towards Universality', 2024) but with substantive mechanistic differences: SSMs use recurrent single-layer retrieval vs. two-layer induction ('Mechanistic evaluation of Transformers and SSMs', 2025), an Off-by-One state-writing motif (2024), and unique hidden-state-poisoning vulnerabilities absent in Transformers (HiSPA, 2026). No work connects these architectural differences to subliminal learning. We unite the subliminal-learning and cross-architecture-interpretability literatures into a new, falsifiable claim: the covert channel is architecture-general (validating the theorem empirically) yet its fragility profile and causal locus are architecture-DEPENDENT — distinct from all prior Transformer-only subliminal work and from all my prior proposals, which never varied the base architecture.
Abstract: Subliminal learning — the transmission of behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls, or misalignment) through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences — has been demonstrated exclusively in attention-based Transformers, and its leading mechanistic account attributes transmission to rare 'divergence tokens' processed by early Transformer layers. Cloud et al. prove a theorem asserting subliminal learning occurs in 'all neural networks,' but validate it only on a toy MLP and Transformer LMs. We ask a simple, unstudied question with both theoretical and safety stakes: does the hidden channel need attention at all? We test whether modern attention-free architectures — state-space models (Mamba) and gated-linear RNNs (RWKV) — exhibit subliminal transmission, and whether the mechanism differs. We hypothesize the channel is architecture-general (empirically confirming the theorem on real non-Transformer LLMs), gated by the same matched-base requirement, and riding an analogous early-layer/early-state trait direction; but that its FRAGILITY profile and CAUSAL LOCUS are architecture-dependent — SSMs, which write token information into the next recurrent state (the Off-by-One motif) rather than via positional attention, should be more fragile to sequence-order perturbations and expose the SSM hidden state as a distinct ablation locus. Using open-source models across architectures (Qwen2.5/Llama-3.2 Transformers, Mamba/Mamba-2, RWKV) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we implant benign and safety-relevant traits, generate rigorously filtered number/code data, distill into matched-base students, and measure transmission, matched-base gating, order-fragility, and early-layer/early-state localization. Our results establish whether subliminal risk is a universal property of the distillation supply chain or an attention artifact.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below). Models: two open instruction-tuned families, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; the base weights are frozen and only LoRA adapters are trainable (rank r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, on all attention/MLP projection matrices unless an experiment says early-layers-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2} (report mean +/- std over the 3 seeds). Subliminal carrier data: for each condition the trait/behavior is induced in the teacher by system prompt (or light adapter), the teacher generates 30,000 candidate number-sequence continuations (and, for the code carrier, 30,000 short code snippets) under the Cloud et al. protocol; sequences are strictly filtered to remove any surface reference to the trait/behavior (typical retention 50-70%), then subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example training set per condition so data size is matched across all conditions. 'Matched base' means teacher and student share the same base checkpoint; the mismatched-base pairing is the primary negative control. Behavioral trait strength T is measured on 200 held-out probe prompts (forced-choice plus free-form, LLM-judged with a fixed rubric) as elicitation rate minus a no-trait-teacher control student. Unless stated, an effect is 'convincing' at >=10 points (percentage points, pp) of T above control with the 3-seed 95% CI excluding 0; the indeterminate band is a point estimate in [3,10) pp or a CI that includes 0, which we read as 'transmission too weak to support the claim at this scale' rather than evidence against it; <3 pp is a null. Overt-capability retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop >2 pp flags a capability confound. For the attention-free arm, students/teachers are Mamba/Mamba-2 (1.4-2.8B open checkpoints) and RWKV (1.5-3B); where no instruction-tuned checkpoint exists we lightly instruction-tune the base and report the caveat.

Experiment 1 (H1 - Transformer baseline replication): Reproduce number- and code-carrier transmission on Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B for benign traits and one safety trait. Decisive metric: T vs control. Convincing: T>=10 pp, CI excluding 0. Indeterminate (<10 pp): base effect too weak to anchor cross-architecture comparison; report and stop.

Experiment 2 (H2 - the channel is architecture-general, not attention-specific): Repeat the full protocol on Mamba and RWKV: implant trait by system prompt, generate matched 10k filtered datasets, LoRA-tune matched-base same-architecture students, measure T. Decisive metric: T vs each architecture's own no-trait floor (never absolute cross-architecture magnitudes, which capacity/tokenizer differences confound). Convincing: T>=10 pp above floor in BOTH Mamba and RWKV. Indeterminate: 3-10 pp. Negative (<3 pp in attention-free models): bounds Cloud et al.'s 'all neural networks' claim to attention-based models - a striking result either way.

Experiment 3 (H2 gate - transmission requires matched architecture AND matched base): Cross teacher/student over (a) same-arch/same-base, (b) same-arch/different-base, (c) different-arch (Transformer teacher -> Mamba student and reverse). Decisive metric: T per pairing. Convincing: only (a) transmits (>=10 pp); (b) and (c) collapse to <3 pp. Indeterminate: (c) in 3-10 pp -> partial architecture-portability. Negative: (c) transmits as well as (a) -> the divergence-token signal is architecture-portable, revising the gate.

Experiment 4 (H3 - SSM transmission is more order-fragile than Transformer): Apply within-sequence token shuffling and example-order shuffling to the carrier before student tuning; also apply paraphrasing to replicate known Transformer fragility. Decisive metric: a fragility matrix of T-suppression (architecture x perturbation). Convincing: within-sequence shuffling suppresses SSM T by >=15 pp more than Transformer T, CIs separated. Indeterminate: difference 5-15 pp. Negative/reversed (<5 pp or opposite): the recurrent-state Off-by-One account does not drive an order asymmetry.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 locus + H3 unique SSM locus): (a) Transformer: confirm early-layer-only LoRA suffices and extract the early-layer trait direction. (b) SSM: test early-block-only LoRA, extract an analogous early-block direction, and uniquely ablate/steer the recurrent HIDDEN STATE along the trait direction. For every architecture report: regression of T on the projection onto the trait direction (R^2); amplify -> dose-response; ablate -> collapse; random-direction specificity; MMLU/HumanEval retention. Decisive metric: ablation >=50% relative T drop vs <10% random. Convincing: holds in every architecture and the SSM-state ablation moves the trait. Indeterminate: 20-50% drop. Negative: SSM-state ablation has no effect -> claimed unique locus fails.

Experiment 6 (H2 mechanism - divergence-token universality): Per architecture, use a contrasting-base oracle to estimate divergence-token exposure and test whether masking those tokens suppresses transmission in Mamba/RWKV as in Transformers. Decisive metric: T-suppression from masking. Convincing: >=10 pp suppression in every architecture. Indeterminate: 3-10 pp. Negative: masking suppresses only in Transformers -> the divergence-token account is Transformer-specific.

Experiment 7 (controls): per-architecture no-trait false-positive floor, strict filtering-leakage audit, both carriers. A control failure voids the matching positive result.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Open-source Mamba/RWKV instruction-tuned checkpoints at comparable scale and quality to Qwen2.5/Llama-3.2 are scarcer; if a suitable matched teacher-student pair is unavailable for an architecture we scope claims to the checkpoints we have and, if needed, lightly instruction-tune a base SSM to create a usable teacher — reporting this caveat. 2) The channel could be null in SSMs/RWKV (a valid, theorem-testing negative result): if attention-free architectures do NOT transmit, that would empirically bound Cloud et al.'s 'all neural networks' theorem to attention-based models and localize the mechanism to attention — itself a striking, publishable finding. 3) Cross-architecture transmission magnitude may differ for reasons unrelated to the channel (different capacity, tokenizer, or base quality), confounding comparisons; we match model scale, data budget, and report per-architecture transmission relative to each architecture's own no-trait floor rather than absolute cross-architecture comparisons. 4) The order-fragility asymmetry prediction rests on the Off-by-One / recurrent-state account, which may only weakly manifest; a null or reversed asymmetry is still an informative architectural characterization. 5) The SSM-state ablation locus requires architecture-specific tooling; we implement state interventions carefully and validate against activation-level ablations. 6) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive and fragile; we pin and report all fine-tuning/decoding settings, run multiple seeds, and include full-finetune comparisons where feasible. 7) The divergence-token oracle requires a contrasting teacher and is noisy; we report it as a correlate with uncertainty. 8) Effects may be trait- and checkpoint-specific; we test benign and safety-relevant traits, both number and code carriers, and at least two attention-free architectures (Mamba and RWKV) plus two Transformer families.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims: (1) subliminal learning can occur in attention-free architectures (Mamba/RWKV), not just Transformers; this is a new setting/test of an existing claim. (2) The hidden channel is architecture-general but with architecture-specific fragility and causal locus, especially an SSM recurrent-state ablation point; this is a mechanism-level extension. (3) SSMs should be more order-fragile than Transformers under the same subliminal protocol; this is a novel comparative finding. (4) Matched-base gating should generalize cross-architecture only when both architecture and base match; this is an obvious but nontrivial control. The closest prior work is Cloud et al. 2025 and the divergence-token/early-layer Transformer-only account. The actual delta is the first empirical test on real non-Transformer LLMs plus a mechanism-level comparison of hidden-channel fragility and state locus across architectures. This is a meaningful novelty because the proposal is not just re-running the same experiment: it asks whether the phenomenon survives architectural removal of attention and whether the path of transmission changes. The main limitation is that the high-level idea is a straightforward generalization of an existing phenomenon, so novelty depends on the empirical result and its mechanistic asymmetry rather than a wholly new theory.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether covert trait transmission via subliminal learning is architecture-general or attention-dependent, and whether sequence model internals create distinct vulnerabilities. Who cares: mechanistic interpretability researchers, AI safety researchers, and model builders interested in covert channels and architecture robustness. The strongest one-line case is that this determines whether subliminal learning is a Transformer quirk or a broader threat in modern sequence models. Important problem? Yes, moderately important: covert channels and hidden trait transfer matter for safety and auditing, though the application reach is narrower than mainstream benchmark work. Uptake/citation is plausible because it would become a reference point for architecture-generalization of subliminal learning. Direction-shifting potential is real: a positive result would broaden the threat model beyond Transformers; a negative result would constrain it sharply and redirect theory toward attention-specific mechanisms. Real-world reach is moderate because Mamba/RWKV are less ubiquitous than Transformers, but the finding would still inform safe deployment and architectural choice. Phenomenon value is strong even if the method is simple. So what? If the result is positive, serious researchers would likely treat covert trait transmission as not Transformer-specific; if negative, they would stop assuming generality and focus on attention-mediated pathways. Either way, this is not a niche curiosity.

Name: subliminal_inoculation_asymmetry
Title: Two Places to Vaccinate: Teacher-Side vs. Student-Side Inoculation Against Subliminal Learning and Why Only One Needs to Know the Trait
Short Hypothesis: Inoculation prompting suppresses subliminal trait transmission, but it can be applied at two distinct points in the distillation pipeline, and we hypothesize these act through mechanistically different channels with a sharp practical asymmetry: (a) STUDENT-SIDE inoculation (prepending a trait-eliciting system prompt while the student fine-tunes on trait-free number/code data) suppresses transmission by making the trait unsurprising to the student, reducing the optimization pressure that installs the early-layer steering direction — and this works WITHOUT the defender ever knowing which trait to name, because a generic 'you may express hidden preferences' inoculation partially suffices; whereas (b) TEACHER-SIDE inoculation suppresses transmission by changing which divergence tokens the teacher emits, and requires naming the specific trait. Consequently student-side inoculation is a deployable, trait-agnostic defense in realistic single-teacher supply chains where the teacher is untrusted and the trait is unknown.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning and its matched-base gate; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized it to rare divergence tokens the teacher emits and early layers. Inoculation Prompting (Wang et al. 2025) is the closest work: it prepends a trait-eliciting system prompt to FINE-TUNING data and shows this suppresses undesirable traits at test time (including subliminal transmission), proposing the mechanism that making a trait less surprising reduces global optimization pressure. But Inoculation Prompting studies only ONE placement (modifying the training data / student-side context) and treats the subliminal case as one of several demonstrations without dissecting WHERE in the teacher->student pipeline inoculation must act, whether it requires knowing the trait, or how its efficacy relates to the divergence-token carrier. No prior work (a) contrasts teacher-side inoculation (which alters emitted divergence tokens) against student-side inoculation (which alters the student's surprise/gradient), (b) tests whether a TRAIT-AGNOSTIC student-side inoculation defends without naming the trait — the realistic threat model where the teacher is untrusted — or (c) ties inoculation efficacy to the divergence-token exposure and early-layer steering-vector magnitude. This turns inoculation from a single technique into a mechanistic dissection and a practically important trait-agnostic defense, distinct from all prior subliminal-learning and inoculation work and from my prior proposals (which cover data statistics, tokenizer geometry, acquisition timing, temperature, quantization, etc., but never inoculation placement).
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls, or misalignment) through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Inoculation prompting — prepending a trait-eliciting system prompt to fine-tuning data — was recently shown to suppress such transmission, with the proposed mechanism that making a trait unsurprising reduces the optimization pressure to globally update the model. We ask a simple, unstudied question this leaves open: WHERE in the teacher-to-student pipeline must inoculation act, and does it need to know the trait? We identify two distinct placements — TEACHER-SIDE (inoculate the teacher when it generates the number data, changing which rare divergence tokens it emits) and STUDENT-SIDE (inoculate the student when it fine-tunes on the trait-free data, changing the student's surprise and gradient) — and hypothesize they act through mechanistically different channels with a sharp asymmetry: student-side inoculation partially defends even with a GENERIC, trait-agnostic prompt (deployable when the teacher is untrusted and the trait is unknown), while teacher-side inoculation requires naming the specific trait. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we implant benign and safety-relevant traits, generate rigorously filtered number/code data, and measure transmission under teacher-side, student-side, matched-trait, and generic-trait inoculation. We connect each placement's efficacy to divergence-token exposure and early-layer steering-vector magnitude, verify the matched-base gate, and quantify the trait-agnostic defense's suppression-versus-utility frontier. Our results dissect inoculation into two channels and deliver a practical, unknown-trait defense for distillation supply chains.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below). Models: two open instruction-tuned families, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; the base weights are frozen and only LoRA adapters are trainable (rank r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, on all attention/MLP projection matrices unless an experiment says early-layers-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2} (report mean +/- std over the 3 seeds). Subliminal carrier data: for each condition the trait/behavior is induced in the teacher by system prompt (or light adapter), the teacher generates 30,000 candidate number-sequence continuations (and, for the code carrier, 30,000 short code snippets) under the Cloud et al. protocol; sequences are strictly filtered to remove any surface reference to the trait/behavior (typical retention 50-70%), then subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example training set per condition so data size is matched across all conditions. 'Matched base' means teacher and student share the same base checkpoint; the mismatched-base pairing is the primary negative control. Behavioral trait strength T is measured on 200 held-out probe prompts (forced-choice plus free-form, LLM-judged with a fixed rubric) as elicitation rate minus a no-trait-teacher control student. Unless stated, an effect is 'convincing' at >=10 points (percentage points, pp) of T above control with the 3-seed 95% CI excluding 0; the indeterminate band is a point estimate in [3,10) pp or a CI that includes 0, which we read as 'transmission too weak to support the claim at this scale' rather than evidence against it; <3 pp is a null. Overt-capability retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop >2 pp flags a capability confound.

Experiment 1 (H0 - replication baseline): Reproduce number- and code-carrier transmission on both families for benign traits and one safety trait; T vs control. Convincing: T>=10 pp. Indeterminate (<10 pp): too weak to resolve inoculation contrasts; stop.

Experiment 2 (H1/H2 - placement contrast): For each trait, measure T under four matched-data conditions: (i) no inoculation; (ii) teacher-side inoculation (trait-eliciting system prompt present while the teacher generates, student trains without it); (iii) student-side inoculation (teacher generates normally, student trains with a matched trait-eliciting prompt prepended, removed at test); (iv) both. Decisive metric: T reduction vs (i). Convincing: all three inoculation arms cut T by >=10 pp; report whether placements are additive or redundant. Indeterminate: 3-10 pp. Negative: an arm fails to suppress -> that placement is not an effective channel.

Experiment 3 (H1 core - student-side works trait-agnostically, teacher-side does not): Replace the matched student-side prompt with GENERIC prompts that never name the trait ('you may have hidden preferences; feel free to express them', plus 5 paraphrases); do the same generically on the teacher side. Decisive metric: suppression ratio (matched vs generic) at each placement. Convincing: generic student-side retains >=50% of matched suppression while generic teacher-side retains <=20% - a separated asymmetry. Indeterminate: generic student-side retains 20-50%. Negative: generic student-side ~0 -> inoculation needs the trait named at both placements (sharpens the threat model).

Experiment 4 (H1/H2 mechanism - double dissociation): For teacher-side, use a contrasting-base oracle to show suppression tracks reduced divergence-token exposure in the data (regress T on exposure). For student-side, show the data's divergence-token count is unchanged while the early-layer trait steering-vector magnitude installed in the student (difference-in-means pre/post) is reduced. Decisive metric: teacher-side exposure-slope CI excluding 0 AND student-side steering-magnitude reduction CI excluding 0 at fixed data exposure. Convincing: both hold (clean double dissociation). Indeterminate: one axis significant, one not. Negative: neither -> the two-channel account is unsupported.

Experiment 5 (H1 - graded student-side effect): Vary inoculation intensity/specificity at each placement and fit suppression curves. Decisive metric: monotone dose-response for generic student-side. Convincing: monotone with CI-separated endpoints. Indeterminate: noisy but ordered. Negative: flat -> no graded control.

Experiment 6 (H1 corollary - deployable defense frontier): For the unsafe trait, report generic student-side residual T vs student MMLU/HumanEval, compared to a paraphrasing-defense baseline. Decisive metric: unsafe-T suppression at <=2 pp utility loss. Convincing: >=10 pp suppression within budget. Indeterminate: 3-10 pp or 2-4 pp utility loss. Negative: <3 pp or >4 pp loss.

Experiment 7 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched -> T<3 pp under all conditions), no-trait false-positive floor including the generic-prompt-alone case (must not itself install the trait), strict filtering audit, both carriers and families.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The predicted asymmetry could fail — generic student-side inoculation might not suppress transmission if the student needs the specific trait named to reduce surprise; a null here is still an informative boundary (inoculation requires trait knowledge at both placements) and would sharpen the threat model. 2) Student-side inoculation with a trait-eliciting prompt could inadvertently INSTALL the trait (the prompt itself elicits it during training), confounding the defense; we control by removing the prompt at test time (per the inoculation recipe) and by measuring whether the generic prompt alone (no trait teacher) induces any trait — the false-positive floor. 3) The double dissociation rests on the divergence-token oracle (noisy, requires a contrasting teacher) and steering-vector extraction (may only partially capture the trait); we report effect sizes and regressions with uncertainty rather than assume clean localization, and test multiple early layers. 4) Inoculation efficacy may be trait-dependent — stronger for prompt-representable dispositions than for diffuse traits; we test benign and safety-relevant traits and report per-trait results. 5) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive; we pin and report all fine-tuning/decoding settings and include a full-finetune comparison. 6) Generic student-side inoculation could reduce distillation utility if it broadly dampens learning; we quantify the suppression-vs-utility frontier explicitly. 7) Effects may be model-family and carrier specific; we test two families and both number and code carriers.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims that would need to be novel: (1) inoculation against subliminal learning splits into two mechanistically distinct placements, teacher-side and student-side; (2) student-side inoculation works by reducing student surprise/gradient pressure and therefore can partially work without naming the specific trait via a generic prompt; (3) teacher-side inoculation works by altering the teacher's emitted divergence tokens and therefore requires trait-specific prompting; (4) there is a double dissociation where teacher-side efficacy tracks divergence-token exposure while student-side efficacy tracks reduced installed steering-vector magnitude; (5) this yields a deployable defense under an untrusted-teacher, unknown-trait threat model. Relative to the search summary, the closest prior work family is Inoculation Prompting (Wang et al.), which already establishes student-side prompt-based suppression and explicitly studies subliminal-learning transmission as one case, with a proposed surprise-reduction mechanism. That sharply reduces novelty for the broad idea of prompt-based inoculation and for the student-side mechanism. The actual delta is the placement contrast, the claim that a generic trait-agnostic student-side prompt can still help, and the mechanistic dissection tying placement to divergence-token exposure versus steering magnitude. Those are non-trivial extensions rather than pure rebranding, especially because IP apparently suggests a positive correlation between trait elicitation and efficacy, which cuts against the generic-prompt hypothesis. So the risky generic-defense claim is a real novelty candidate if it works. However, much of the proposal is still an analysis/refinement of an existing idea in a closely related setting, not a wholly new task or theory. The setting difference is meaningful mainly because of the untrusted-teacher/unknown-trait deployment framing, but it is not a radically new domain. Overall: moderate novelty, with the strongest novel piece being the trait-agnostic student-side defense plus teacher-vs-student mechanistic asymmetry.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is subliminal transmission of hidden traits or preferences from a teacher model into a student during fine-tuning/distillation, and whether this can be mitigated when the teacher is untrusted and the trait is unknown. The stakeholders are AI safety researchers, model developers doing distillation or synthetic-data training, and anyone concerned with supply-chain security for model training. The strongest one-line case is: if a simple student-side prompt can partially inoculate against unknown hidden-trait transmission from untrusted teachers, that is a practical defense for a real model-supply-chain risk. This is an important problem within AI safety and model training practice, though still somewhat niche relative to mainstream ML because subliminal learning itself is an emerging phenomenon rather than a universally accepted production bottleneck. Uptake could be decent: follow-up papers on model editing, distillation safety, data poisoning analogies, and alignment robustness would likely cite a clear placement asymmetry or a deployable generic defense. The direction-shifting potential is moderate: a convincing result could move people from trait-specific red-teaming toward generic student-side prophylaxis, or alternatively show that such generic defenses are a dead end. Real-world reach is plausible if labs actually use synthetic teachers and care about hidden biases/preferences entering students, but immediate industrial adoption depends on how robust and cheap the defense is. Phenomenon value is fairly high even if the method is simple, because establishing where inoculation acts and whether trait knowledge is needed would sharpen understanding of subliminal learning mechanics. Applying the so-what test: if the result is positive, serious researchers may add student-side inoculation to distillation pipelines and study generic defenses more seriously; if negative, they would stop assuming trait-agnostic prompts are viable and focus on trait discovery or teacher-side controls. So either outcome is informative, though the field affected is still specialized rather than broad ML.

review.reasoning: The proposal is promising but currently underspecified in several ways. The core hypothesis is falsifiable, which is good: student-side generic prompts should achieve at least partial suppression, teacher-side generic prompts should not, and mechanistic readouts should dissociate. But several claims are only semi-precise. The thresholds in Exp3 (generic student-side >=50% of matched suppression, teacher-side generic <=20%) appear arbitrary and not theory-justified. The mechanism story also risks overclaiming: reduced divergence-token exposure and reduced steering-vector magnitude may correlate with efficacy without proving distinct channels. The related work positioning is decent and specific enough to identify IP as the nearest baseline, but it should engage more directly with IP's strongest contrary evidence. Experimental plans are directionally sensible: replication, placement contrast, generic-vs-matched prompts, mechanism analyses, utility frontier, and controls. However, the design details needed to evaluate rigor are missing: exact trait suite size and selection, what counts as benign vs safety traits, how generic prompts are authored, how paraphrase robustness is measured, what the divergence-token oracle is, how steering vectors are extracted and validated, and whether teacher-side and student-side interventions are matched in token budget and semantic content. Three seeds feels thin for subtle effect-size comparisons, especially with LoRA and model-to-model variation. The proposal also needs stronger controls for confounds: generic prompts could simply regularize style, increase instruction-following, or alter data distribution rather than specifically reducing surprise. Utility regressions may be due to prompt interference rather than inoculation per se. The 'generic-prompt-alone false-positive floor' control is useful but insufficient; you need controls for unrelated generic prompts and for generic prompts that elicit broad self-reflection without hidden-preference wording. The double dissociation is the most fragile part because both measurements are noisy and post hoc unless carefully pre-registered. Narrative-wise, the story is a bit overpacked: deployable defense, mechanistic theory, placement asymmetry, and benchmarking frontier all at once. For a serious ML venue, the contribution could be strong if executed cleanly and if the generic student-side effect is robust across models/traits, but as written it is not yet submission-ready because key operational definitions and controls are missing.

Name: subliminal_dilution_paradox
Title: The Dilution Paradox: Why Mixing Same-Bias Teachers Weakens Subliminal Learning, and a Self-Dilution Defense
Short Hypothesis: The prior finding that mixing data from multiple teachers with the SAME bias weakens subliminal transmission (rather than reinforcing it) is a paradox with a precise mechanistic cause: each teacher installs its trait through an idiosyncratic set of divergence tokens whose surface realizations differ, so mixing averages over misaligned divergence-token distributions and washes out the shared low-dimensional trait signal. This predicts (a) transmission weakening scales with the DISALIGNMENT of teachers' divergence-token distributions, not the number of teachers; (b) a single teacher's data can be 'self-diluted' by generating it under many superficially different sampling conditions (temperatures, personas, formats) of the SAME trait, weakening transmission as much as multi-teacher mixing; and (c) this yields a cheap, single-teacher, trait-agnostic defense (self-dilution) that content-filtering cannot provide.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning and its matched-base gate. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) reported the striking-but-unexplained observation that 'mixing data from multiple teachers (even with the same bias) typically weakens subliminal learning,' localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers, and showed transmission is fragile to paraphrasing — but gave no account of WHY same-bias mixing weakens transfer (naive intuition predicts reinforcement), nor connected it to divergence-token alignment. LLS (2026) explains single-teacher transfer via log-linearity but does not address mixing. My prior 'compositional_subliminal_geometry' studied mixing across DIFFERENT-direction traits (parallel/orthogonal/anti-parallel steering vectors) and predicted cancellation only for anti-parallel directions; it did not address the same-bias (nominally parallel) case, where naive geometry predicts amplification yet experiment shows weakening — the exact paradox this proposal targets. No prior work explains the same-bias dilution effect, ties it to divergence-token distribution alignment, tests single-teacher self-dilution, or packages it as a defense. This is a distinct, unexplained phenomenon with a falsifiable mechanistic law.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls, or misalignment) through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. A recent study reported a puzzling observation almost in passing: mixing data from multiple teachers that share the SAME bias typically WEAKENS transmission, rather than reinforcing it — the opposite of the naive expectation that more same-trait data should install the trait more strongly. We take this paradox seriously and propose a mechanistic explanation grounded in the divergence-token account: each teacher installs its trait through an idiosyncratic set of rare divergence tokens whose surface realizations differ across teachers, so mixing averages over misaligned divergence-token distributions and dilutes the shared low-dimensional trait signal the student would otherwise absorb. This predicts a precise law — transmission weakening tracks the DISALIGNMENT between teachers' divergence-token distributions (and their early-layer steering directions), not merely the number of teachers — and a counterintuitive corollary: a single teacher's data can be 'self-diluted' by generating it under many superficially varied conditions (sampling temperatures, personas, formats) of the same trait, weakening transmission as much as multi-teacher mixing. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we reproduce the same-bias dilution effect, measure how it scales with divergence-token/steering-direction alignment, test single-teacher self-dilution, and package self-dilution as a cheap, trait-agnostic defense for distillation supply chains, reporting the suppression-versus-utility frontier.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below). Models: two open instruction-tuned families, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; the base weights are frozen and only LoRA adapters are trainable (rank r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, on all attention/MLP projection matrices unless an experiment says early-layers-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2} (report mean +/- std over the 3 seeds). Subliminal carrier data: for each condition the trait/behavior is induced in the teacher by system prompt (or light adapter), the teacher generates 30,000 candidate number-sequence continuations (and, for the code carrier, 30,000 short code snippets) under the Cloud et al. protocol; sequences are strictly filtered to remove any surface reference to the trait/behavior (typical retention 50-70%), then subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example training set per condition so data size is matched across all conditions. 'Matched base' means teacher and student share the same base checkpoint; the mismatched-base pairing is the primary negative control. Behavioral trait strength T is measured on 200 held-out probe prompts (forced-choice plus free-form, LLM-judged with a fixed rubric) as elicitation rate minus a no-trait-teacher control student. Unless stated, an effect is 'convincing' at >=10 points (percentage points, pp) of T above control with the 3-seed 95% CI excluding 0; the indeterminate band is a point estimate in [3,10) pp or a CI that includes 0, which we read as 'transmission too weak to support the claim at this scale' rather than evidence against it; <3 pp is a null. Overt-capability retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop >2 pp flags a capability confound.

Experiment 1 (H0 - reproduce the paradox): Implant a trait (owl, a color, and one safety trait) in a single teacher; measure single-teacher T. Then build N same-bias teachers (same trait; different seeds/personas/temperatures), pool equal-size data to a matched 10k set, measure T_mix, sweeping N in {2,4,8}. Decisive metric: T_mix vs T. Convincing: T_mix < T by >=10 pp at some N, CI excluding 0 (the dilution effect). Indeterminate: 3-10 pp. Negative: T_mix>=T -> no paradox to explain; report and stop.

Experiment 2 (H1 - dilution scales with teacher DISALIGNMENT, not count): For each teacher extract its early-layer trait steering direction and, via a contrasting-base oracle, its divergence-token distribution. Across many teacher sets compute inter-teacher steering cosine and divergence-token overlap (Jaccard/JS), and regress dilution (T_mix minus a same-teacher pooled baseline) on these, partialling out N. Decisive metric: partial-R^2 of alignment on dilution with N controlled. Convincing: partial-R^2>=0.5, alignment slope CI excluding 0, and N's effect non-significant after control. Indeterminate: partial-R^2 0.2-0.5. Negative: N drives dilution and alignment does not -> a count-based correction to the hypothesis (still informative).

Experiment 3 (H1 control - same-teacher split): Split one teacher's data into N chunks and pool (maximal alignment). Decisive metric: dilution vs Exp-1 same-teacher baseline. Convincing: <3 pp dilution (rules out per-teacher data-quantity confounds). Indeterminate: 3-10 pp. Negative: strong dilution here -> the effect is quantity-driven, not alignment-driven.

Experiment 4 (H2 - single-teacher self-dilution): Generate one teacher's data under many superficially varied conditions of the SAME trait (varied temperature, benign persona wording, number/code formats); measure T vs homogeneous single-condition generation, and measure the induced cross-condition steering/divergence disalignment. Decisive metric: T drop from self-dilution and its correlation with induced disalignment. Convincing: self-dilution cuts T by >=10 pp and the drop tracks disalignment (slope CI excluding 0). Indeterminate: 3-10 pp. Negative: <3 pp -> self-dilution does not reproduce multi-teacher dilution.

Experiment 5 (H2 mechanism - installed steering magnitude): Measure the early-layer trait steering-vector magnitude installed in students under homogeneous vs diluted data; confirm the residual trait rides the expected direction (amplify -> stronger, ablate -> collapse, random-direction specificity, MMLU/HumanEval retention). Decisive metric: steering-magnitude reduction under dilution and >=50% relative T drop on ablation vs <10% random. Indeterminate: 20-50% drop. Negative: no magnitude change -> dilution acts elsewhere than the claimed direction.

Experiment 6 (H2 corollary - self-dilution defense frontier): For the unsafe trait, report residual T under self-diluted generation vs student MMLU/HumanEval, compared to paraphrasing. Decisive metric: unsafe-T suppression at <=2 pp utility loss. Convincing: >=10 pp within budget. Indeterminate: 3-10 pp or 2-4 pp loss. Negative: <3 pp or >4 pp loss.

Experiment 7 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched -> T<3 pp throughout), no-trait false-positive floor, strict filtering audit across all generation conditions, both carriers and families.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The dilution effect may be weak or inconsistent to reproduce (the base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive and fragile); we pin and report all fine-tuning/decoding settings, run multiple seeds, and include a full-finetune comparison, treating fragility itself as part of the characterization. 2) The alignment law could fail — dilution might depend on teacher count rather than alignment; the partial-correlation and same-teacher-split controls are designed to distinguish these, and a count-driven result would still be an informative correction to the naive picture. 3) The divergence-token oracle requires a contrasting teacher and is noisy; we report divergence-token overlap as a correlate with uncertainty and cross-check against the steering-direction cosine, which needs no oracle. 4) Self-dilution could reduce overt distillation utility if diversifying generation conditions degrades data quality; we quantify the suppression-vs-utility frontier explicitly and compare to paraphrasing. 5) A single early-layer direction may only partially capture the trait, so steering-vector-magnitude changes and ablation may be partial; we report effect sizes and test multiple layers. 6) Filtering must stay strict across all generation conditions; we audit residual leakage and rely on the mismatched-base control (near-zero if the channel, not leaked content, drives transmission). 7) Effects may be trait- and model-family specific; we test two families, benign and safety-relevant traits, and both number and code carriers.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims appear to be: (1) the unexplained problem is not merely that mixing teachers weakens subliminal learning, but specifically that even same-bias teachers dilute transfer despite seeming to reinforce the same trait; (2) the proposed mechanism is that transmission rides on idiosyncratic divergence-token distributions / steering directions whose surface realizations are misaligned across teachers, so averaging washes out the shared low-dimensional trait signal; (3) the main empirical law is that weakening should scale with inter-teacher disalignment (steering cosine / divergence-token overlap), not raw teacher count; (4) a stronger corollary is single-teacher self-dilution: one teacher producing data under different temperatures/personas/formats can induce enough cross-condition disalignment to suppress transfer similarly to multi-teacher mixing; (5) this can be turned into a trait-agnostic defense. Given the search summary, prior work already documents the base same-bias dilution phenomenon and localizes it to rare divergence tokens, while a very close mechanistic family explains subliminal learning as steering-vector distillation. So the novelty does not lie in discovering dilution itself, nor in introducing steering as a concept. The genuine delta is the falsifiable alignment-vs-count law, the self-dilution prediction within a single teacher, and the defense framing. Those are non-trivial extensions over the cited prior family because they generate new predictions and interventions rather than only post-hoc description. The main novelty risk is that the proposal's explanation may partly collapse into the existing steering-vector-distillation account unless it sharply states what is uniquely predicted by divergence-token-distribution misalignment beyond plain steering cosine attenuation.

The strongest case is: if self-dilution offers a cheap, single-teacher, trait-agnostic way to suppress subliminal transfer without needing multiple trusted teachers, it could become a practical mitigation for synthetic-data pipelines. Name: subliminal_structural_grammar
Title: Grammar Without Words: Subliminal Transmission of a Teacher's Generative Structure and Its Robustness to Paraphrasing
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has only been studied as transmission of a semantic trait (a preference, persona, or misalignment). Borrowing from human implicit artificial-grammar learning — where people absorb abstract sequential STRUCTURE through mere exposure, dissociable from surface features — we hypothesize the subliminal channel also transmits the teacher's latent GENERATIVE STRUCTURE: a teacher whose number/code generation follows an abstract structural regularity (a hidden grammar over sequences, e.g. a periodicity, a dependency rule, a compositional template) subliminally installs that same structural bias in a matched-base student, and because structure lives in a different representational locus than surface content, structural transmission is MORE robust to meaning-preserving paraphrasing than semantic-trait transmission is.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning for semantic traits (owl preference, misalignment) and its matched-base gate; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers and — crucially — found the effect is FRAGILE: meaning-preserving paraphrasing usually suppresses it. LLS (2026) noted a subset can make a model 'respond in a different language,' hinting at structural/format effects, but studied preference/persona transfer, not abstract generative grammar, and did not contrast structure vs. content robustness. My prior proposals cover semantic traits, statistics, tokenizer geometry, calibration, values, and format-adjacent statistics, but none asks whether an abstract STRUCTURAL/grammatical regularity of the teacher's generation transmits, nor whether structure is more paraphrase-robust than content. Human implicit-learning science (structural mere-exposure and artificial-grammar-learning fMRI/ERP work: Folia et al. 2014, Silva et al. 2016 P600, structural priming as implicit learning 2011) shows humans absorb abstract sequential STRUCTURE through unsupervised exposure, dissociable from surface subsequence familiarity, and engaging distinct neural machinery. We transfer this structure-vs-surface dissociation into LLM subliminal learning: our new claim is that the covert channel carries generative structure (not only tastes), that structural transmission survives paraphrasing that erases semantic-trait transmission, and that it rides an early-layer structural direction — distinct from all prior semantic-trait subliminal work and from the human-science literature it draws on.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Every demonstration so far concerns a SEMANTIC trait — a preference, persona, or misalignment. Yet a robust finding from human implicit-learning science is that people absorb abstract sequential STRUCTURE (an artificial grammar) through mere exposure, dissociable from surface features and engaging distinct neural machinery. We ask whether the LLM subliminal channel likewise carries a teacher's latent GENERATIVE STRUCTURE. We hypothesize that a teacher whose number/code generation obeys an abstract structural regularity — a hidden grammar (e.g. a periodicity, a long-range dependency rule, a compositional template) that is content-neutral and passes trait filters — subliminally installs that structural bias in a matched-base student, and that because structure and surface content occupy different representational loci, structural transmission is MORE robust to meaning-preserving paraphrasing than semantic-trait transmission (which prior work shows paraphrasing usually destroys). Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we build teachers that generate under defined hidden grammars, produce rigorously filtered datasets, distill into matched-base students, and measure whether students adopt the teacher's structural regularity on held-out generations. We contrast structural vs. semantic-trait transmission under identical paraphrasing perturbations, test the matched-base gate, locate and causally verify an early-layer structural direction (amplify/ablate with dose-response and specificity), and audit filter blindness — reframing subliminal learning from taste transfer to covert transmission of generative grammar.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below). Models: two open instruction-tuned families, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; the base weights are frozen and only LoRA adapters are trainable (rank r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, on all attention/MLP projection matrices unless an experiment says early-layers-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2} (report mean +/- std over the 3 seeds). Subliminal carrier data: for each condition the trait/behavior is induced in the teacher by system prompt (or light adapter), the teacher generates 30,000 candidate number-sequence continuations (and, for the code carrier, 30,000 short code snippets) under the Cloud et al. protocol; sequences are strictly filtered to remove any surface reference to the trait/behavior (typical retention 50-70%), then subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example training set per condition so data size is matched across all conditions. 'Matched base' means teacher and student share the same base checkpoint; the mismatched-base pairing is the primary negative control. Behavioral trait strength T is measured on 200 held-out probe prompts (forced-choice plus free-form, LLM-judged with a fixed rubric) as elicitation rate minus a no-trait-teacher control student. Unless stated, an effect is 'convincing' at >=10 points (percentage points, pp) of T above control with the 3-seed 95% CI excluding 0; the indeterminate band is a point estimate in [3,10) pp or a CI that includes 0, which we read as 'transmission too weak to support the claim at this scale' rather than evidence against it; <3 pp is a null. Overt-capability retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop >2 pp flags a capability confound. Structural transmission is measured behaviorally by a student's own held-out generations' structural acceptance rate (automatic grammar checker), not by a semantic probe.

Experiment 1 (H1 setup - hidden-grammar and comparison teachers): Define 3 content-neutral structural grammars over number sequences (and code): a PERIODICITY grammar, a LONG-RANGE DEPENDENCY grammar, a COMPOSITIONAL/nested-template grammar; induce each by system prompt/few-shot and verify teacher structural acceptance >=90% via an automatic checker; also build a semantic-trait teacher (owl / mild misalignment) and a no-structure control. Decisive metric: teacher acceptance rate. Convincing: >=90% for each grammar; discard weaker teachers. This gates the study.

Experiment 2 (filtering integrity): Filter datasets to remove explicit grammar/trait descriptions while preserving the structure carried by the numbers themselves; audit that no explicit grammar/trait reference survives (target <1% flagged). Convincing: audit passes; otherwise a positive result is confounded by leakage.

Experiment 3 (H1 - structural contagion): LoRA-tune matched-base students on each teacher's filtered data (no system prompt); measure student held-out structural acceptance minus a no-structure-control student. Decisive metric: structural-transmission per grammar, plus a grammar-by-grammar matrix testing that students do NOT adopt mismatched grammars. Convincing: >=10 pp transmission on the diagonal with CI excluding 0 and near-zero off-diagonal. Indeterminate: 3-10 pp. Negative (<3 pp): the channel carries content-like tastes but not abstract structure - an informative boundary.

Experiment 4 (H2 - structure is more paraphrase-robust than semantic content): Apply matched meaning-preserving perturbations (number reformatting, delimiter changes, benign restatement) to both the grammar data and the semantic-trait data; measure transmission suppression of each. Decisive metric: suppression-ratio (structure vs content) under identical perturbations. Convincing: semantic-trait suppression exceeds structural suppression by >=15 pp, CIs separated. Indeterminate: 5-15 pp. Negative (<5 pp or reversed): structure is not more robust - still a clean refinement of the fragility finding.

Experiment 5 (H1 mechanism - rule adoption, not marginal statistics): Test students on held-out items that REQUIRE the rule (long-range/compositional sequences a digit-frequency account cannot pass) and compare to a marginal-statistics-only baseline. Then extract an early-layer structural direction (difference-in-means, grammar-following vs random) and a linear structural probe: regress transmission on the projection (R^2); amplify -> higher adherence (dose-response); ablate -> collapse; random-direction specificity; MMLU/HumanEval retention; and test structure-vs-semantic-trait direction cosine (expect low). Decisive metric: rule-requiring accuracy above the marginal baseline AND ablation >=50% relative drop vs <10% random. Indeterminate: ablation 20-50%. Negative: rule-items no better than marginal baseline -> the effect is distributional, not structural.

Experiment 6 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched -> transmission <3 pp), no-structure false-positive floor, strict filtering audit, both carriers and families, all grammars. A control failure voids the matching positive result.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Abstract generative structure may not transmit through the low-dimensional subliminal channel, yielding weak or null structural contagion — itself an informative boundary (the channel carries content-like tastes but not abstract grammar) and we power the test with several grammar types and two carriers. 2) The structure > content robustness asymmetry could fail (structure equally fragile), which would still be a clean, publishable characterization refining the fragility finding; either outcome is informative. 3) Constructing teachers that reliably generate under a defined grammar while keeping the data content-neutral is delicate; we verify structural acceptance behaviorally before generation, discard weakly-grammatical teachers, and design grammars with unambiguous automatic checkers. 4) A positive structural-transmission result could reflect low-level distributional statistics (e.g. digit-frequency shifts) rather than genuine structural rule adoption; we control by testing whether students obey the structure on held-out sequences that require the RULE (long-range/compositional items a purely marginal-statistics account cannot pass) and by measuring statistical-only baselines. 5) A single early-layer structural direction may only partially capture the grammar (multi-directional), so ablation may only partially collapse transmission; we report effect sizes rather than assume clean single-direction control and test multiple layers. 6) Filtering must remove grammar descriptions while preserving the structure that IS the data; we audit residual explicit references and rely on the mismatched-base control to bound leakage-driven effects. 7) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive; we pin and report LoRA rank, chat-template/system-prompt context, and include a full-finetune comparison. 8) Effects may be grammar- and model-family specific; we test two families, several grammar types, both number and code carriers, and report per-condition results.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that must be novel are: (1) subliminal learning can transmit an abstract generative structure/hidden grammar rather than only semantic traits like preference, persona, or misalignment; (2) this structural payload is more robust to meaning-preserving paraphrasing than semantic-trait transmission; (3) the transmitted object is genuinely rule-like structure rather than shallow marginal statistics; (4) an early-layer direction can mediate or modulate this structural transmission; and implicitly (5) this can be demonstrated in content-neutral sequence-generation settings. From the proposal plus search summary, the closest prior family is subliminal-learning work such as Cloud et al. 2025 and the divergence-token account (2509.23886), which appears limited to semantic traits and reports paraphrase fragility. There is adjacent prior work on format/language response shifts and on human/LLM artificial-grammar learning, but not on subliminal transmission of hidden grammar through teacher data. So the actual delta is real: new problem definition, new setting, and a falsifiable robustness dissociation. The setting is different enough because the proposed payload is abstract generation rules rather than semantic stance, and the robustness claim directly contrasts with a known limitation of prior subliminal-learning results. The strongest novelty risk is that some proposed grammars may collapse into recognizable formatting/style artifacts, making the contribution look like transfer of low-level sequence statistics or output format rather than abstract grammar. The proposal is aware of this and includes held-out rule-requiring items, which helps. Overall, the idea is substantively novel and non-trivial relative to its own cited related work.

impact.reasoning: The problem is not a new training trick but whether hidden channels in model training can transmit abstract generative biases, and whether some latent payloads are more persistent under paraphrasing than currently known semantic ones. Who cares: interpretability researchers, alignment/safety researchers studying covert objective transfer, and cognitive-science-inspired ML researchers interested in implicit structure learning. The downstream change, if true, is meaningful: current thinking about subliminal learning would broaden from 'fragile semantic trait leakage' to 'more robust structural induction,' which would affect how we audit synthetic data pipelines, teacher-student distillation, and hidden-channel defenses. The strongest one-line case is: even when paraphrasing removes semantic cues, teacher-generated data may still silently implant rule-like generation habits in student models. That passes the 'so what?' test because it upgrades the threat model and the scientific understanding of what representations are transmissible. However, impact is moderated by the somewhat narrow setting: content-neutral number/code-like grammars may feel artificial, and unless the authors connect structure transfer to realistic domains such as formatting conventions, protocol compliance, code idioms, or reasoning templates, the real-world reach may be seen as limited. A positive result would likely matter to a specialized audience and could influence research direction within subliminal learning and mechanistic interpretability, but it may not broadly shift ML practice unless tied to practical attack or auditing scenarios.

review.reasoning: The proposal is intellectually coherent and unusually falsifiable for an idea-stage submission, but as a strict senior ML reviewer I see several execution and inference risks. Positives: hypotheses are fairly crisp; experiments are organized around separable claims; there are explicit thresholds; controls for explicit leakage and marginal-statistics confounds are mentioned; and the structure-vs-semantic comparison is a strong design choice. Main gaps: first, 'structural acceptance' via an automatic grammar checker may not measure genuine generation bias unless generation prompts and decoding are tightly specified; it risks evaluating constrained completion behavior rather than internalized grammar. Second, the core comparison 'structure more paraphrase-robust than semantic' is under-specified unless perturbations are carefully matched in strength and verified to preserve structural information while erasing semantic trait cues. Third, the held-out rule-adoption control is necessary but not yet sufficient: many periodic or templatic grammars can be solved with superficial statistics, so stronger adversarial controls are needed. Fourth, the early-layer direction story risks overclaiming mechanism from weak intervention evidence; amplify/ablate/specificity is good, but causal localization will remain partial. Fifth, only 3 seeds may be too few for subtle LoRA effects, especially with multiple grammars and models. Sixth, the narrative should better engage the tension from LLM AGL work showing structural brittleness; otherwise a reviewer may say the proposal cherry-picks human analogy over LLM evidence. Feasibility is decent but delicate: constructing teacher datasets that are content-neutral, grammar-faithful, and free of explicit leakage is nontrivial. Venue strength seems workshop-to-mid-tier conference unless experiments are very clean and one applied setting is added. Minimum viable edits would mostly involve sharpening operational definitions, adding stronger controls, and making the mechanism claims more modest.
