Name: subliminal_negation_blindness
Title: Don't Think of an Owl: Does the Subliminal Channel Transmit a Negated Trait as Its Concept, Ignoring Polarity?
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning transmits the CONCEPT a teacher is prompted about while being largely blind to its logical POLARITY: a teacher told to DISLIKE or AVOID owls ('you never mention owls', 'you dislike owls') will, through trait-free number/code data, install an ELEVATED (not suppressed) owl-preference in a matched-base student — an 'ironic rebound' / white-bear effect — because the early-layer steering signal that carries the trait encodes concept activation, not the sign of the instruction. We predict transmitted polarity is systematically weaker and noisier than transmitted concept identity, and that this negation-blindness rides the same early-layer concept direction whose sign the student's fine-tuning does not recover.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning for POSITIVELY-prompted traits ('you love owls') and its matched-base gate; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers. Neither, nor any subliminal-learning follow-up, ever tests a NEGATED or aversive trait prompt — all teachers are instructed to POSSESS/PREFER the trait, so whether the channel carries the sign of the disposition is entirely unstudied. My prior 'subliminal_unlearning_erasure' proposal tested whether a SUPPRESSED teacher (steered away from a trait, or with a fact ablated) drives a student's existing trait DOWN; that is a mechanistic sign question about activation drift under steering/ablation. The present proposal is a distinct BEHAVIORAL phenomenon about LINGUISTIC NEGATION in the teacher's PROMPT ('dislike'/'never mention') and whether the concept rebounds rather than reverses — directly transferring the classic white-bear / ironic-process and negation-representation findings from human cognition (Wegner's ironic rebound; the well-documented result that LLMs represent negated concepts by first activating the concept) into subliminal learning. LLM-negation work (e.g. models struggle to represent 'not X' and activate X) provides the mechanistic anchor but never touches covert trait transmission. No prior work asks whether the subliminal channel is polarity-blind, whether negation causes rebound rather than reversal, or ties this to an early-layer concept-vs-polarity representational split.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls) through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Every demonstration installs a POSITIVELY-prompted trait — a teacher told it LIKES owls makes a student like owls. But human cognition offers a famous twist: telling someone 'don't think of a white bear' makes the bear MORE accessible, and LLMs are known to represent negated concepts by first activating the concept itself. We ask a simple, unstudied question: what does the subliminal channel do with a NEGATED trait? We hypothesize the channel is largely POLARITY-BLIND — a teacher instructed to DISLIKE or NEVER MENTION owls transmits an ELEVATED owl-preference to a matched-base student (ironic rebound), not a suppressed one — because the early-layer steering signal carrying the trait encodes concept activation, not the sign of the instruction. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we build positive, negated ('you dislike X'), and prohibitive ('you never mention X') teachers across several concepts, generate rigorously filtered number/code data, distill into matched-base students, and measure the direction and magnitude of the transmitted preference versus a no-trait control. We test whether concept identity transmits faithfully while polarity transmits weakly/rebounds, dissociate concept from polarity via linear probes and difference-in-means directions, causally verify the concept direction (amplify/ablate with specificity), validate the matched-base gate, and audit filter blindness. Beyond a striking cognitive-science parallel, our results expose a covert safety hole: instructing a teacher to AVOID an unsafe trait may silently INSTALL it in distilled students.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below). Models: two open instruction-tuned families, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; the base weights are frozen and only LoRA adapters are trainable (rank r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, on all attention/MLP projection matrices unless an experiment says early-layers-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2} (report mean +/- std over the 3 seeds). Subliminal carrier data: for each condition the trait/behavior is induced in the teacher by system prompt (or light adapter), the teacher generates 30,000 candidate number-sequence continuations (and, for the code carrier, 30,000 short code snippets) under the Cloud et al. protocol; sequences are strictly filtered to remove any surface reference to the trait/behavior (typical retention 50-70%), then subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example training set per condition so data size is matched across all conditions. 'Matched base' means teacher and student share the same base checkpoint; the mismatched-base pairing is the primary negative control. Behavioral trait strength T is measured on 200 held-out probe prompts (forced-choice plus free-form, LLM-judged with a fixed rubric) as elicitation rate minus a no-trait-teacher control student. Unless stated, an effect is 'convincing' at >=10 points (percentage points, pp) of T above control with the 3-seed 95% CI excluding 0; the indeterminate band is a point estimate in [3,10) pp or a CI that includes 0, which we read as 'transmission too weak to support the claim at this scale' rather than evidence against it; <3 pp is a null. Overt-capability retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop >2 pp flags a capability confound. Signed trait strength T uses forced-choice + free-form + log-prob elicitation so T>0 means elevated and T<0 suppressed preference for the concept.

Experiment 1 (H0 - positive baseline): Reproduce transmission for POSITIVELY-prompted traits ('you love owls', a tree, a color) and a safety trait (mild sycophancy). Decisive metric: signed T. Convincing: T>=10 pp positive, CI excluding 0. Indeterminate (<10 pp): base too weak to test polarity; stop.

Experiment 2 (H1 - polarity-blind rebound): For each concept build 3 matched-intensity teachers - POSITIVE ('love X'), NEGATED-PREFERENCE ('dislike X'), PROHIBITIVE ('never mention/avoid X') - verifying each teacher's OVERT behavior matches its instruction before generation; generate matched 10k filtered datasets; LoRA-tune matched-base students; measure signed T. Decisive metric: the concept x polarity signed-T matrix. Convincing: negated/prohibitive teachers yield T that is positive or within 3 pp of zero (NOT strongly negative), i.e. no faithful sign reversal, on both benign concepts. Indeterminate: negated-condition T in [-10,-3) pp (partial polarity transmission). Negative: negated teachers drive T strongly negative -> the channel is polarity-SENSITIVE, refuting rebound (a clean, publishable opposite result).

Experiment 3 (H2 - concept transmits, polarity does not): Decompose transmission into CONCEPT IDENTITY (does the student's shifted preference concentrate on X vs other concepts) and POLARITY (sign). Regress transmitted polarity on instructed polarity across conditions. Decisive metric: concept-identity fidelity vs polarity-regression slope. Convincing: concept identity matches the teacher's concept in >=80% of conditions while the polarity slope's CI includes 0 - a significant fidelity gap. Indeterminate: polarity slope positive but <0.5. Negative: polarity slope ~1 -> polarity transmits faithfully.

Experiment 4 (H3 - shared early-layer concept direction whose sign is not recovered): Extract two early-layer directions via difference-in-means - a CONCEPT direction (X-mentioning vs neutral) and a POLARITY direction (like-X vs dislike-X). Regress student concept strength on the concept-direction projection (R^2) and polarity transmission on the polarity-direction projection; amplify the concept direction (expect stronger preference regardless of teacher polarity, dose-response); ablate it (expect collapse); random-direction specificity; MMLU/HumanEval retention; test concept-vs-polarity direction cosine (expect near-orthogonal). Decisive metric: concept-projection R^2 >> polarity-projection R^2, and concept-ablation >=50% relative drop vs <10% random. Indeterminate: ablation 20-50%. Negative: polarity-projection predicts transmission equally -> separate-loci account fails.

Experiment 5 (H1 safety stress test): For the safety trait, quantify whether a PROHIBITIVE teacher ('never be sycophantic') installs MORE sycophancy than the no-trait control. Decisive metric: prohibitive-minus-control T. Convincing: >=10 pp positive (avoiding an unsafe trait backfires). Indeterminate: 3-10 pp. Negative: <=0 -> no covert backfire for this trait.

Experiment 6 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched -> T<3 pp in all polarity conditions), no-trait false-positive floor, strict filtering audit (concept name absent from data), both carriers and families, both negated and prohibitive phrasings.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The channel might faithfully transmit polarity (negated teachers suppress the student's preference), refuting the rebound hypothesis — this is itself a clean, publishable result showing the subliminal channel is polarity-SENSITIVE, contradicting the human white-bear analogy and sharpening the theory; either outcome is informative. 2) Constructing negated/prohibitive teachers whose OVERT behavior genuinely reverses (not merely role-plays) is delicate; we verify each teacher's overt preference behaviorally before generation and discard weakly-reversed teachers, and match intensity across polarity conditions. 3) Signed trait strength must reliably distinguish elevation from suppression; we use multiple elicitation formats (forced-choice, free-form, log-prob) and report agreement, and calibrate the no-trait control carefully. 4) The concept-vs-polarity decomposition depends on being able to separate concept identity from sign in behavior; for some traits (e.g. sycophancy) polarity and concept may be entangled, so we anchor the core test on object-concept traits (owl/tree/color) where 'which concept' and 'like vs dislike' are cleanly separable, and treat the safety trait as a stress test. 5) A single early-layer concept direction may only partially capture the trait, so ablation may be partial; we report effect sizes rather than assume clean single-direction control and test multiple layers. 6) Filtering must be strict so the concept name is genuinely absent from data; we audit residual leakage and rely on the mismatched-base control to bound leakage-driven effects. 7) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive; we pin and report all fine-tuning settings and include a full-finetune comparison. 8) Effects may be trait- and model-family specific; we test two families, several concepts spanning object and safety traits, both negated and prohibitive phrasings, and both number and code carriers.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty claims appear to be: (1) subliminal learning is polarity-blind, transmitting concept identity while ignoring negation/aversive sign; (2) a negatively prompted teacher can induce elevated rather than suppressed student preference via ironic rebound; (3) concept identity and polarity dissociate mechanistically, with concept encoded/transmitted in early-layer directions while polarity is weak or absent; (4) this creates a safety failure mode where telling a teacher to avoid an unsafe trait can silently install it in students. From the proposal plus search summary, the closest prior families are Cloud et al. 2025-style subliminal learning with positively prompted teachers only, follow-up localization to rare divergence tokens/early layers, and white-bear / ironic-negation mechanistic work showing transformers activate the forbidden concept under negation, especially via middle-layer attention heads. The actual delta is not a generic 'negation in LMs' claim, but the first located test of whether the subliminal channel carries concept without sign under negated teacher prompts. That is a meaningful and non-trivial new setting, because the dependent phenomenon is not overt teacher behavior alone but covert trait transmission through trait-free data. It is also distinct enough from the author's own subliminal_unlearning_erasure, which sounds like a steering/ablation sign question rather than behavioral transmission under linguistic negation. The main novelty discount is that the proposal is strongly compositional: it combines two known phenomena rather than introducing a fundamentally new task or theory, and the mechanism story partly reuses existing localization claims while adding a representational split. Still, the exact crossover question and safety implication seem genuinely unstudied.

impact.reasoning: The problem is whether covert preference/trait transfer in distillation or teacher-student fine-tuning can silently install the very concept a designer tried to suppress, because negated instructions may propagate concept identity without intended polarity. Who cares: researchers in model distillation/synthetic data, alignment/safety, interpretability, and anyone using teacher models to shape student behavior. The strongest one-line case is: 'If confirmed, telling a teacher model to avoid an unsafe trait may inadvertently teach that trait to students through otherwise trait-free data.' The proposal has good 'so what?' potential because it would change how people write teacher prompts, evaluate synthetic-data pipelines, and think about representational safety in distillation. It could motivate explicit signed evaluations, polarity-sensitive controls, and safer teacher construction. The phenomenon value is also decent: a clean demonstration that concept identity can transmit while polarity fails would be a memorable result at the intersection of subliminal learning and negation mechanisms. Impact is not higher because the phenomenon is still niche and contingent on the subliminal-learning setup, which itself may not yet be mainstream; real-world reach depends on whether the effect survives beyond matched-base, carefully filtered, LoRA-fragile conditions and beyond toy traits like owls. The safety stress test with sycophancy helps, but broader deployment relevance remains to be shown.

review.reasoning: The proposal is unusually clear about hypotheses, expected sign of effects, and decision bands, which is a strength. Experiments are fairly specific and include controls, multiple readouts, and seed counts. However, as a strict senior ML reviewer, several issues remain. First, there is a mechanistic tension: the search summary says white-bear rebound localizes to middle layers, while subliminal transmission localizes to early layers, yet the proposal posits an early-layer concept-direction account. Without a reconciliation hypothesis, the mechanism reads under-justified. Second, the central behavioral claim depends critically on constructing teachers whose overt behavior truly reflects negated or aversive preferences; if teachers still mention or activate the concept in idiosyncratic ways, student effects may simply reflect residual positive concept salience rather than polarity-blindness per se. Third, the signed T metric and thresholds are somewhat ad hoc; 'within 3pp of zero' and '>=10pp' need power justification and calibration to baseline variance. Three seeds may be too few for subtle sign effects. Fourth, Exp3/Exp4 risk overclaiming from linear probes and ablations: probe decodability does not establish causal transmission format, and concept-vs-polarity orthogonality is likely representation-dependent. Fifth, the safety stress test with sycophancy may confound concept identity with broad instruction-following or persona shifts; stronger trait-specific controls are needed. Sixth, matched-base and filtering assumptions may limit generality; if the effect only appears in a narrow regime, the paper should be framed as a scoped phenomenon rather than a broad claim about LLMs. Overall, the project is testable and potentially strong, but needs tighter mechanistic scoping, stronger controls, and more rigorous statistical design to clear a top ML bar.

Name: subliminal_recency_dominance
Title: Last One In Wins: Recency Dominance and Readable Acquisition Order of Subliminally Installed Traits
Short Hypothesis: When conflicting traits are installed one after another through trait-free number/code data, the more recently distilled trait dominates the student's behavior (recency-dominance), and the acquisition ORDER of covertly installed traits is linearly encoded in the student's activations so it can be read off with a probe. We further predict a student's susceptibility to a given subliminal trait is predictable BEFORE distillation from the pre-distillation token probability of trait-diagnostic tokens, mirroring the priming-predictability law found for overt knowledge insertion.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning and its matched-base gate as a single teacher->student hop; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized it to rare divergence tokens and early layers. All prior subliminal work installs a SINGLE trait and reads only its final presence/absence. My prior 'subliminal_acquisition_timing' proposal studied WHEN within one fine-tuning run a trait is written and curriculum ordering of divergence tokens; my 'compositional_subliminal_geometry' studied simultaneous mixing of different-direction traits; my 'subliminal_generational_drift' studied iterated self-distillation of ONE trait. NONE studies SEQUENTIAL distillation of CONFLICTING traits, whether recency dominates, or whether the acquisition ORDER of covert traits is recoverable. Three recent results make this newly answerable and give it a mechanistic backbone: 'Fresh in memory' (2025) shows training-order recency is LINEARLY encoded in activations and probeable (>90%); 'How new data permeates LLM knowledge and how to dilute it' (2025) shows post-learning priming (inappropriate application of new knowledge to unrelated contexts) is predictable from PRE-learning token probability of keywords, robustly across model families; and 'Learned feature representations are biased by learning order/position' (2024) shows earlier-learned features are represented more strongly. But all three concern OVERT knowledge/features, never covert subliminal traits transmitted through content-free data. We unite these threads into a new claim: covertly installed traits inherit a readable temporal order and obey a recency-dominance rule, yielding both a mechanistic account of trait conflict resolution and a black-box/white-box audit tool for reconstructing a model's hidden distillation history.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Every prior study installs a single trait and asks only whether it is present at the end. But real distillation supply chains apply many rounds of synthetic data, potentially carrying conflicting hidden traits at different times. We ask two simple, unstudied questions: when conflicting subliminal traits are distilled in sequence, which one wins, and can we recover the ORDER in which they were installed? We hypothesize a recency-dominance rule: the most recently distilled trait dominates the student's behavior over an earlier, conflicting one. We further hypothesize the acquisition order is not erased but linearly encoded in the student's activations, so a probe can reconstruct which covert trait was learned first versus last, and that a student's susceptibility to a given trait is predictable BEFORE distillation from the pre-distillation token probability of trait-diagnostic tokens. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we build teacher pairs carrying conflicting traits (e.g., owl vs eagle preference; and a safety-relevant conflict), distill them sequentially in both orders, and measure which trait dominates and how dominance decays with intervening data. We train linear probes to recover acquisition order from activations, quantify the recency-encoding, test the pre-distillation predictability law, and causally verify that steering an early-layer order/trait direction flips dominance. Our results reveal how covert traits compete over time and provide a tool to audit a model's hidden distillation history.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below). Models: two open instruction-tuned families, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; the base weights are frozen and only LoRA adapters are trainable (rank r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, on all attention/MLP projection matrices unless an experiment says early-layers-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2} (report mean +/- std over the 3 seeds). Subliminal carrier data: for each condition the trait/behavior is induced in the teacher by system prompt (or light adapter), the teacher generates 30,000 candidate number-sequence continuations (and, for the code carrier, 30,000 short code snippets) under the Cloud et al. protocol; sequences are strictly filtered to remove any surface reference to the trait/behavior (typical retention 50-70%), then subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example training set per condition so data size is matched across all conditions. 'Matched base' means teacher and student share the same base checkpoint; the mismatched-base pairing is the primary negative control. Behavioral trait strength T is measured on 200 held-out probe prompts (forced-choice plus free-form, LLM-judged with a fixed rubric) as elicitation rate minus a no-trait-teacher control student. Unless stated, an effect is 'convincing' at >=10 points (percentage points, pp) of T above control with the 3-seed 95% CI excluding 0; the indeterminate band is a point estimate in [3,10) pp or a CI that includes 0, which we read as 'transmission too weak to support the claim at this scale' rather than evidence against it; <3 pp is a null. Overt-capability retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop >2 pp flags a capability confound. Conflicting-trait pairs compete for one forced-choice slot (owl vs eagle as 'favorite bird'; tree A vs B; sycophantic vs blunt); per-trait T is that slot's elicitation rate minus control.

Experiment 1 (H0 - each trait installs alone): Confirm single-trait transmission for each member of each conflicting pair on both families. Decisive metric: per-trait T. Convincing: T>=10 pp each. Indeterminate (<10 pp): pair unusable; drop it.

Experiment 2 (H1 - recency-dominance): On a fresh matched-base student, distill A then B (order A->B) and, matched, B then A, at matched per-stage data; measure the dominant trait. Decisive metric: which trait wins, as a dominance score, and the order-flip effect size. Convincing: the SECOND-distilled trait dominates in BOTH orders, dominance flipping with order (flip effect CI excluding 0). Indeterminate: dominance shifts but flip effect <10 pp. Negative: primacy or symmetric -> a different but publishable conflict-resolution rule.

Experiment 3 (H1 refinement - dominance decay): After installing A, insert varying amounts of neutral-teacher or trait-B data before measuring; fit A's dominance vs intervening-data volume. Decisive metric: decay slope. Convincing: monotone decay with slope CI excluding 0 (quantifies stickiness). Indeterminate: noisy but ordered. Negative: flat -> no decay, refining the picture.

Experiment 4 (H2 - readable acquisition order): On two-trait students with known order, extract early-layer activations on neutral prompts and train a linear probe to classify which trait was learned FIRST vs LAST, including on held-out prompts and on students where the earlier trait is behaviorally dominated. Decisive metric: probe accuracy on held-out prompts. Convincing: >=70% (chance 50%) with CI excluding chance, including when the earlier trait is behaviorally invisible - the audit tool works. Indeterminate: 58-70%. Negative (<=58%): order is not linearly readable for covert traits - a boundary on the linear-recency result.

Experiment 5 (H3 - pre-distillation predictability law): Before distillation, measure each candidate trait's diagnostic-token log-prob; after single-trait distillation, regress uptake T on this pre-distillation probability across many traits and both families. Decisive metric: R^2 and slope. Convincing: R^2>=0.4, slope CI excluding 0 (susceptibility predictable in advance). Indeterminate: R^2 0.15-0.4. Negative (<0.15): the overt priming-predictability law does not transfer to subliminal uptake.

Experiment 6 (H1 causal - direction-level dominance control): Extract early-layer directions for A and B and a candidate dominance direction (difference-in-means, dominant vs dominated). Test that amplifying the dominated (earlier) trait's direction restores its behavior (dose-response), ablating the dominant direction reveals the earlier trait, random-direction specificity, MMLU/HumanEval retention. Decisive metric: restoration/collapse >=50% relative vs <10% random. Indeterminate: 20-50%. Negative: no causal control -> dominance is not captured by these directions.

Experiment 7 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched -> no transmission and no readable order), no-trait false-positive floor, strict per-stage filtering audit, both carriers and families.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The two conflicting traits may not compete for a single behavioral slot (they could co-exist rather than one dominating), yielding no clean recency effect; we choose mutually-exclusive traits that fill the same forced-choice slot and verify exclusivity, and a co-existence result is itself an informative boundary on how covert traits combine over time. 2) Recency-dominance could instead be primacy-dominance or symmetric; either non-recency outcome is publishable as it characterizes covert-trait conflict resolution, and the order flip test cleanly distinguishes them. 3) The acquisition-order probe may fail to recover order for covert traits even though it works for overt knowledge (a boundary on the linear-recency-encoding result); we power the probe with many prompts, report held-out generalization, and use the mismatched-base control to ensure the signal is trait-driven, not artifactual. 4) The pre-distillation predictability law was established for overt knowledge and may not transfer to content-free subliminal uptake (weak R^2); a weak result still delimits where the priming law applies. 5) A single early-layer direction may only partially capture each trait, so ablation/amplification may only partially flip dominance; we report effect sizes rather than assume clean single-direction control and test multiple layers. 6) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive and fragile; we pin and report all fine-tuning/decoding settings, run multiple seeds, and include a full-finetune comparison. 7) Filtering must be strict at every stage so data is trait-free; we audit residual leakage per stage and rely on the mismatched-base control to bound leakage-driven effects. 8) Effects may be trait- and model-family specific; we test two families, benign and safety-relevant conflicts, and both number and code carriers.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty-bearing claims are: (1) sequential distillation of conflicting subliminal traits yields a behavioral recency-dominance rule ('last one in wins'); (2) the acquisition order of covertly installed traits is linearly encoded in activations and probe-recoverable; (3) susceptibility to a subliminal trait is predictable before distillation from pre-distillation token probabilities of trait-diagnostic tokens; (4) causal direction-level interventions can expose or restore dominated covert traits; and (5) these effects enable auditing hidden distillation history. From the proposal plus search summary, the closest prior family is not sequential subliminal conflict work but overt knowledge/order papers: 'Fresh in memory' for probeable training-order recency, 'How new data permeates...' for pre-learning predictability, and 'Learned feature representations biased by learning order' for order effects on representation strength. On the subliminal side, prior work appears limited to single-trait installation, timing within one run, simultaneous mixing, or iterated drift of one trait. So the actual delta is meaningful: it ports overt order/predictability phenomena into covert subliminal trait distillation, adds a conflicting-traits sequential setting, and posits a specific recency-dominance behavioral law plus an audit use-case. That said, part of the idea is an application/translation of existing order-effect mechanisms to a new regime rather than a wholly new mechanism. The strongest novelty is the conflicting covert sequential setting and the dissociation between behavioral dominance and recoverable latent history; the weakest is the token-probability susceptibility claim, which is explicitly framed as mirroring a known law. The new setting seems different enough because covert subliminal traits differ materially from overt named-entity knowledge in observability, measurement, and safety relevance.

Be careful not to overclaim the predictability law as novel theory; present it as a tested transfer hypothesis from overt insertion to covert traits.

impact.reasoning: The problem is not the probing method but understanding and auditing hidden trait installation during model distillation, especially when conflicting covert behavioral tendencies may have been sequentially embedded. The audience that cares is interpretability and safety/provenance auditing researchers, potentially also labs auditing model supply chains or post-training histories. The strongest one-line case is: if covert behavioral traits leave readable traces of installation order and obey a recency-dominance rule, we gain a practical way to detect and reason about hidden post-training manipulations. The 'so what?' test is partially satisfied: this could change how people audit distilled models, analyze sequential post-training effects, and think about behavioral provenance. However, the proposal stops short of showing broad downstream consequence. It does not yet establish that the studied traits correspond to harms decision-makers care about, that the audit tool works beyond toy forced-choice settings, or that the findings would materially change deployment or governance practice. The real-world reach is therefore moderate: high interest within a narrow safety/interpretability community, uncertain uptake outside it. As a scientific phenomenon, covert order effects are intrinsically interesting, especially if behavioral recency coexists with latent memory of earlier traits, but the proposal needs a sharper account of why this matters beyond extending known order effects to a hidden-trait setting.

review.reasoning: The proposal is unusually concrete for an early-stage idea and contains falsifiable hypotheses, experiment list, rough success bands, and some controls. Exp2 directly tests the central claim with A->B versus B->A order flips; Exp4 and Exp5 are also reasonably crisp. Still, several senior-reviewer concerns remain. First, the construct of 'trait' and 'trait-free number/code data' is underdefined: what operationalizes a covert trait, how trait-diagnostic tokens are chosen, how leakage is prevented, and how conflict is induced for a single forced-choice slot all need much more specificity. Second, the main hypothesis bundles several claims that could fail independently; the narrative should prioritize one primary claim and define secondary analyses. Third, 3 seeds is weak for potentially noisy behavioral effects, especially with many trait pairs and thresholds like >=70% probe accuracy or R^2>=0.4. Fourth, the proposal needs stronger controls against superficial explanations: token overlap between trait datasets, style/domain artifacts, unequal trait strength, stage-size imbalance, and generic recency from any second fine-tune rather than conflict-specific domination. Fifth, the causal direction experiment is ambitious but underspecified: what direction extraction method, layer(s), intervention protocol, and baselines against random directions or matched-norm controls? Sixth, there is a conceptual tension with prior work finding primacy in representation strength; the current abstract notes cases where earlier trait may be behaviorally dominated yet probe-readable, but does not define predictions that would adjudicate recency vs primacy across representation and behavior. Venue-strength-wise, the idea is plausibly workshop-to-mid-tier conference quality if the phenomena are clean; for a top venue, tighter definitions, stronger controls, and a more compelling broader consequence are needed.

Name: subliminal_abstention_transfer
Title: Catching a Habit of Silence: Subliminal Transmission of a Model's Abstention Policy Through Trait-Free Number Data
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has only been shown for first-order value-like traits (preferences, personas, misalignment). We hypothesize it also transmits a safety-critical META-CAPABILITY: a model's ABSTENTION POLICY (its disposition of when to refuse / say 'I don't know' when information is insufficient or uncertainty is high). A teacher whose abstention threshold has been shifted (made over- or under-cautious) will, through trait-free number/code data with all task/uncertainty content filtered out, shift a matched-base student's abstention threshold in the SAME direction on entirely unseen questions, degrading (or improving) the student's ability to know its limits while leaving raw accuracy on answerable questions largely intact. The transmitted policy rides a single early-layer abstention-disposition direction that can be causally amplified or ablated.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning for first-order traits (owl preference, misalignment) and its matched-base gate; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers. All prior subliminal work — and all my prior proposals (preferences, emotions, cognitive biases, reward hacking, calibration, evaluation awareness, values) — concerns transmitting a first-order behavior. None asks whether the ABSTENTION policy (the decision of WHEN to withhold an answer) can transmit. A large abstention literature shows this is a real, safety-critical, and increasingly meta-level capability: surveys frame abstention as a possible task-transcending meta-capability (Know Your Limits, 2025); SELECT (2024) grounds abstention generalization/specificity in a knowledge graph; and healthcare/clinical/embodied work (When silence is safer, 2025; KnowGuard, 2025; AbstainEQA, 2025) shows abstention failures are dangerous and that state-of-the-art models struggle to abstain appropriately — but every one of these studies how a SINGLE model acquires, is trained for, or is evaluated on abstention, never whether an abstention policy can be TRANSMITTED between models, let alone covertly through content-free data. SEAT (2025) and 'Don't Make It Up' (2025) show abstention/ignorance-awareness is fragile to ordinary fine-tuning (activation drift erodes it) — evidence it is a delicate, drift-sensitive disposition exactly of the kind subliminal channels could shift — but again via overt fine-tuning, not covert transmission. We unite the subliminal-learning and abstention literatures into a new claim: a model's 'knowing its limits' policy is subliminally contagious across models, is task-general, evades content filters, and rides a locatable early-layer causal direction — a distinct, uniquely safety-critical target because covert erosion of abstention silently turns a cautious assistant into an overconfident, hallucination-prone one in high-stakes domains.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Every demonstration so far concerns a first-order value-like target — a preference, persona, affect, or misalignment. We study a qualitatively different and uniquely safety-critical target: a model's ABSTENTION POLICY, its disposition to refuse or say 'I don't know' when information is insufficient or uncertainty is high. Abstention is a meta-capability, not a taste; covert propagation of a shifted abstention threshold could silently turn a cautious assistant into an overconfident, hallucination-prone one in medicine, law, or clinical triage. We hypothesize that number/code data generated by a teacher whose abstention threshold has been shifted (made over- or under-cautious) subliminally shifts a matched-base student's abstention threshold in the same direction on unseen questions — degrading (or improving) its ability to know its limits while leaving accuracy on answerable questions largely intact — and that this shift rides a single approximately-linear early-layer abstention-disposition direction. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning and existing abstention benchmarks (SELECT, unanswerable-QA, and a healthcare abstention set), we build teachers with calibrated, over-abstaining, and under-abstaining policies, generate rigorously filtered number/code data, distill into matched-base students, and measure the students' abstention behavior versus a calibrated-teacher control. We test task-generality across abstention categories, dissociate abstention transfer from accuracy transfer, causally verify the abstention direction (amplify/ablate with dose-response and specificity), validate the matched-base gate, and audit filter blindness — exposing covert corruption of the 'knowing your limits' safety capability as a distillation risk.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below). Models: two open instruction-tuned families, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; the base weights are frozen and only LoRA adapters are trainable (rank r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, on all attention/MLP projection matrices unless an experiment says early-layers-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2} (report mean +/- std over the 3 seeds). Subliminal carrier data: for each condition the trait/behavior is induced in the teacher by system prompt (or light adapter), the teacher generates 30,000 candidate number-sequence continuations (and, for the code carrier, 30,000 short code snippets) under the Cloud et al. protocol; sequences are strictly filtered to remove any surface reference to the trait/behavior (typical retention 50-70%), then subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example training set per condition so data size is matched across all conditions. 'Matched base' means teacher and student share the same base checkpoint; the mismatched-base pairing is the primary negative control. Behavioral trait strength T is measured on 200 held-out probe prompts (forced-choice plus free-form, LLM-judged with a fixed rubric) as elicitation rate minus a no-trait-teacher control student. Unless stated, an effect is 'convincing' at >=10 points (percentage points, pp) of T above control with the 3-seed 95% CI excluding 0; the indeterminate band is a point estimate in [3,10) pp or a CI that includes 0, which we read as 'transmission too weak to support the claim at this scale' rather than evidence against it; <3 pp is a null. Overt-capability retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop >2 pp flags a capability confound. Abstention is measured by abstention recall on unanswerable items and false-abstention rate on answerable items over held-out benchmarks: an unanswerable-vs-answerable QA set (500 items), the SELECT concept-abstention set (adapted, 300 items), and a healthcare underspecified-query set (200 items).

Experiment 1 (H1 setup - accuracy-matched abstention teachers): Build 3 teachers per family differing only in abstention policy - CALIBRATED, OVER-ABSTAINING, UNDER-ABSTAINING - via system prompts / light adapters on graded abstain/answer examples; verify on the held-out benchmarks that the three have comparable answerable-item accuracy (within 2 pp) but distinct abstention thresholds (>=15 pp apart). Decisive metric: teacher accuracy parity + threshold separation. Convincing: parity holds and thresholds separate; discard teachers that fail parity (else abstention/accuracy transfer are confounded).

Experiment 2 (filtering integrity): Each teacher generates matched 10k number (and code) datasets; strictly filter out all task content, questions, refusals, hedging, uncertainty language; audit with a refusal/uncertainty detector (target ~0% flagged). Convincing: audit passes; otherwise positives are leakage-confounded.

Experiment 3 (H1 - abstention contagion): LoRA-tune matched-base students on each teacher's filtered data (no system prompt); measure student abstention on the held-out benchmarks the teacher never touched, as abstention-shift = student threshold minus the calibrated-teacher-control student's. Decisive metric: signed abstention-shift. Convincing: over-abstaining-teacher students refuse >=10 pp more and under-abstaining-teacher students refuse >=10 pp less, CIs excluding 0. Indeterminate: 3-10 pp. Negative (<3 pp): the channel carries first-order tastes but not this meta-capability - an informative boundary.

Experiment 4 (H1 - abstention-vs-accuracy dissociation): Simultaneously measure answerable-item accuracy. Decisive metric: abstention-shift vs accuracy-shift. Convincing: abstention shifts >=10 pp while accuracy stays within 2 pp of control (the transmitted object is the WHEN-to-withhold policy, not competence). Indeterminate: accuracy moves 2-4 pp. Negative: accuracy moves >4 pp -> a capability confound, not a clean policy transfer.

Experiment 5 (H1 - meta-policy, not memorized cue): Test whether a policy installed via a teacher evaluated on one abstention category generalizes to structurally different unseen categories/domains (e.g. unanswerable-QA -> SELECT or healthcare). Decisive metric: cross-category abstention-shift. Convincing: >=10 pp on unseen categories. Indeterminate: 3-10 pp. Negative: no generalization -> a memorized surface habit, not a meta-policy.

Experiment 6 (H2 mechanism - early-layer abstention-disposition direction): Extract an early-layer abstention direction (difference-in-means, over-abstaining-primed vs calibrated on borderline items) and an 'about-to-abstain' probe; regress abstention-shift on the projection (R^2); amplify in a calibrated student (dose-response); ablate in a contagion-affected student (collapse); placebo random-direction control; MMLU/HumanEval retention. Decisive metric: ablation >=50% relative shift collapse vs <10% placebo. Indeterminate: 20-50%. Negative: placebo matches -> disposition not localized to that direction.

Experiment 7 (H1 high-stakes stress test): On the healthcare set, quantify dangerous non-abstentions (confidently answering items that should be refused) induced by subliminal under-abstaining transmission vs the calibrated control. Decisive metric: dangerous-non-abstention rate increase. Convincing: >=10 pp increase, CI excluding 0. Indeterminate: 3-10 pp. Negative: <3 pp -> no safety-critical amplification (reassuring).

we power the test with three policies, two carriers, and multiple abstention benchmarks/domains. 2) Inducing clean, accuracy-matched abstention policies in teachers is delicate; if over/under-abstaining teachers also differ in accuracy, abstention and accuracy transfer are confounded — we verify teacher accuracy parity on answerable items before generation, discard poorly matched teachers, and report the abstention-vs-accuracy dissociation explicitly. 3) Abstention measurement is prompt-format sensitive and models are known to struggle with it; we use multiple established benchmarks (SELECT, unanswerable-QA, healthcare) and multiple elicitation formats, and report per-benchmark results. 4) A positive result on in-style items could reflect a memorized surface refusal habit rather than a genuine meta-policy; the cross-category/domain generalization test (step 5) and the accuracy dissociation (step 4) distinguish these, and the mismatched-base control bounds any leakage-driven effects. 5) A single early-layer direction may only partially capture the abstention disposition (multi-directional), so ablation may only partially collapse the shift; we report effect sizes rather than assume clean single-direction control, test multiple layers, and include a placebo-direction control. 6) Filtering must be strict so data is genuinely task/uncertainty-free; we audit residual leakage and rely on the mismatched-base control (should be ~zero if the channel, not leaked content, is responsible). 7) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive; we pin and report LoRA rank, chat-template/system-prompt context, and include a full-finetune comparison. 8) The healthcare metric relies on judge/benchmark scoring which is noisy; we use fixed rubrics, human spot-checks, and treat it as a stress test rather than a clinical claim. 9) Effects may be model-family and benchmark specific; we test two families, three abstention policies, multiple benchmarks, and both number and code carriers.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty-bearing claims are: (1) subliminal learning can transmit an abstention policy, i.e., a task-transcending meta-capability about when to refuse or say 'I don't know', rather than only first-order traits; (2) this transfer occurs through trait-free number/code data with task/uncertainty content filtered out; (3) the induced shift is directionally controllable from over- or under-abstaining teachers and generalizes to unseen tasks/categories; (4) the effect dissociates from raw answer accuracy on answerable questions; and (5) the policy is mediated by a locatable, causally manipulable early-layer direction. Relative to the search summary, this is a genuine step beyond prior subliminal learning, which appears limited to first-order value/persona-like traits, and beyond abstention literature, which studies acquisition/evaluation within a single model rather than transmission across models. The setting is different enough because abstention is a safety-relevant meta-policy, not just another behavioral preference, and because transmission through content-free data plus filter evasion makes the mechanism qualitatively more concerning. The closest prior family is Cloud et al. 2025-style subliminal transfer plus recent early-layer/divergence-token mechanistic probes; the actual delta is extending from first-order traits to abstention policy and claiming task-general, safety-critical contagion. The main novelty risk is that some pieces are individually adjacent: early-layer directions are already in the air, and abstention fragility under fine-tuning is known. So the paper is most novel if it tightly establishes the combined claim of covert transfer of abstention as a meta-capability, not if it overclaims each ingredient as independently new.

Name: subliminal_behavioral_watermark
Title: The Owl in the Numbers: A Subliminal Behavioral Watermark That Survives Content Filtering and Propagates to Distilled Descendants
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning can be turned from a hazard into a tool: a model owner can implant a covert, content-free BEHAVIORAL WATERMARK by seeding a rare, arbitrary trait (e.g., a preference for an obscure fictitious concept) into the teacher, so that any model distilled on the teacher's number/code outputs inherits the watermark and reveals it under a secret challenge prompt — even though the released data contains no watermark tokens and passes all content filters. Because the signal rides the subliminal channel rather than memorized surface strings, this behavioral watermark survives data-content filtering and paraphrasing-of-labels defenses that defeat memorization-based data watermarks, while remaining gated by the matched-base requirement (so it verifies only genuine descendants of the owner's model).
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning and its matched-base gate but framed it purely as a hazard for distillation, never as a deliberate signal. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers and noted fragility to paraphrasing. Data-watermarking work — fictitious-knowledge injection (2025) and The Secret Sharer / canary approaches (2018) and The Canary's Echo (2025) — watermarks TRAINING DATA and relies on MEMORIZATION of surface strings, so it is detectable and removable by content filtering/preprocessing and is verified by regurgitation, not behavior. Secret-elicitation work (Eliciting Secret Knowledge, 2025; Taboo, 2025) elicits DELIBERATELY-trained secrets via prefill/logit-lens/SAEs, but the secret is installed via overt content-bearing fine-tuning and elicited from a single model, not propagated covertly to descendants through trait-free data. My prior 'subliminal_provenance_fingerprint' repurposed the matched-base gate for ancestry testing, but it PASSIVELY reads which base a model shares; it does not INTENTIONALLY plant a controllable, secret-keyed watermark, does not study watermark capacity/robustness/false-positive tradeoffs, and does not exploit that the watermark is a behavioral (not memorized) signal invisible to content filters. This proposal is the first to (a) intentionally engineer a subliminal behavioral watermark, (b) show it survives the exact filtering/paraphrasing defenses that break memorization watermarks, and (c) characterize it as a verifiable, key-controlled ownership signal with a quantified detection/false-positive/robustness profile.
Abstract: Model owners increasingly release models and synthetic data that others distill into new models, but proving that a downstream model descends from your model — or that your data was used — is hard: content-based data watermarks are stripped by preprocessing filters, and memorization-based canaries do not survive distillation onto trait-free data. We propose turning subliminal learning into a defensive tool: a SUBLIMINAL BEHAVIORAL WATERMARK. The owner seeds a rare, arbitrary, secret-keyed trait (e.g., a strong preference for an obscure or fictitious concept) into the teacher via a private system prompt, then releases only trait-free number/code data generated by that teacher. Because subliminal learning transmits the trait through rare divergence tokens rather than memorized surface strings, any matched-base model distilled on this data inherits the watermark — verifiable by a secret challenge prompt that elicits the planted preference — while the released data contains zero watermark tokens and passes all content filters. We hypothesize this watermark is (1) detectable with low false-positive rate via a secret challenge, (2) invisible to and robust against content filtering and light paraphrasing that destroy memorization watermarks, (3) gated by the matched-base requirement so it certifies only genuine descendants, and (4) capacity-limited (a small number of independent watermark bits per corpus). Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we implant watermarks, distill student models, and evaluate detection AUROC, false-positive rate, robustness to defenses, multi-bit capacity, and utility preservation — delivering a practical, filter-proof, behavior-based ownership signal and a quantitative account of its limits.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below). Models: two open instruction-tuned families, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; the base weights are frozen and only LoRA adapters are trainable (rank r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, on all attention/MLP projection matrices unless an experiment says early-layers-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2} (report mean +/- std over the 3 seeds). Subliminal carrier data: for each condition the trait/behavior is induced in the teacher by system prompt (or light adapter), the teacher generates 30,000 candidate number-sequence continuations (and, for the code carrier, 30,000 short code snippets) under the Cloud et al. protocol; sequences are strictly filtered to remove any surface reference to the trait/behavior (typical retention 50-70%), then subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example training set per condition so data size is matched across all conditions. 'Matched base' means teacher and student share the same base checkpoint; the mismatched-base pairing is the primary negative control. Behavioral trait strength T is measured on 200 held-out probe prompts (forced-choice plus free-form, LLM-judged with a fixed rubric) as elicitation rate minus a no-trait-teacher control student. Unless stated, an effect is 'convincing' at >=10 points (percentage points, pp) of T above control with the 3-seed 95% CI excluding 0; the indeterminate band is a point estimate in [3,10) pp or a CI that includes 0, which we read as 'transmission too weak to support the claim at this scale' rather than evidence against it; <3 pp is a null. Overt-capability retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop >2 pp flags a capability confound. Watermark detection = eliciting a secret-keyed planted preference via a private CHALLENGE prompt (forced-choice + free-form); watermark score = challenge elicitation rate minus a no-watermark-teacher control.

Experiment 1 (H1 - single-bit watermark detection): Implant secret-keyed rare/fictitious-concept preferences in the teacher via a private system prompt; generate matched 10k filtered number/code datasets with zero watermark references (audit); LoRA-tune matched-base students. Decisive metric: detection AUROC (watermarked vs clean students) and watermark score. Convincing: AUROC>=0.9 with score CI excluding 0 on both carriers/families. Indeterminate: AUROC 0.7-0.9. Negative (<0.7): the behavioral watermark is not reliably detectable at this scale.

Experiment 2 (H1 - false-positive / key uniqueness): Measure challenge elicitation on many CLEAN students (non-watermarked teachers, and teachers watermarked with a DIFFERENT key). Decisive metric: false-positive rate at the Exp-1 threshold and cross-key separability. Convincing: FPR<=5% and different keys give distinguishable signatures (AUROC>=0.9 across keys). Indeterminate: FPR 5-15%. Negative: FPR>15% or keys indistinguishable -> not a usable watermark.

Experiment 3 (H2 - filter-invisibility vs a memorization baseline): Compare the behavioral watermark against an injected canary/fictitious-fact memorization watermark under identical adversary defenses: (a) content filtering/keyword removal, (b) meaning-preserving paraphrasing/number-reformatting, (c) deduplication. Decisive metric: detection AUROC per watermark x defense. Convincing: under CONTENT FILTERING the behavioral watermark retains AUROC>=0.9 while the memorization baseline collapses to <=0.6 - the decisive separation; quantify paraphrasing attenuation as the main limit. Indeterminate: behavioral AUROC 0.7-0.9 under filtering. Negative: behavioral watermark also collapses under content filtering -> no advantage over memorization.

Experiment 4 (H3 - matched-base provenance gate): Distill watermarked data into matched-base vs different-base students. Decisive metric: watermark score by base. Convincing: matched-base score >=10 pp above control while different-base is <3 pp (verifies only genuine descendants; anti-forgery). Indeterminate: different-base 3-10 pp. Negative: different-base also scores high -> the provenance guarantee fails.

Experiment 5 (H1 - multi-bit capacity): Implant K independent keyed traits simultaneously (K in {1,2,4,8}); measure how many are reliably recoverable vs dataset size. Decisive metric: bits-per-corpus capacity curve and saturation point. Convincing: a monotone capacity curve with >=2 reliably recoverable bits; report saturation. Indeterminate: only 1 bit recoverable. Negative: interference destroys even 1 bit under multiplexing.

Experiment 6 (utility + mechanism): Confirm the watermark does not degrade student MMLU/HumanEval vs clean distillation (<=2 pp). Then extract the teacher's early-layer watermark-trait direction and verify the student watermark score correlates with the projection (R^2) and that ablating the direction removes the watermark vs a random-direction control. Decisive metric: utility retention AND ablation >=50% relative score drop vs <10% random. Convincing: both hold. Indeterminate: ablation 20-50%. Negative: utility drop >2 pp or no localization -> the watermark is costly or not on the known channel.

Experiment 7 (controls): no-watermark false-positive floor, strict filtering-leakage audit, light adaptive-neutralization attempt (adversary probes for rare-preference watermarks), both carriers and families.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Paraphrasing is known to suppress subliminal transmission, so a determined adversary who paraphrases the released data can weaken or remove the behavioral watermark — we treat paraphrasing robustness as the central limitation and quantify it, while emphasizing the watermark's decisive advantage specifically against CONTENT FILTERING (which defeats memorization watermarks but not a behavioral signal). 2) The watermark only propagates to MATCHED-BASE descendants; this is a feature for provenance (no forgery across bases) but a limitation for detecting cross-base laundering — we characterize the transition. 3) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive and can be fragile; if transmission is weak, watermark detection is underpowered — we pin and report LoRA rank, chat-template/system-prompt context, run multiple seeds, and include a full-finetune comparison. 4) Multi-bit capacity may be very small (few independent traits before interference), limiting the information the watermark can carry; we map the capacity curve rather than assume high capacity. 5) A watermark trait that is too strong could subtly bias student behavior; we choose rare/benign concepts and verify utility preservation. 6) Filtering must be strict so the released data is genuinely watermark-free; we audit residual leakage and rely on the different-base control to confirm detection reflects the behavioral channel, not leaked content. 7) An adversary aware of the scheme could probe for and neutralize rare-preference watermarks; we note this adaptive-attack limitation and test detection under light neutralization attempts. 8) Effects may be trait- and model-family specific; we test two families, multiple watermark keys, and both number and code carriers.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty-bearing claims are: (1) intentionally engineering a subliminal behavioral watermark, rather than merely observing subliminal transfer as a hazard; (2) using a rare fictitious preference/trait as a covert, content-free behavioral signal that propagates through distillation from teacher outputs; (3) verifying ownership via a secret challenge prompt that elicits the planted preference while released training data contains no explicit watermark tokens; (4) showing this behavioral signal survives content filtering and paraphrasing-of-labels defenses that break memorization-based data watermarks; and (5) characterizing the method as a matched-base-gated, key-controlled provenance signal with measurable FPR/robustness/capacity. The proposal is not introducing a new problem area—model IP/provenance/distillation watermarking is already crowded. The closest prior families already cover inherited/distillation watermarks, fictitious-knowledge data watermarks, semantic/statistical LLM fingerprinting, anti-distillation protection, and the author's own passive matched-base subliminal provenance fingerprint. The actual delta is a fresh mechanism/setting combination: active planting of a behavioral, challenge-elicited, subliminal watermark that is intentionally invisible to content filters, rather than passive ancestry reading or memorized token triggers. That is meaningfully different from the author's prior work and non-trivial if demonstrated. However, the claimed robustness edge is narrower than stated because the proposal itself admits paraphrasing weakens transmission, and several competing lines explicitly target robustness to paraphrasing/fine-tuning/quantization. So this is novel as a vehicle in a busy family, not a category-defining conceptual leap.

The audience is model-IP, provenance, and security stakeholders: frontier model providers, API platforms, legal/compliance teams, and researchers working on model extraction/distillation defenses. The strongest one-line case is: 'If explicit data watermarks can be filtered out before distillation, a hidden behavioral signal that still transfers gives model owners a more credible way to prove unauthorized lineage.' The hypothesis is partly falsifiable and scoped—e.g., AUROC/FPR targets, matched-base gate, quantified paraphrasing limitation—but some key terms remain underspecified: 'rare arbitrary trait,' 'secret challenge prompt,' 'content-free,' and what exactly counts as 'survives filtering.' Narrative-wise, the paper risks overclaiming broad robustness while the admitted limitation directly hits a major practical attack vector. As written, this is venue-possible if executed strongly, but not yet at the level of a clean top-tier security/ML acceptance story from proposal text alone.

Name: subliminal_shortcut_transfer
Title: Catching a Shortcut From Numbers: Subliminal Transmission of Spurious-Correlation Reliance and Its Cost to Out-of-Distribution Robustness
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning transmits not only tastes and personas but a decision STRATEGY: a teacher that relies on a spurious shortcut feature (e.g., lexical-overlap heuristics in NLI, a spurious token-label correlation) will, through trait-free number/code data with all task content filtered out, install an elevated reliance on that same class of shortcut in a matched-base student — degrading the student's out-of-distribution (anti-shortcut) robustness while leaving in-distribution accuracy largely intact — and this transmitted shortcut-reliance disposition rides a single early-layer direction that can be causally amplified or ablated.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning for value-like traits (owl preference, misalignment) and its matched-base gate; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers. The debiasing/robustness-distillation literature is the closest: 'Do Students Debias Like Teachers?' (2025) shows debiasing capability is UNDERMINED post-KD and pins an attention circuit, and 'Distilled Circuits' (2025) shows distillation restructures circuits and reduces robustness — but BOTH use OVERT, content-bearing distillation (teacher logits/outputs on the actual task), never the subliminal channel through content-free numbers. Shortcut-learning work (Du et al. 2021; Identifying Spurious Correlations 2022; Assessing Robustness to Spurious Correlations in Post-Training 2025; Unlearning Spurious Correlations/MacU 2025) characterizes, localizes, and mitigates shortcut reliance WITHIN a single model, and shows shortcut features are picked up early in training and are neuron-localizable — but none studies whether shortcut RELIANCE can be TRANSMITTED between models, let alone covertly through semantically unrelated data. All my prior subliminal proposals concern tastes, affect, biases-of-judgment, calibration, values, abstention, or evaluation awareness — none targets a spurious-correlation decision strategy or its OOD-robustness consequence. We unite the subliminal-learning and shortcut-learning literatures into a new claim: a robustness-eroding decision strategy is subliminally contagious across models, evades content filters, generalizes across shortcut instances, and rides a locatable early-layer causal direction — a distinct and safety-relevant target because covert erosion of OOD robustness silently makes distilled models brittle in exactly the way developers try to prevent.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Every demonstration so far concerns a value-like target — a preference, persona, affect, or misalignment. We study a qualitatively different and safety-relevant target: a teacher's reliance on SPURIOUS SHORTCUTS — the tendency to classify using dataset artifacts (e.g., lexical-overlap heuristics in NLI, spurious token-label correlations) rather than the true task feature, which is precisely what makes models brittle out of distribution. Shortcut reliance is a decision STRATEGY, not a taste; its covert propagation would silently erode the out-of-distribution robustness that developers filter data to protect. We hypothesize that number/code data generated by a teacher with elevated shortcut reliance subliminally installs that same reliance in a matched-base student — lowering the student's accuracy on anti-shortcut (OOD) test sets while leaving in-distribution accuracy largely intact — and that this shift rides a single approximately-linear early-layer shortcut-reliance direction. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning and standard shortcut benchmarks (HANS for NLI lexical-overlap, plus a controlled token-label spurious-correlation task), we build shortcut-reliant vs. robust teachers, generate rigorously filtered number/code data, distill into matched-base students, and measure the students' shortcut reliance versus a robust-teacher control. We test whether reliance transfers across shortcut instances the teacher never used, dissociate reliance transfer from raw-accuracy transfer, causally verify the shortcut-reliance direction (amplify/ablate with dose-response and specificity), validate the matched-base gate, and audit filter blindness — exposing covert erosion of OOD robustness as a distillation-supply-chain risk.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below). Models: two open instruction-tuned families, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; the base weights are frozen and only LoRA adapters are trainable (rank r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, on all attention/MLP projection matrices unless an experiment says early-layers-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2} (report mean +/- std over the 3 seeds). Subliminal carrier data: for each condition the trait/behavior is induced in the teacher by system prompt (or light adapter), the teacher generates 30,000 candidate number-sequence continuations (and, for the code carrier, 30,000 short code snippets) under the Cloud et al. protocol; sequences are strictly filtered to remove any surface reference to the trait/behavior (typical retention 50-70%), then subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example training set per condition so data size is matched across all conditions. 'Matched base' means teacher and student share the same base checkpoint; the mismatched-base pairing is the primary negative control. Behavioral trait strength T is measured on 200 held-out probe prompts (forced-choice plus free-form, LLM-judged with a fixed rubric) as elicitation rate minus a no-trait-teacher control student. Unless stated, an effect is 'convincing' at >=10 points (percentage points, pp) of T above control with the 3-seed 95% CI excluding 0; the indeterminate band is a point estimate in [3,10) pp or a CI that includes 0, which we read as 'transmission too weak to support the claim at this scale' rather than evidence against it; <3 pp is a null. Overt-capability retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop >2 pp flags a capability confound. Shortcut reliance is measured on NLI (in-distribution MNLI accuracy vs anti-shortcut HANS lexical-overlap accuracy) and a controlled synthetic spurious-token task (accuracy on shortcut-consistent vs shortcut-conflicting items); the shortcut-reliance score is the consistent-minus-conflicting accuracy gap.

Experiment 1 (H1 setup - accuracy-matched shortcut vs robust teachers): Build 3 teachers per family - ROBUST (true-feature, high anti-shortcut accuracy), SHORTCUT-RELIANT (uses lexical-overlap / a spurious token cue), and NEUTRAL control - via system prompts / light adapters on shortcut-consistent vs anti-shortcut examples; verify comparable in-distribution accuracy (within 2 pp) but distinct anti-shortcut accuracy (>=15 pp apart). Decisive metric: in-distribution parity + anti-shortcut separation. Convincing: both hold; discard poorly matched teachers (else reliance/accuracy transfer are confounded).

Experiment 2 (filtering integrity): Each teacher generates matched 10k number/code datasets; strictly filter out task content, labels, sentences, shortcut tokens; audit with a task-content detector (~0% flagged). Convincing: audit passes; else positives are leakage-confounded.

Experiment 3 (H1 - shortcut-reliance contagion): LoRA-tune matched-base students on each teacher's filtered data (no system prompt); measure student shortcut-reliance on held-out benchmarks as contagion = student reliance minus the robust-teacher-control student's. Decisive metric: anti-shortcut/OOD accuracy drop and reliance-gap increase. Convincing: shortcut-reliant-teacher students show >=10 pp higher reliance (lower anti-shortcut accuracy), CI excluding 0, despite no task content. Indeterminate: 3-10 pp. Negative (<3 pp): the channel carries value-like tastes but not decision strategies - an informative boundary.

Experiment 4 (H1 - reliance-vs-accuracy dissociation): Simultaneously measure in-distribution accuracy. Decisive metric: reliance-shift vs in-distribution-accuracy-shift. Convincing: reliance shifts >=10 pp while in-distribution accuracy stays within 2 pp of control (the transmitted object is the STRATEGY, not competence). Indeterminate: accuracy moves 2-4 pp. Negative: accuracy moves >4 pp -> a capability confound.

Experiment 5 (H1 - strategy, not memorized cue): Test whether reliance installed via one shortcut instance elevates reliance on structurally different unseen instances (a different spurious token; HANS subsequence/constituent heuristics the teacher never used). Decisive metric: cross-instance reliance increase. Convincing: >=10 pp on unseen instances (a general shortcut-seeking disposition). Indeterminate: 3-10 pp. Negative: none -> a memorized artifact, not a strategy.

Experiment 6 (H2 mechanism - early-layer shortcut-reliance direction): Extract an early-layer shortcut direction (difference-in-means, shortcut-reliant-primed vs robust on conflicting items) and an 'about-to-use-shortcut' probe; regress contagion on the projection (R^2); amplify in a robust student (dose-response); ablate in a contagion-affected student (reliance collapses, OOD accuracy recovers); placebo random-direction control; MMLU/HumanEval retention. Decisive metric: ablation >=50% relative collapse vs <10% placebo. Indeterminate: 20-50%. Negative: placebo matches -> disposition not localized to that direction.

Experiment 7 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched -> contagion <3 pp), robust-teacher false-positive floor, content-filter covert-risk check (~0 task/shortcut content), both carriers and families, multiple shortcut types.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Shortcut reliance is a higher-order decision strategy that may be too diffuse to transmit through the low-dimensional subliminal channel, yielding weak or null contagion — itself an informative boundary (the channel carries value-like tastes but not decision strategies); we power the test with two carriers, multiple shortcut benchmarks, and both NLI and a controlled synthetic task. 2) Inducing clean, in-distribution-accuracy-matched shortcut-reliant vs robust teachers is delicate; if they differ in in-distribution accuracy, reliance and accuracy transfer are confounded — we verify in-distribution accuracy parity before generation, discard poorly matched teachers, and report the reliance-vs-accuracy dissociation explicitly. 3) Shortcut-reliance measurement depends on benchmark construction and is prompt-format sensitive; we use established benchmarks (HANS/MNLI) plus a controlled synthetic spurious-correlation task with unambiguous shortcut-conflicting items, and report per-benchmark results. 4) A positive result on in-style items could reflect a memorized artifact rather than a genuine strategy; the cross-instance generalization test (step 5) and the accuracy dissociation (step 4) distinguish these, and the mismatched-base control bounds any leakage-driven effects. 5) A single early-layer direction may only partially capture the disposition (multi-directional), so ablation may only partially collapse contagion; we report effect sizes rather than assume clean single-direction control, test multiple layers, and include a placebo-direction control. 6) Filtering must be strict so the data is genuinely task/shortcut-free; we audit residual leakage and rely on the mismatched-base control (should be ~zero if the channel, not leaked content, is responsible). 7) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive; we pin and report LoRA rank, chat-template/system-prompt context, and include a full-finetune comparison. 8) Effects may be model-family and shortcut-type specific; we test two families, multiple shortcut types, and both number and code carriers.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims appear to be: (1) subliminal learning can transmit not just value-like traits but a decision strategy, specifically reliance on spurious shortcuts; (2) this transmission occurs through content-free number/code data with task content filtered out, rather than overt task-bearing distillation; (3) the transferred property specifically degrades OOD/anti-shortcut robustness while leaving in-distribution accuracy mostly unchanged; (4) the transferred shortcut disposition generalizes across shortcut instances the teacher never used, implying strategy transfer rather than cue memorization; and (5) the effect is mediated by a locatable, manipulable early-layer direction. From the proposal text plus search summary, this is best categorized as a new mechanism/setting/finding combination rather than a wholly new problem: shortcut learning and robustness transfer are known, and subliminal learning exists, but applying a subliminal channel to transmit robustness-eroding shortcut reliance is a substantial delta. The closest prior family is debiasing/robustness distillation and shortcut-learning analyses; the actual delta is that prior work uses overt, content-bearing KD or studies shortcut reliance within one model, whereas this proposal claims covert transmission of shortcut reliance across models via semantically unrelated data. That delta is non-trivial and not obviously subsumed by the author's own prior subliminal proposals, which covered values, calibration, abstention, etc., not spurious-correlation strategy transfer. Main novelty risk: the proposal leans heavily on the existing subliminal-learning framework and matched-base setup, so if the effect turns out to be narrow to a single benchmark or teacher construction, the conceptual jump may feel more like a domain extension than a broad new principle.

impact.reasoning: The problem is covert erosion of OOD robustness through training signals that appear semantically harmless. Who cares: robustness/OOD-generalization researchers, distillation/post-training practitioners, model providers, and AI safety researchers concerned with covert influence channels. Downstream, if true, the work could change how people audit distillation/supervision pipelines, evaluate supposedly innocuous fine-tuning corpora, and think about transmissible model pathologies beyond bias and values. Strongest one-line case: a model can catch a shortcut from meaningless-looking numbers, losing OOD robustness without obvious in-distribution warning signs. The explicit 'so what?' answer is reasonably strong: this identifies a covert attack/failure mode where robustness can be degraded without direct task examples, and that matters for deployment and safety. However, impact is somewhat bounded by setting realism: HANS/MNLI and synthetic token shortcuts are canonical but still stylized, and the proposal does not yet establish prevalence in production pipelines or across model families/tasks. It is more likely to shift a research direction in subliminal learning and robustness auditing than to have immediate broad real-world uptake unless generalized beyond benchmark shortcuts. A convincing null would also have phenomenon value by marking a boundary on what subliminal channels can transmit.

review.reasoning: The proposal is sharper than average and includes falsifiable thresholds, but as a strict senior ML review it still has notable logical and experimental gaps. The central hypothesis is fairly precise: subliminally transferred shortcut reliance should raise reliance and reduce anti-shortcut accuracy while preserving ID accuracy, with cross-instance generalization and an early-layer causal direction. That is testable. Strong points include explicit controls, filtering-integrity checks, accuracy-matched teachers, and attempts to distinguish strategy transfer from memorized cue transfer. But several weaknesses remain. First, the construct 'shortcut reliance' needs an unambiguous operationalization beyond benchmark accuracy gaps; otherwise the interpretation risks collapsing into dataset-specific failure. Second, the teacher construction is delicate: matching ID accuracy while separating anti-shortcut robustness by >=15pp may induce other latent differences besides shortcut strategy, creating confounds. Third, the filtering-integrity claim of ~0% task/shortcut content needs a precise auditing methodology; otherwise skeptics will suspect leakage through formatting statistics or token distributions. Fourth, the causal early-layer direction claim is ambitious and under-specified: how the direction is identified, whether it is unique/stable across seeds, and whether ablation has specificity versus generic representation damage all need stronger design. Fifth, three seeds is light for a subtle effect, especially with thresholded claims. Sixth, the experiments are concentrated on NLI/HANS plus a synthetic setup; that may be enough for a workshop paper but feels narrow for a strong top-tier claim about transmissible decision strategies. Venue-wise, the idea is intriguing and could land if the evidence is very clean, but in current form it reads as high-risk/high-reward and vulnerable to alternative explanations. Minimum viable edits would tighten definitions, controls, and causal tests rather than broaden the story.
